title: Advanced Mathematics for Competitive Programming
text:
You already know how to write a fast segment tree, how to squeeze a flow algorithm under the time limit, and how to debug a tricky DP at two in the morning. Then a problem says count the labelled forests modulo \(998244353\), or find \(x\) with \(x^2 \equiv a \pmod p\), and the difficulty is no longer engineering. The obstacle is a piece of mathematics that editorials name in one line and never explain.
This book is the missing explanation. It develops the algebra, number theory, counting, and probability behind hard ICPC, Codeforces, and AtCoder problems, starting from definitions and assuming no university mathematics — only that you are a confident programmer who can follow a careful argument.
Start with mathematical foundations, then follow the learning path. Keep the notation and algebra contracts open as a reference.

title: Advanced Mathematics for Competitive Programming
text:
What a chapter looks like
Every chapter follows the same rhythm, because that is the order in which ideas actually become usable:

A problem you cannot yet solve. Concrete, contest-shaped, and deliberately just out of reach.
The object that solves it, introduced in plain words before any notation, with a small example you can check by hand.
Why the central formula is true. Not a citation — a derivation you could reproduce on paper during a contest.
The algorithm’s contract: what it assumes, what it returns, what it costs, and the inputs on which it silently returns garbage.
Practice, from recognizing the model to combining several of them.

The failure modes are not an appendix. Knowing that Fermat inversion breaks the moment the modulus is composite, or that a formula needs \(n < p\) because it divides by a factorial, is exactly the knowledge that separates a correct submission from a wrong-answer verdict you cannot explain.

title: Advanced Mathematics for Competitive Programming
text:
How to study
Read the derivations with a pen. When a chapter says why this is true, close the page and try to rebuild the argument; the gap you find is the part you did not actually understand. Work the small numerical examples by hand — they are chosen so that a misconception produces a visibly wrong number.
Attempt the original exercises before opening their solutions. Use the external contest problems to practice modelling under uncertainty. Difficulty labels are relative to this course; they are not predicted contest ratings. Some exercise pages deliberately point forward to applications that need a later chapter, and identify those extra prerequisites.
The book assumes you already have a tested competitive-programming library, so it contains almost no code. It teaches mathematical models, correctness invariants, input/output contracts, and resource bounds; the implementations stay in your library. No routine should be selected merely because its name resembles a phrase in the problem statement.

text:

Chapter numbers are the reading order: chapter \(n\) relies only on earlier chapters. Detours are still allowed — the learning path lists, for each chapter, the few earlier ones it genuinely uses.

title: Advanced Mathematics for Competitive Programming
text:
Chapters

I · Arithmetic and counting

00 · Mathematical foundations and proof: notation, logic, induction, invariants, extremal arguments, Bézout, double counting.
01 · Modular algebra: units, fields, CRT, orders, valuations, logarithms, modular roots.
02 · Multiplicative number theory: factorization, arithmetic functions, gcd filters, divisor inversion, Gaussian integers.
03 · Combinatorics and practice: inclusion–exclusion, Stirling and Catalan models, partitions, binomial transforms, rook polynomials.
04 · Binomial coefficients modulo anything: Lucas, Kummer carries, prime-power factorials, composite moduli by CRT.
05 · Group actions and practice: orbits, stabilizers, Burnside, Pólya, induced graph symmetries.



II · Algebraic engines

06 · Polynomials and practice: convolution, Fourier evaluation, division, product trees, interpolation, Taylor shift.
07 · Linear algebra: vector spaces, rank, determinants, XOR bases, tree counts, recurrences and black-box methods.
08 · Transforms: subset and divisor inversion, OR/AND/XOR, ranked disjoint convolution.
09 · Formal power series and practice: precision, Newton lifting, inverse, logarithm, exponential, composition and reversion.
10 · Generating functions and practice: labelled and unlabelled models, rational sequences, coefficient extraction, Lagrange inversion.
11 · Set power series: disjoint multiplication, connected components, set exponential and logarithm.



III · Models and synthesis

12 · Probability: sample spaces, indicators, conditioning, variance, stochastic DP and absorbing systems.
13 · Discrete sums and Diophantine tools: interpolation, differences, floor sums, rational approximation, Pell equations.
14 · Summatory sieves: quotient states, prefix recurrences, prime sums, multiplicative enumeration, powerful support.
15 · Mixed capstones: modelling workshops with complete reduction guidance.



IV · Frontier topics

16 · q-Analogues and subspace counting: Gaussian binomials, division-free recurrences, rank distributions.
17 · Finite-field polynomials: quotient fields, Frobenius, factorization and irreducibility certification.
18 · Algebraic graph methods: polynomial identity testing, Pfaffians, Tutte matrices, weighted matching.
19 · Holonomic methods: differential equations, polynomial-coefficient recurrences, guessing and certification.
20 · Frontier capstones: synthesis with explicit hypotheses, small models and validation plans.

title: Advanced Mathematics for Competitive Programming
text:
What mastery means
For each chapter, record whether you can define its objects, reproduce its central proof, solve its local exercises, recognize its model in a contest statement, and explain a counterexample to its misuse. Revisit a difficult problem after two and six weeks; successful recall of the derivation is more informative than recognizing an editorial.
The course concentrates on algebra, number theory, counting, and probability. Geometry and continuous optimization are outside this curriculum. No finite toolkit covers every future contest problem; the transferable skill is deriving a new variant from well-understood objects and assumptions.
See the source and verification policy for reference standards.

title: Sources and maintenance policy
text: The textbook’s proofs are written from definitions and checked independently; a linked editorial is supporting evidence, not permission to copy its claims. The rewrite found mistakes even in official-hosted explanatory material. Small exhaustive calculations complement proofs but do not certify arbitrary instances or randomized error bounds.

title: Sources and maintenance policy
text:
Verification records
The repository maintains CONTENT_AUDIT.md as the complete original chapter inventory and disposition tracker, CURRICULUM.md as the editorial dependency plan, and VALIDATION_REPORT.md as the integrated result. Detailed AUDIT and VALIDATION documents record chapter findings and checks. Exact small-instance oracles live under tests/; site checks under scripts/. HTTP reachability and mathematical relevance are recorded separately.
Original exercises include local solutions. External statements are linked instead of reproduced. Where a site blocks automated access, the validation report states that limitation; it is neither a confirmed broken link nor a successful content check.

text:
Link conventions

Link directly to a task, not a search result.
Link an official editorial separately from the statement.
Mark [JA], [ZH], or another language code when the target is not English.

title: Sources and maintenance policy
text:
Copyright and spoilers
Problem statements and editorials are not mirrored. Each practice entry says what skill it trains and supplies progressively stronger hints in collapsed blocks. Those hints should reconstruct the decisive reduction, not reproduce an implementation or the original editorial.

title: Sources and maintenance policy
text:
Link rot
Contest sites occasionally move PDF editorials. If a link dies, retain the contest, year, round, and problem letter in the entry so it remains searchable; then prefer a new official URL over an unofficial mirror. The last mechanical link audit is recorded in the repository handoff rather than claimed permanently inside these notes.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
text:
By now you have the machinery. What these problems test is the step no chapter can hand you: looking at a statement that mentions none of it and deciding which object you are actually counting. Nothing here announces “take a logarithm of a set power series” or “this is a Tutte matrix” — the statements are about cards, bitstrings, chessboards and graphs, and the algebra only appears once you have modelled them correctly.
So the failure mode to train against is not a slow implementation; it is a model that counts almost the right thing. Each guide below therefore spends most of its length on the reduction and its boundary cases, and ends with a hand-checkable instance you can compare against a brute-force oracle.
The skill tested here is choosing and certifying a mathematical model. Attempt each statement before reading its guide. Write down the objects, coefficient domain, invariant, target complexity, and smallest brute-force oracle. A successful solution explains why the algebra counts or detects exactly the requested objects.
Required chapters vary by problem: 16 for subspaces, 17 for binary polynomial orders, 11 for components, 18 for matching, and 19 for differential equations. Review labelled generating functions when a coefficient is factorial-normalized.
The objectives are to combine two or more chapters, carry a reduction through its boundary cases, and distinguish a mathematically valid model from an algorithm meeting the statement’s limits. The following guides contain spoilers and full reduction reasoning; they are not implementation templates.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
section: First inclusion in a span: make 1
text:
First inclusion in a span: make 1
Official problem: ABC278 Ex — make 1.
View each card as a vector in \(\mathbb F_2^B\) and let \(e\) be the vector represented by integer one. A sequence becomes good precisely when its span first contains \(e\). Cards cannot repeat. These are two separate constraints: counting subspaces alone does not count ordered distinct draws.
Let \(F_s\) count length-\(s\) distinct-card sequences whose span avoids \(e\). Each such length-\(N-1\) prefix has \(2^B-(N-1)\) unused final cards. Subtract the extensions still avoiding \(e\):
\[\text{answer}=F_{N-1}(2^B-N+1)-F_N.\]
To compute \(F_s\), temporarily allow repetitions and call the count \(G_s\). Group equal positions into a partition of the \(s\) positions. Ordering its blocks by first occurrence assigns a unique distinct-card sequence to its blocks, giving
\[G_s=\sum_{t=0}^s {s\brace t}F_t,\qquad
F_s=\sum_{t=0}^s [z^t](z(z-1)\cdots(z-s+1))\,G_t.\]
The inverse relation is the signed Stirling change of basis between ordinary powers and falling factorials. It is not inclusion–exclusion on independent equality events.
For rank \(r\), the number of \(r\)-subspaces avoiding \(e\) is \(2^r{B-1\brack r}_2\). To prove this, project onto the quotient by the line spanned by \(e\). Such a subspace projects injectively to an \(r\)-subspace of the quotient. After choosing that image, its lifts are graphs of \(2^r\) linear maps into the one-dimensional kernel. In a fixed \(r\)-space, the number of length-\(s\) spanning vector sequences is \(\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^s-2^i)\): count rank-\(r\) matrices by choosing \(r\) independent rows in \(\mathbb F_2^s\).
Put \(Q_0=1\) and \(Q_j=\prod_{i=1}^j(2^i-1)\). Simplifying the product gives
\[G_s=Q_s\sum_{r=0}^{\min(s,B-1)}
\frac{2^{r(r+1)/2}\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}(2^{B-1-j}-1)}{Q_r}\,
\frac1{Q_{s-r}}.\]
This is one ordinary convolution, after computing the two input arrays. Empty products are one. Over the statement’s modulus \(998244353\), verify that the \(Q_j\) used through \(j=N\) are nonzero before inversion; the bound \(N\le200000\) permits this directly. A product tree builds the falling-factorial polynomial of degree \(N\); divide by its last linear factor to obtain the degree-\(N-1\) row. Two dot products with \(G\) then give the answer. With multiplication cost \(M(N)\), this route costs \(O(M(N)\log N)\) plus \(O(N+\log B)\) preparation; no loop through all \(2^B\) vectors is needed.
Hand check. For \(B=2,N=2\), the avoiding length-one cards are \(0,2,3\), so \(F_1=3\). Among their six ordered distinct pairs, \((2,3)\) and \((3,2)\) already span one, giving \(F_2=4\). The answer is \(3\cdot3-4=5\), agreeing with the official example.
Failure to catch: using replacement counts \(G_s\) directly ignores repeated cards. An oracle enumerates all distinct sequences for \(B\le3\) and checks XOR spans after each prefix. The official editorial describes the subspace/Stirling/convolution route.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
text:
Binary shifts and repeated factors
Official problem: CF1698G — Long Binary String.
Index bits from zero and encode a string by \(s(x)=\sum_i s_ix^i\) over \(\mathbb F_2\). XORing a copy shifted by \(j\) adds \(x^js(x)\). Thus reachable targets are polynomial multiples of \(s\), with the operation positions restricted to the finite string. If \(s=0\), no two-bit target exists.
Otherwise write \(s=x^ag\) with \(g(0)=1\). Every target’s first nonzero bit is at index at least \(a\). A target with bits at \(a,a+L\) is reachable exactly when \(g\mid1+x^L\). The earliest first bit maximizes lexicographic order; among targets with that first bit, the smallest positive \(L\) is best.
Factor \(g=\prod_i h_i^{e_i}\). Since \(g(0)=1\), the residue of \(x\) is a nonzero element of each field modulo \(h_i\). Let its odd order be \(o_i\mid2^{\deg h_i}-1\). For \(L=2^tu\) with \(u\) odd,
\[x^L+1=(x^u+1)^{2^t}.\]
The derivative of \(x^u+1\) is \(x^{u-1}\), coprime to \(x^u+1\), so the latter is square-free. Therefore divisibility is equivalent to \(o_i\mid u\) and \(2^t\ge e_i\) for all \(i\). The minimum gap is
\[L=\operatorname{lcm}_i(o_i)\cdot2^{\lceil\log_2(\max_i e_i)\rceil}.\]
For constant \(g=1\), the empty lcm is one and take the power-of-two factor as one. Find each \(o_i\) by factoring \(2^{\deg h_i}-1\) and repeatedly testing whether a prime factor can be removed from the candidate order using polynomial modular powering.
Worked instance. For input 1111, \(s=1+x+x^2+x^3=(x+1)^3\). The factor’s order is one but its multiplicity is three, so \(L=4\). The quotient \((1+x^4)/s=1+x\) means applying the string at shifts zero and one. The answer’s one-based positions are 1 and 5.
The original input length is at most 35. The lcm of distinct-factor orders is less than \(2^{\sum\deg h_i}\), while the repetition correction is at most 64. These bounds keep the constructed target and the last shifted operation far below \(10^{100}\), even allowing trailing zeros of the input pattern. This proves the finite-string boundary rather than silently replacing the task by an infinite ideal. Small string enumeration should test zero input, a monomial, a repeated factor, and a product of distinct factors.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
text:
Connected bipartite subgraphs
Official problem: ARC105 F — Lights Out on Connected Graph.
Assign each vertex its flip parity. A retained edge changes colour exactly when its endpoints have different parities, so the retained graph must be bipartite. The target is the number of connected bipartite spanning subgraphs of the given graph.
For each vertex subset \(S\), count graphs together with a valid two-colouring:
\[A[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}2^{e(T,S\setminus T)}.\]
Here \(T\) is the first colour class and \(e(T,S\setminus T)\) counts original crossing edges; each is independently retained or deleted. Every bipartite graph with \(k\) components appears \(2^k\) times. Its unique component partition makes the coloured count a partition exponential. Use the distinguished-component recurrence or the fast set-series logarithm of Chapter 11 to obtain \(C\), then return \(C[U]/2\) for the nonempty full set.
Complete four-vertex check. Among connected bipartite subgraphs of \(K_4\), a \(1+3\) bipartition contributes only its star, giving four. Each of the three unordered \(2+2\) bipartitions contributes the full four-cycle or one of its four spanning paths, giving \(3\cdot5=15\). A connected graph has a unique bipartition up to swapping, so these groups are disjoint. The total is 19, matching the official sample.
Precompute induced-edge counts so \(e(T,S\setminus T)=e(S)-e(T)-e(S\setminus T)\). Enumerating the cut terms costs \(O(3^n)\); connected extraction costs \(O(3^n)\) directly or \(O(n^22^n)\) with ranked multiplication. The official \(n\le17\) permits the subset model. The failed model is dividing every \(A[S]\) by two first: disconnected graphs have more than two colourings. An oracle enumerates all edge subsets on up to five vertices, then checks connectivity and bipartiteness independently.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
section: Degree constraints become a minimum matching
text:
Degree constraints become a minimum matching
Official problem: ABC412 G — Degree Harmony.
Vertex \(i\) must have degree at most \(A_i\), with the same parity as \(A_i\). Make \(A_i\) labelled copies of it. Pair copies internally at cost zero, or externally at cost one when their original vertices are adjacent. Every perfect matching consumes all copies. The copies used externally give the selected degree, and the rest occur in internal pairs, proving the bound and parity condition.
Conversely, any valid simple subgraph uses that many external copies and leaves an even number to pair internally. A matching could initially encode a multigraph, but any two external edges between the same original vertices can be replaced by internal pairs at both ends. This lowers the weight by two. Thus a minimum-weight matching never repeats an original edge and its weight equals the desired minimum simple-subgraph edge count.
If \(X=\sum_iA_i\) is odd, reject immediately. For even \(X\), a weighted Tutte matrix has weights zero and one. Its determinant has degree at most \(X\) in the weight variable. Interpolate from \(X+1\) distinct field values, keeping edge samples fixed; half its lowest nonzero degree is the answer. The baseline is \(O(X^4)\) field operations with cubic determinants, and each trial has false-zero/raised-minimum probability at most \(X/|S|\). The official bound is \(X\le150\).
Small instance. On a triangle with \(A=(1,2,3)\), retain just edge \(13\). The degrees \((1,0,1)\) satisfy all bounds and parities. A zero-edge answer cannot satisfy vertices 1 and 3, so the optimum is one. In the expanded matching, use one external \(13\) pair and pair the remaining copies internally. The determinant’s lowest degree is two.
Oracle and failure case. Enumerate original edge subsets and compare their optimum with explicit perfect matchings of the expanded graph for tiny \(X\). This catches both duplicate-edge handling and the forgotten division by two. The official editorial confirms the reduction.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
section: Bridge: carry strings and run counts
text:
Bridge: carry strings and run counts
Official problem: CF1761D — Carry Bit.
Let \(c_0=0\) and let \(c_i\) be the carry out of bit \(i-1\), for \(1\le i\le n\). Equal adjacent carry bits arise from three choices of the two input bits; a change arises from one. The requested total is the weighted count of length-\(n\) carry strings with exactly \(k\) ones.
For \(k=0\) the answer is \(3^n\). For \(k>0\), suppose the ones have \(t\) nonempty runs. Their lengths can be chosen in \(\binom{k-1}{t-1}\) ways. If the final carry is zero, the zero gaps require \(t\) positive gaps (between runs and at the end), with a possibly empty initial gap, giving \(\binom{n-k}{t}\) choices and \(2t\) carry changes. If the final carry is one, there are \(t-1\) positive internal zero gaps, giving \(\binom{n-k}{t-1}\) choices and \(2t-1\) changes. Hence
\[\sum_{t=1}^{k}\binom{k-1}{t-1}
\left(\binom{n-k}{t}3^{n-2t}
+\binom{n-k}{t-1}3^{n-2t+1}\right).\]
Skip a term when its binomial coefficient vanishes; a feasible term always has nonnegative exponent. Each summand counts an explicitly specified run pattern and then the bit-pair choices at unchanged carries. Precomputed factorials and powers give \(O(n)\) time and memory; the modulus is prime and \(n\le10^6<p\).
For \(n=3,k=1\), only \(t=1\) contributes: \(2\cdot3+1\cdot9=15\). A brute-force oracle enumerates input pairs and computes \(\operatorname{popcount}(a)+\operatorname{popcount}(b)-\operatorname{popcount}(a+b)\). The tempting \(O(nk)\) carry DP is a useful oracle, but misses the full constraint target.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
section: Rectangular components and a differential equation
text:
Rectangular components and a differential equation
Verified problem: QOJ60 — Chinese Elephant Chess. Count binary \(n\times m\) matrices with at most two ones per row and column. The associated bipartite graph has maximum degree two, so every connected component is an isolated vertex, a path, or an even cycle.
Use \(x\) for labelled rows and \(y\) for labelled columns, and put \(z=xy\). For \(k\) vertices of each colour, an alternating path has \(k!k!\) orders: start at its row endpoint, which removes reversal ambiguity. Its EGF contribution is \(z^k\), \(k\ge1\). A path with \(k+1\) row vertices and \(k\) column vertices has \((k+1)!k!/2\) orders for \(k\ge1\); reversing the path gives the same graph. The analogous column-heavy paths give the other term. Isolated vertices need separate treatment, since their reversal does not give two representations. An alternating cycle with \(k\) vertices of each colour, \(k\ge2\), has \(k!k!/(2k)\) representations after quotienting rotations and reversal.
Consequently the connected EGF is
\[C(x,y)=(x+y)\frac{2-z}{2(1-z)}
+\frac{z}{1-z}-\frac z2-\frac12\log(1-z).\]
Each term came from a distinct component type. The all-graph EGF is \(A=\exp C\), and the required answer is \(n!m![x^ny^m]A\). Defining
\[J(z)=\frac{2-z}{2(1-z)},\qquad
H(z)=\frac{\exp(z/(1-z)-z/2)}{\sqrt{1-z}},\]
we have \(A(x,y)=H(xy)\exp((x+y)J(xy))\).
Assume \(m=n+d\) with \(d\ge0\), swapping dimensions if necessary. Selecting \(r\) powers from the \(x\) exponential forces \(r+d\) from the \(y\) exponential. Therefore the diagonal-offset generating series is
\[D_d(z)=H(z)J(z)^d B_d(zJ(z)^2),\qquad
B_d(t)=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{t^r}{r!(r+d)!},\]
and the answer is \(n!m![z^n]D_d(z)\). This is an actual coefficient extraction, not the substitution \(x=y\).
The successive coefficient ratio of \(B_d\) gives
\[tB_d''+(d+1)B_d'-B_d=0.\]
This produces a constant-order differential equation for \(D_d\) constructively. Let \(t(z)=zJ(z)^2\), \(h(z)=H(z)J(z)^d\), and let the prime denote differentiation in \(z\). All of the following are rational functions:
\[q=\frac{h'}h=\frac1{(1-z)^2}-\frac12+\frac1{2(1-z)}+d\frac{J'}J,
\qquad a=\frac{t''}{t'}-(d+1)\frac{t'}t,
\qquad b=\frac{(t')^2}{t}.\]
Applying the chain rule to \(D_d=hB_d(t)\) yields
\[D_d''-(2q+a)D_d'+(q^2-q'+aq-b)D_d=0.\]
Multiply by a common polynomial denominator and extract coefficients using Chapter 19. Its order and coefficient degrees are bounded constants independent of \(n,m,d\); thus each new coefficient uses a fixed number of previous coefficients. At zero, \(J=H=t'=1\), \(a=-(d+1)/z+O(1)\), and \(b=1/z+O(1)\). After clearing denominators without adding an unnecessary factor of \(z\), the coefficient solving for \([z^{k+1}]D_d\) is a fixed nonzero scalar times \((k+1)(k+d+1)\). Start with \(D_d(0)=1/d!\). For the official bounds \(n,m\le10^6\) modulo \(998244353\), these integers and factorials are units. Constructing the fixed-size rational operator, then scanning coefficients and preparing factorials, costs \(O(n+m)\) field operations.
Small checks. For \(n=1,m=3\), choose at most two of the three cells: \(1+3+3=7\). For \(n=m=2\), every binary matrix is valid, giving 16. These test both the isolated-path correction and the factorial normalization. Enumerating all binary matrices through \(3\times3\) checks the component model independently. A failed approach is an undifferentiated ordinary component GF: row and column labels are separate, and their factorials matter.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
text:
Grafy: a certified finite sum
Verified problem: QOJ11139 — Grafy, meaning “Graphs.” Its linked original statement asks for simple directed graphs with every in-degree and out-degree two, no loops, and permits opposite edges. The bound is \(n\le500\); a cubic counting method is appropriate. This problem is retained as an inclusion–exclusion synthesis exercise, not evidence that every graph count needs a holonomic recurrence.
Give each vertex two labelled outgoing stubs and two labelled incoming stubs. A bijection between the \(2n\) outgoing and incoming stubs is a permutation. Every valid simple graph corresponds to \(2^{2n}\) such bijections: independently order its two outgoing and two incoming edges at every vertex.
For one vertex’s outgoing pair, let \(L_1,L_2\) indicate that the first/second stub forms a loop; let \(E\) indicate that both stubs reach the same destination vertex. Let \(B\) indicate that both are loops. The local validity indicator is
\[1-L_1-L_2-E+2B.\]
To verify it, a single bad event gives zero; any intersection of two of \(L_1,L_2,E\) forces all three and equals \(B\), for which \(1-3+2=0\). Otherwise it is one. Multiply these local indicators over all source vertices and sum over stub permutations.
In the product expansion choose \(i\) vertices contributing \(2B\), \(j\) contributing one of \(-L_1,-L_2\), and \(k\) contributing \(-E\). The remaining vertices contribute one. The multinomial coefficient assigns these categories. A \(B\) vertex contributes coefficient two and two ways to match its own incoming stubs, hence \(4^i\). Each single-loop vertex has two choices of outgoing stub and two of its own incoming stub, hence \((-4)^j\). A double-destination event needs two still-free incoming stubs: its destination cannot be one of the \(i+j\) vertices whose incoming capacity has been partly used. Choose distinct destinations for the \(k\) selected sources in \(\binom{n-i-j}{k}k!\) ways, with two incoming orders and negative sign per source. The remaining unmatched stubs can be bijected arbitrarily.
This proves the exact formula
\[\frac1{4^n}\sum_{\substack{i,j,k\ge0\\i+j+k\le n}}
\binom{n}{i,j,k,n-i-j-k}
4^i(-4)^j(-2)^k
\binom{n-i-j}{k}k!\,
(2n-2i-j-2k)!.\]
All factorial arguments are nonnegative on these bounds. Precompute factorials/inverses through \(2n\), powers, and use three nested loops; the cost is \(O(n^3)\) field operations and \(O(n)\) storage. The statement’s prime modulus exceeds \(2n\), and four is a unit. The accessible QOJ editorial gives the same cubic sum; the indicator derivation above supplies the missing interpretation of its factors.
Checks. At \(n=3\), every vertex must connect to both other vertices, giving one. At \(n=4\), deleting the selected edges from the complete loop-free digraph leaves one outgoing and one incoming edge at every vertex, hence a derangement permutation. There are nine derangements of four elements, matching the official sample. An independent oracle enumerates two outgoing neighbours per vertex and checks column sums. Counting ordered pairs of permutations without correcting their multiple decompositions would overcount graphs according to their component structure.

title: 20 — Frontier Capstones
text:
Exercises and postmortem

Choose the invariant. Explain why the graph-colouring logarithm is valid while dividing every disconnected count by two is not.
Solution: the unique component partition gives multiplicative colour choices, one factor two per component. The logarithm isolates a single component; only then is the multiplicity uniformly two.
Boundary exercise. What does the binary-shift formula give for input 001?
Solution: \(s=x^2\), so \(g=1\) and the least gap is one. Apply at shifts zero and one to obtain one-based positions 3 and 4. The initial power of \(x\) changes the first position but not the gap.
Certification exercise. Why is verifying the first 100 coefficients of the QOJ60 recurrence insufficient by itself?
Solution: any sequence can share a finite prefix and diverge. The component EGF, coefficient extraction, Bessel-type equation, and chain-rule operator form an identity proof; small coefficients test its algebra and indexing.
Optimization exercise. Which of the Grafy and carry-bit models needs a guessed recurrence to meet its stated limits?
Solution: neither. Grafy’s verified cubic sum fits its intended scale; Carry Bit’s run decomposition is linear. A more sophisticated technique is useful only when it preserves a proved contract and improves a relevant bottleneck.

For each attempted problem, record the recognition clue, exact counted object, coefficient domain, critical invariant, complexity, division/randomness conditions, and smallest independent oracle. Include the first tempting model that failed and the counterexample that exposed it.

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
“Does this graph have a perfect matching?” has a classical combinatorial algorithm, and it is fiddly. Here is a different one, complete in three lines:

put an independent variable \(x_{ij}\) in entry \((i,j)\) and \(-x_{ij}\) in \((j,i)\) for each edge, zero elsewhere;
substitute uniformly random field values for the variables;
answer yes if the determinant is nonzero.

This is correct with one-sided error that you can make astronomically small, and it is a single Gaussian elimination. Why should it work? Because a determinant is a signed sum over permutations, each permutation draws as a set of directed cycles in the graph, and the antisymmetric signs make every cycle configuration that is not a matching cancel against its own reversal. What survives is exactly one monomial per perfect matching — and monomials in distinct variables cannot cancel each other.
That is the pattern of the chapter: design a polynomial whose nonvanishing is the combinatorial property you care about, then test it by random evaluation. Keep the two halves apart in your head, because they fail differently — the identity is exact, and only the evaluation is probabilistic.
Recognition signals include a graph-existence question with awkward combinatorial constraints, an answer determined by the first nonzero coefficient, and a DP that needs to know whether an enormous count is zero. The distinction to preserve is between an exact polynomial identity and a probabilistic evaluation of that identity.
Prerequisites: determinants, rank, and linear maps, conditional probability, and polynomial degree and interpolation.
After this chapter you should be able to prove a matching polynomial is nonzero, calculate a randomized error budget, recover a bounded-weight optimum by interpolation, and recognize when signs prevent an algebraic object from being a counting formula.

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
section: Polynomial identity testing: why random values help
text:
Polynomial identity testing: why random values help
The engine behind step 3 above: a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish at many points, so a random point is unlikely to be a root.
Let \(P(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) be a nonzero polynomial over a field \(F\), of total degree at most \(d\). Total degree means the maximum sum of exponents in one monomial, not the maximum exponent of a single variable. Choose each variable independently and uniformly from a finite nonempty set \(S\subseteq F\).






NoteSchwartz–Zippel bound



The probability that \(P\) evaluates to zero is at most \(\min(1,d/|S|)\). A nonzero evaluation proves the symbolic polynomial is nonzero. A zero evaluation may be unlucky.


For one variable this is the fact that a degree-\(d\) polynomial has at most \(d\) roots. For the induction, write
\[P=\sum_{j=0}^k Q_j(x_1,\ldots,x_{m-1})x_m^j,\qquad Q_k\ne0.\]
The leading coefficient \(Q_k\) has total degree at most \(d-k\), so it vanishes after the first substitutions with probability at most \((d-k)/|S|\). If it does not vanish, the remaining univariate polynomial has at most \(k\) roots. Adding these two possible causes of failure gives \(d/|S|\).
Repeating the whole test \(t\) times with independent samples, and declaring nonzero if any trial is nonzero, gives error at most \((d/|S|)^t\) when \(d<|S|\). Repetition is not useful if the chosen field makes a nonzero polynomial vanish everywhere: \(x^p-x\) on \(\mathbb F_p\) is an example. Its formal degree is \(p\), so the theorem correctly gives no useful guarantee.
Small exact example. For \(P(x,y)=x-y\) over \(\mathbb F_5\), exactly five of the 25 pairs vanish. The error is \(1/5\), matching the total-degree-one bound. If you sample one value and reuse it for both variables, the error becomes one: independence is a hypothesis, not an implementation detail.
crumbs: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
Pairings, Pfaffians, and hafnians
Next we need the object whose nonvanishing encodes a matching. For antisymmetric matrices the determinant is a perfect square, and its square root — the Pfaffian — is literally a sum over pairings of the vertices.
A perfect matching partitions an even number \(n=2r\) of vertices into pairs that are edges. An alternating matrix has \(A_{ii}=0\) and \(A_{ji}=-A_{ij}\). In characteristic different from two this is a skew-symmetric matrix; in characteristic two the zero diagonal must still be imposed.
For each pairing, order its pairs \((i_1,j_1),\ldots,(i_r,j_r)\) so \(i_k<j_k\) and \(i_1<\cdots<i_r\). Its sign is the sign of the permutation \((i_1,j_1,\ldots,i_r,j_r)\). Define
\[\operatorname{Pf}(A)=\sum_{\text{pairings }M}\operatorname{sgn}(M)\prod_{(i,j)\in M}A_{ij}.\]
The hafnian replaces every pairing sign by \(+1\). It directly counts weighted pairings when the weights count choices; a general Pfaffian does not.
Four vertices. The three pairings give
\[\operatorname{Pf}(A)=A_{12}A_{34}-A_{13}A_{24}+A_{14}A_{23}.\]
If every upper-triangular entry is one, the Pfaffian is \(1-1+1=1\), although the complete four-vertex graph has three perfect matchings. Replacing distinct edge variables by one can therefore destroy counting information.

Why its square is a determinant
The identity is \(\det A=\operatorname{Pf}(A)^2\). One proof route parallels elimination. For an invertible leading alternating block
\[J=\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A=\begin{pmatrix}J&B\\-B^T&D\end{pmatrix},\]
simultaneous row and column elimination produces the remaining alternating matrix \(D+B^TJ^{-1}B\). The determinant becomes \(a^2\det(D+B^TJ^{-1}B)\), while the Pfaffian becomes \(a\operatorname{Pf}(D+B^TJ^{-1}B)\).
The Pfaffian rule follows from its pairing expansion: it is multilinear and alternating in the indexed vectors of an alternating bilinear form. Adding one vector to another changes no value (the extra term repeats a vector); swapping two indexed vectors changes the sign. These are the simultaneous row/column operations used in the elimination. Induction from the empty matrix, whose Pfaffian and determinant are both one, proves the identity for matrices with available pivots. Applying this to the matrix of independent symbolic entries proves a polynomial identity, so specialization also covers singular matrices and characteristic two.
This gives cubic field-operation Pfaffian elimination with pair pivots. If the remaining matrix has no nonzero entry, its positive-size Pfaffian is zero. Track permutation signs; each pair pivot contributes \(a\), not \(a^2\). General hafnian computation has no analogous cubic cancellation algorithm; direct pairing recursion is exponential. Special graph classes may admit special sign choices, but arbitrary matching counts cannot be replaced by a determinant.
crumbs: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
The Tutte matrix
For a simple undirected graph on vertices \(1,\ldots,n\), assign an independent variable \(x_{ij}\) to each edge with \(i<j\). Put \(x_{ij}\) in entry \((i,j)\), \(-x_{ij}\) in entry \((j,i)\), and zero elsewhere. This is the Tutte matrix \(T\). For perfect matching, reject odd \(n\) immediately; the pairing argument below uses even \(n\). The rank result also applies to odd-size graphs.
Its Pfaffian has one monomial for every perfect matching, each with coefficient \(+1\) or \(-1\). Distinct matchings use different edge sets, so these monomials cannot cancel. Therefore the Pfaffian, and hence the determinant, is nonzero exactly when the graph has a perfect matching. This argument also works in characteristic two: signs coincide, but distinct monomials remain distinct.
There is a useful direct explanation from the determinant’s cycle covers. Pair every term containing an odd cycle of length at least three with the term obtained by reversing the odd cycle containing the smallest possible vertex. The permutation sign is unchanged while the product of alternating entries changes sign, so the pair cancels. The remaining even cycles admit alternating matching edges. Conversely, a perfect matching contributes its unique product of squared edge variables through two-cycles, with nonzero coefficient.
Sample every edge variable independently from \(S\) and evaluate the determinant. Its total degree is \(n\), so a graph with a perfect matching is incorrectly rejected with probability at most \(n/|S|\). A graph without one is always rejected. This certifies existence, not an explicit list of matching edges. Recovering the matching requires an additional algorithm.

Rank and maximum matching
If the maximum matching size is \(\nu\), the symbolic rank is \(2\nu\). A matching of size \(\nu\) supplies a nonsingular principal \(2\nu\)-vertex minor. For the other inequality, pair elimination of an alternating matrix shows its rank is even and equals the size of some nonsingular principal submatrix. Such a principal submatrix has a perfect matching by the preceding theorem, so its size is at most \(2\nu\).
Evaluation cannot increase symbolic rank: every larger minor is identically zero. A fixed nonzero \(2\nu\) minor remains nonzero with probability at least \(1-2\nu/|S|\). Thus the evaluated rank divided by two is a lower estimate of \(\nu\), equal to it with that probability. Do not equate the rank itself with the number of matched edges.
crumbs: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
section: Weighted matching: the first nonzero coefficient
text:
Weighted matching: the first nonzero coefficient
Suppose each edge has a nonnegative integer weight \(w_{ij}\le W\). Replace its variable in the Tutte matrix by \(x_{ij}y^{w_{ij}}\), retaining opposite signs below the diagonal. Let the resulting matrix be \(B(y)\). In its Pfaffian, each perfect matching contributes an edge-variable monomial times \(y\) raised to its total weight.
Let \(\mu\) be the minimum matching weight. The coefficient of \(y^\mu\) in the Pfaffian is a nonzero polynomial in edge variables because its matching monomials are distinct. Hence
\[\min\{k:[y^k]\det B(y)\ne0\}=2\mu.\]
The factor two comes from squaring the Pfaffian. For a graph of two vertices joined by an edge of weight three, \(\det B(y)=x_{12}^2y^6\): the answer is three, not six.
Now sample the edge variables once per trial, keeping them fixed across every evaluation of \(y\). With probability at least \(1-n/|S|\), the lowest determinant coefficient survives. The univariate determinant has degree at most \(nW\), so \(nW+1\) distinct field points recover it by interpolation. This requires enough field elements; for integer points modulo \(p\), require \(p>nW\). Cubic determinant evaluation at each point gives a baseline \(O((nW+1)n^3)\) field operations, plus interpolation; this is \(O(Wn^4)\) when \(W\ge1\). When all weights are zero, one determinant suffices. This is useful for small weights; huge binary-encoded weights make this approach infeasible even though the formula remains true.
Sampling new edge values at each interpolation point would evaluate different polynomials and invalidate interpolation. Random cancellation can only raise the reported minimum degree or erase the polynomial; it cannot create a lower-degree term. Independent repetitions may therefore take the smallest finite answer, with a one-sided error bound.
Worked weighted example. On four vertices give edges \(12,34\) weight one; edges \(13,24\) weight two; omit the other edges. Then
\[\operatorname{Pf}B(y)=x_{12}x_{34}y^2-x_{13}x_{24}y^4.\]
The determinant starts at degree four, so the minimum matching weight is two. Even though the two matchings can interact in higher coefficients after squaring, they cannot cancel the unique lowest edge monomial.
crumbs: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
Determinant polynomials and rank-one changes
For \(n\times n\) constant matrices \(A,B\), \(\det(A+xB)\) has degree at most \(n\): each determinant term multiplies \(n\) entries of degree at most one. Thus \(n+1\) distinct evaluations and interpolation give a general \(O(n^4)\) baseline. Singular \(A\) is allowed; factoring out \(A\) would wrongly assume it invertible.
For column vectors \(u,v\) and invertible \(A\), column multilinearity gives the determinant lemma
\[\det(A+uv^T)=\det(A)\bigl(1+v^TA^{-1}u\bigr).\]
To see the scalar factor, factor out \(A\) and expand \(\det(I+ab^T)\) with \(a=A^{-1}u\). Terms selecting two updated columns vanish because those columns are parallel; choosing no updated column contributes one and choosing column \(i\) contributes \(a_ib_i\). If \(1+v^TA^{-1}u\ne0\), multiplication verifies
\[ (A+uv^T)^{-1}=A^{-1}-
\frac{A^{-1}uv^TA^{-1}}{1+v^TA^{-1}u}.\]
This is Sherman–Morrison. The denominator condition is essential. The adjugate is the transpose of the matrix of signed minors; cofactor expansion gives \(A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I\) even for singular \(A\). The division-free form
\[\det(A+uv^T)=\det A+v^T\operatorname{adj}(A)u\]
therefore remains valid without an inverse, by the same column expansion.

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
A contest workflow

Define the exact polynomial and prove that the required object makes it nonzero. Distinct formal variables can prevent cancellations that numerical counts suffer.
Bound its total degree in the variables you randomize. Record the field, sampling set, independence, and number of trials.
Choose between one evaluation, rank computation, and univariate interpolation; state which quantities remain fixed during a trial.
Interpret zero correctly and calculate a union bound over the actual outputs you need to certify.
Compare tiny instances with explicit graph enumeration before trusting large random instances.

title: 18 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization
text:
Exercises, solutions, and contest guidance

Cancellation. Compute the Pfaffian and hafnian of the alternating four-by-four matrix whose upper entries are all one.
Hint: there are three pairings. Solution: the Pfaffian is \(1-1+1=1\); the hafnian is \(1+1+1=3\). Its determinant is one, not the matching count.
Probability budget. A nonzero target polynomial has degree at most 100 and samples use all of \(\mathbb F_{1000000007}\). Bound two independent false-zero trials.
Solution: \((100/1000000007)^2<10^{-14}\). This is a worst-case mathematical bound, independent of any observed success rate.
Singular update. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) and \(u=v=(0,1)^T\). Find the new determinant without using \(A^{-1}\).
Hint: use the adjugate. Solution: \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\), so the new determinant is \(0+1=1\); the updated matrix is the identity.
Application — Degree Harmony, ABC412 G. Replace vertex \(i\) by \(A_i\) copies. Join copies of the same vertex with weight-zero edges; join copies of adjacent original vertices with weight-one edges. A perfect matching assigns some stubs to original edges and pairs unused stubs internally. Internal pairs consume an even number, so the selected degree at \(i\) is at most \(A_i\) and has the same parity. Conversely, any graph satisfying those conditions matches its used stubs externally and the remaining even number internally. A general matching might create repeated original edges. However, two edges between the same original vertices can be replaced by one internal pair at each endpoint, decreasing weight by two. A minimum-weight matching therefore creates no repeated edge and corresponds to a simple subgraph as required. The official editorial gives the reduction and determinant method. The degree/interpolation contract above is the needed algebraic implementation guidance; see Chapter 20 for a worked instance.
Alternate method — No Need, ABC056 D. Card \(i\) matters exactly when the other cards contain a subset of sum in \([K-a_i,K)\). Work modulo \(x^K\) and use
\[F(x)=\prod_j(1+r_jx^{a_j}).\]
Hint: divide out card \(i\); its factor has constant term one. Solution guidance: the coefficient for any subset sum is a sum of distinct square-free monomials in the formal variables \(r_j\), so existence is equivalent to a nonzero polynomial even modulo a fixed prime. Assign independent uniform values in \(\mathbb F_p\). For each necessary card, choose one existing witness sum before sampling. Its coefficient has degree at most \(N-1\), and missing that card implies this witness coefficient vanished. A union bound over at most \(N\) cards gives \(N(N-1)/p\), without an extra factor \(K\). The products and quotients can be maintained in \(O(NK)\) field operations by coefficient recurrences. Ordinary coefficients modulo \(p\) can instead hide every witness through cancellation. This modelling method is documented in the editorial on AtCoder.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
A problem gives you \(n\) binary vectors and asks how many sequences of them have XOR-span of a given dimension. Another asks how many \(\mathbb F_2\) matrices have rank exactly \(r\). Both look like they want a clever DP over bitmasks, and both are hopeless that way: the objects being counted are subspaces, and there are far too many subsets to sort into them.
Subspaces have their own counting theory, and it is startlingly close to the one you already know. Choosing an \(r\)-element subset of \(n\) has \(\binom nr\) answers; choosing an \(r\)-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb F_q^n\) has \(\binom nr_q\) answers — the Gaussian binomial coefficient — and the two satisfy almost the same recurrences and almost the same identities. Set \(q=1\) and the subspace formulas degenerate into the subset formulas.
That is what “q-analogue” means: a formula in a variable \(q\) that recovers a classical counting formula at \(q=1\) and counts a field-flavoured object at a prime power \(q\). The payoff is practical — once a contest quantity is recognized as a subspace or rank count, it collapses into a short product.
One warning governs the whole chapter, and it is the same one as in binomials modulo anything: the tidy product formula divides, the object being counted does not. When a denominator vanishes in your working modulus, the count still exists; only that route to it has failed.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read units and valuations, binomial counting, and vector spaces, span, and rank, which supplies every geometric fact used below. The harder practice also uses convolution and Stirling transforms.
Learn to derive a subspace count by counting ordered bases, read a Gaussian binomial as an inversion or partition statistic, use the division-free recurrence when the product formula is singular, and turn a rank question into a product over independent row choices.
Throughout, \(q\) is a positive prime power (or a formal variable), \(0\le r\le
n\), and the answer modulus — when there is one — is an unrelated number. Keep those two apart: \(q\) lives inside the objects, the modulus only compresses the final count.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
1. Gaussian binomial coefficients
When \(q\) is a prime power, the Gaussian (or q-) binomial coefficient counts \(r\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_q^{n}\):
\[\binom nr_q=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}\frac{q^{n-i}-1}{q^{r-i}-1}.\]
Set the value to 1 for \(r=0\) and to zero for out-of-range \(r\). The product states an exact integer count; it is not a licence for arbitrary modular division.
To see the product, count ordered independent vectors in two ways. The first vector has \(q^n-1\) choices, the next must avoid the line already spanned and has \(q^n-q\) choices, and so on; divide by the number \((q^r-1)(q^r-q)\cdots(q^r-q^{r-1})\) of ordered bases of one fixed \(r\)-subspace, since each subspace is produced exactly that many times.
The same polynomial is the inversion generating polynomial for binary strings with \(r\) ones, and the area generating polynomial for partitions inside an \(r\times(n-r)\) rectangle. Thus \(\binom42_q=1+q+2q^2+q^3+q^4\) records how many such objects have each statistic value.
To connect binary strings, define an inversion as a pair of positions with a 1 before a 0. Splitting by the first bit: a leading 0 leaves a length-\(n-1\) string with \(r\) ones; a leading 1 leaves \(r-1\) ones and adds \(n-r\) inversions. This gives the recurrence below and the same boundary values, proving the polynomial identity by induction. Record, for each successive 1, how many zeros follow it; these counts form a nonincreasing list bounded by \(n-r\). Its Ferrers rows form a partition inside an \(r\times(n-r)\) rectangle, and their sum is the inversion count. For \(n=4,r=2\), the strings \(0011,0101,0110,1001,1010,1100\) have respectively \(0,1,2,2,3,4\) inversions. At \(q=2\), their weighted total is 35, the number of 2-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_2^4\); the six strings themselves are not the 35 subspaces.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
2. The division-free recurrence
The recurrence
\[\binom nr_q=\binom{n-1}r_q+q^{n-r}\binom{n-1}{r-1}_q\]
remains valid even when the product formula appears to divide by zero. Fix a hyperplane \(H\cong\mathbb F_q^{n-1}\). An \(r\)-subspace is either contained in \(H\), giving the first term, or meets \(H\) in an \((r-1)\)-subspace; the latter case has \(q^{n-r}\) extensions, giving the second term. It is often the safest way to compute a whole table.
To justify the extension count, fix \(W=U\cap H\) of dimension \(r-1\). In the quotient vector space \(V/W\), an extension \(U/W\) is a line outside the hyperplane \(H/W\). There are \(q^{n-r+1}-q^{n-r}\) vectors outside that hyperplane, and each line contains \(q-1\) such nonzero vectors. Division gives \(q^{n-r}\) lines.
The recurrence with the boundary values computes a table through \(n,r\) in \(O(nr)\) ring operations with \(O(r)\) rolling memory, assuming powers of \(q\) are available; evaluate rows in an order preserving both prior-row entries. For a fixed numerical \(q\) modulo a prime \(P\), precompute q-integers and q-factorials only while their factors are invertible. If some \(q^i-1\) vanishes modulo \(P\), ordinary division is invalid even though the Gaussian binomial itself remains defined. Use the division-free recurrence, a proved q-Lucas theorem when its hypotheses match, or cancel cyclotomic-factor exponents before evaluation.
Define the q-integer \([i]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{i-1}\) directly as a polynomial. At \(q=1\), it is \(i\), although the expression \((q^i-1)/(q-1)\) is \(0/0\). Thus at \(q=1\) the q-factorial method reduces to ordinary factorials when \(1,\ldots,n\) are units, and the Gaussian coefficient equals \(\binom nr\). When \(q\ne1\) and \(q-1\) is a unit, a q-integer vanishes exactly when \(q^i=1\). For example at \(q=2\) modulo 7, \([3]_q=7\) vanishes; the Gaussian polynomial \(\binom32_q=1+q+q^2\) is still defined and evaluates to zero. Do not “cancel zeros” after evaluation. The optional q-Lucas/cyclotomic methods require their own hypotheses; the division-free recurrence is the complete safe contract taught here.






NoteA vanishing denominator is not a vanishing count



Over \(\mathbb F_2\) with answer modulus 7, the factor \(q^3-1=7\) in the product formula is zero, so the quotient is undefined. The recurrence still returns \(\binom32_2=7\equiv0\): the count is genuinely divisible by the modulus here, but had the modulus been 5 the recurrence would have returned \(2\) while the product route still divided by a unit-free factor. Failure of the formula and vanishing of the answer are independent events.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
3. Small characteristic and q-factorials
Factorial-scaled formulas require \(1,\ldots,N\) to be invertible, and q-factorials additionally require the q-integers to be invertible. When that fails, decide which of two situations you are in.
A Gaussian binomial has an integer polynomial definition and survives a failed product denominator: the object exists and only the route failed, so the division-free recurrence recovers it. By contrast, over \(\mathbb F_2\) the derivative of every polynomial has zero coefficient at \(x\) — differentiating \(a_2x^2\) gives \(2a_2x=0\) — so there is no formal antiderivative of \(x\) at all. There the failed division by 2 signifies nonexistence, not a missing trick. Determine which case you face before choosing a fallback; see small characteristic for the same distinction on ordinary factorials.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
section: 4. Rank distributions as a counting model
text:
4. Rank distributions as a counting model
How many \(a\times b\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_q\) have rank \(r\)? Their column space is an \(r\)-subspace of \(\mathbb F_q^a\), with \(\binom ar_q\) choices. For a fixed basis of that space, the \(b\) columns form an \(r\times b\) coordinate matrix of full row rank. Choose its \(r\) independent rows successively, giving
\[N_{a,b}(r)=\binom ar_q\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(q^b-q^i),
\qquad 0\le r\le\min(a,b).\]
Changing the chosen basis is not another matrix choice: coordinates transform with it, so fixing one basis for each subspace counts each matrix once. For binary \(2\times2\) matrices, ranks 0,1,2 occur \(1,9,6\) times, totaling \(16=2^4\) — a useful check, since the rank classes must partition all \(q^{ab}\) matrices. This is the bridge from subspaces to random linear maps and XOR sequence counting. A naive rank sum or table can still be too slow; the advanced problems require compressing the products or recognizing a convolution.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
Decision checklist

Identify whether the q-object counts subspaces, inversions, or partitions before writing any formula; the three share a polynomial but not a model.
Separate the field size \(q\) from the answer modulus, and list every factor you intend to invert in the latter.
If any \(q^i-1\) is a non-unit modulo the answer modulus, switch to the division-free recurrence rather than patching the product.
For a rank question, ask what is fixed per subspace (a basis, a coordinate matrix) so that each object is counted exactly once.
Sanity-check totals: rank classes sum to \(q^{ab}\), subspace counts sum to the Galois number.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
Ordered practice

Mastery — Even XOR, ARC146 C. Count independent sets of vectors.


Hints

Append a parity coordinate: an even-cardinality subset with XOR zero becomes an ordinary linear dependence among \((x,1)\in\mathbb F_2^{N+1}\). Count independent choices before forgetting order.

Mastery — Many Xor Optimization Problems, ARC139 F. Ranks of random binary matrices and Gaussian coefficients.


Hints

Classify sequences by span dimension; count matrices of each rank, then count which leading answer bits become attainable.

Capstone — October 18, 2017, CF1603F. Large-dimensional subspace avoidance.


Hints

Separate \(x=0\): then the vectors must be independent. For \(x\ne0\), project modulo the line generated by \(x\) and track spans that lift without containing \(x\).

Capstone — make 1, ABC278 Ex. Basis/rank enumeration under a process constraint.


Hints

Replace values by vectors over \(\mathbb F_2\) and classify by rank. First count histories allowing repetition, then use Stirling inversion to recover the distinct-choice process; factor the rank sum into a convolution.


The official ABC278 Ex editorial provides the advanced q-binomial/Stirling/convolution guidance and links the other subspace applications. The following original exercises teach the necessary model before those larger reductions.

title: 16 — q-Analogues and Subspace Counting
text:
Exercises with hints and solutions

1. Concept check: a subspace count by hand
Count the 2-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb F_2^3\) two ways: by the product formula, and by the recurrence. Hint: a 2-subspace of \(\mathbb F_2^3\) is the kernel of a nonzero linear functional.






NoteSolution





The product gives \(\binom32_2=\frac{(2^3-1)(2^2-1)}{(2^2-1)(2-1)}=7\). The recurrence gives \(\binom32_2=\binom22_2+2^{1}\binom21_2=1+2\cdot3=7\). Directly: each 2-subspace is the kernel of a nonzero functional, there are \(2^3-1=7\) nonzero functionals, and proportional functionals share a kernel — over \(\mathbb F_2\) no two distinct nonzero functionals are proportional, so the count is 7. The three routes agree, and the last one explains why planes through the origin are as numerous as lines here.





2. Application: subspaces avoiding a vector
In \(\mathbb F_q^n\), fix a nonzero vector \(v\). How many \(r\)-subspaces do not contain \(v\)? Hint: first count those containing its one-dimensional span.






NoteSolution





Subspaces containing \(\langle v\rangle\) correspond bijectively to \((r-1)\)-subspaces of \(V/\langle v\rangle\), so the count avoiding \(v\) is \(\binom nr_q-\binom{n-1}{r-1}_q=q^r\binom{n-1}r_q\). For the latter identity, project an avoiding subspace to the quotient: its image is an \(r\)-subspace, and its lifts are graphs of the \(q^r\) linear maps from that subspace to \(\langle v\rangle\), after fixing a complementary hyperplane. For \(q=2,n=3,r=1\), there are \(7-1=6\) lines avoiding \(v\). For \(r=0\) the zero subspace always avoids a nonzero vector.





3. Synthesis: forbid an even zero-XOR subset
Among subsets of \(\mathbb F_2^N\), count those with no nonempty even-sized subset of XOR zero. Derive a count by cardinality. Hint: append one parity bit to every chosen vector.






NoteSolution





Map \(x\) to \((x,1)\in\mathbb F_2^{N+1}\). A dependence among these vectors is exactly an even zero-XOR subset. For \(r\) previously independent augmented vectors, their span has \(2^r\) elements. If \(r\ge1\), exactly half have last coordinate one: the last-coordinate map is a nonzero linear functional, so its two fibers both have size \(2^{r-1}\). The next allowed vector therefore has \(2^N-2^{r-1}\) choices. The first has \(2^N\) choices. For cardinality \(s\ge1\) the unordered count is
\[\frac{2^N\prod_{r=1}^{s-1}(2^N-2^{r-1})}{s!},
\qquad 1\le s\le N+1.\]
Add one for the empty set. Division by \(s!\) is exact over integers; the ARC146 C modulus and indexing bounds also make it a unit. Prefix products and inverse factorials evaluate all cardinalities in \(O(N)\) field operations. For \(N=2\), the counts are \(1,4,6,4\), totaling 15; the full four-element set is the only forbidden subset of the four-vector universe.





4. Synthesis: nonzero forbidden XOR versus zero
Count ordered length-\(m\) sequences in \(\mathbb F_2^k\) with no nonempty subsequence XOR equal to a specified \(x\). Derive a rank-sum expression for \(x\ne0\) and a separate formula for \(x=0\). Hint: use the preceding avoiding subspace count and full-row-rank coordinate matrices.






NoteSolution





For \(x\ne0\), the condition is \(x\) outside the span. The exact count is
\[\sum_{r=0}^{\min(m,k-1)}2^r\binom{k-1}r_2
\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(2^m-2^i).\]
Each term chooses an avoiding \(r\)-subspace and a sequence spanning it. For \(x=0\), the empty subsequence is excluded, so the vectors must be independent: the count is \(\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(2^k-2^i)\) when \(m\le k\), otherwise zero. Treating zero as an ordinary forbidden span vector would wrongly return zero for every instance. For \(k=1,x=1\), only the all-zero sequence survives; for \(k=1,x=0\), only the length-one sequence (1) survives among positive lengths. These formulas are the mathematical reduction, not a complete multi-query algorithm for CF1603 F’s largest bounds: its product/rank-sum evaluations need batch preprocessing and further algebraic simplification. Use the official contest tutorial linked on its statement for that optimization.

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
You are asked for \(\sum_{n \le 10^{11}}\varphi(n)\). A linear sieve computes \(\varphi\) for every \(n\) — but \(10^{11}\) values will not fit in memory, and will not finish in time either. The catch is that you were never asked for the table. You were asked for one number.
That distinction is the whole chapter. Whenever a recurrence for the prefix \(F(N) = \sum_{n\le N}f(n)\) only ever refers to itself at arguments of the form \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\), the recursion touches fewer than \(2\sqrt N\) distinct arguments, because \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\) takes only that many values. A prefix over \(10^{11}\) terms then costs about \(N^{2/3}\) operations — seconds, not centuries.
So “summatory sieve” never means skipping information by magic. It means: find a recurrence whose arguments close under floor division. Three standard ways to find one, each keyed to a different piece of structure:

Du Jiao sieve — an easy Dirichlet convolution \(f * g = h\) isolates \(F(N)\).
Min_25 sieve — \(f\) is multiplicative and \(f(p)\) is a low-degree polynomial in \(p\).
Powerful-number sieve — subtract off an easy function that agrees with \(f\) on primes; what remains lives only on numbers whose prime exponents are all at least two, and there are only \(O(\sqrt N)\) of those.

Before this chapter, be comfortable with multiplicative functions, Möbius inversion, and quotient grouping from Chapter 02 — this chapter is those ideas pushed until they become algorithms.

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read multiplicative functions and divisor sums. For weighted prefixes, the discrete-sums chapter supplies polynomial block sums. You should learn to derive a prefix recurrence, prove that its recursive states close under floor division, distinguish a prime-sum sieve from full multiplicative enumeration, and justify a cutoff using the actual time and storage model.

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
Definitions and notation
\(N\ge1\) is the fixed query bound. An arithmetic function \(f\) has prefix \(F(x)=\sum_{1\le n\le x}f(n)\) for integer \(x\ge0\), with \(F(0)=0\). \(f*g\) means Dirichlet convolution. Coefficients lie in a commutative ring; integer formulas are evaluated exactly before reduction unless their denominators are units. In prime enumeration, \(p_i\) is the \(i\)th prime with zero-based index \(p_0=2\). A cutoff \(B\) is an integer preprocessing bound. Operation counts below treat exact coefficient operations as constant time.

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
1. The \(O(\sqrt{N})\) quotient-state space
This section is the reason all three methods work, so it is worth pinning down before any of them.
Every recursive call in these methods should normally be one of the distinct values \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\). This is a small state space because values below \(\sqrt N\) can occur directly, while every value above it equals \(\lfloor N/i\rfloor\) for some \(i<\sqrt N\). There are fewer than \(2\sqrt N\) values in total. Two common indexing schemes are:

store large values in a hash map and precompute all values up to a cutoff;
map \(v\) to \(v\) itself if \(v≤\sqrt{N}\), otherwise to \(N/v\) in a second array.

For \(N=20\), the distinct states are \(20,10,6,5,4,3,2,1\), rather than twenty different arguments. This is the object being memoized; quotient grouping is what makes a recurrence over all divisors practical.
Never accidentally memoize arbitrary arguments: that can turn an intended \(O(\sqrt{N})\) state set into linear space.
Closure follows from the identity \(\lfloor\lfloor N/a\rfloor/b\rfloor=\lfloor N/(ab)\rfloor\) for positive integers \(a,b\): both sides count how many complete blocks of \(ab\) fit in \(N\). Thus recursively dividing an existing quotient cannot create a new kind of state. The map using a second array is injective on the distinct large quotients: their producing indices are at most \(\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor\), and different large quotient blocks have different right endpoints \(N/v\). This is a property of this state set, not of arbitrary integers \(v\).

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
section: 2. Du Jiao sieve from a convolution identity
text:
2. Du Jiao sieve from a convolution identity
The idea in one line: if \(f\) is hard but \(f\) convolved with something easy is also easy, then the convolution identity gives \(F(N)\) in terms of \(F\) at smaller quotients.
Suppose \(h=f*g\) and the prefixes of \(h\) and \(g\) are cheap. We want \(F(N)=\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\). Start by summing the definition of convolution:
\[H(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\sum_{d\mid n}f(n/d)g(d).\]
Writing \(n=dk\) makes the meaning visible: for each possible \(d\), the allowed \(k\) run through \(1,\ldots,\lfloor N/d\rfloor\). Swapping those two sums gives
\[H(N)=\sum_{d\le N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If \(g(1)=1\), the \(d=1\) term is exactly \(F(N)\); move every other term to the other side:
\[F(N)=H(N)-\sum_{d=2}^{N}g(d)F(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
If instead \(g(1)\) is another unit, divide the whole equation by \(g(1)\) after isolating \(g(1)F(N)\); without an invertible \(g(1)\) this recurrence is not an algorithmic contract. Commutativity lets you swap the names of \(f,g\) if the other factor has easier prefix sums. The remaining formula appears to have \(N\) terms, but all indices \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\) repeat. Group a block \(l\le d\le r\) with one quotient \(q\); its total coefficient is \(G(r)-G(l-1)\). That quotient grouping is the speedup, not the recurrence alone.

Mertens and totient prefixes
Let \(M(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu(n)\). The identity \(\mu*1=\varepsilon\) says that the convolution prefix \(H(N)\) is \(1\) for every \(N\ge1\). Here \(g=1\), so a block of indices \([l,r]\) has coefficient \(r-l+1\). Substitution gives
\[
M(N)=1-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)M(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\qquad r_N(l)=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{\lfloor N/l\rfloor}\right\rfloor.
\]
Here \(\mathcal B_N\) is the set of quotient-block starts: begin with \(l=2\) and repeatedly replace \(l\) by \(r_N(l)+1\). It is not the set of every integer from \(2\) through \(N\).
Let \(\Phi(N)=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)\). The identity \(\varphi*1=\operatorname{id}\) says its convolution prefix is \(1+2+\cdots+N=T(N)=N(N+1)/2\), giving
\[
\Phi(N)=T(N)-\sum_{l\in\mathcal B_N}
(r_N(l)-l+1)\Phi(\lfloor N/l\rfloor),
\]
with the same definitions of \(\mathcal B_N\) and \(r_N(l)\).
Precompute through \(B\ge\sqrt N\) and memoize only larger quotient states. Such a state is \(x=\lfloor N/k\rfloor\) for \(k\le N/B\). Its quotient loop takes \(O(\sqrt x)\) operations, so all memoized work is at most
\[
O\left(\sum_{k\le N/B}\sqrt{N/k}\right)
=O\left(\sqrt N\sqrt{N/B}\right)
=O(N/\sqrt B).
\]
The middle bound follows by comparing \(\sum_{k\le K}k^{-1/2}\) with its integral, which is at most \(2\sqrt K\) up to a constant. Total time is \(O(B+N/\sqrt B)\) and storage is \(O(B+N/B)\), assuming \(O(1)\) prefix access and memo lookup. Choosing \(B\) near \(N^{2/3}\) balances the terms and gives \(O(N^{2/3})\) time and space for one query. This bound does not automatically amortize across unrelated query bounds.
Worked recurrence. For \(N=6\), \(\mu(1),\ldots,\mu(6)\) are \(1,-1,-1,0,-1,1\). The block formula uses \([2,2],[3,3],[4,6]\): \(M(6)=1-M(3)-M(2)-3M(1)=1-(-1)-0-3=-1\). The corresponding totient formula gives \(\Phi(6)=21-\Phi(3)-\Phi(2)-3\Phi(1)=21-4-2-3=12\). The weights are lengths of blocks, not numbers of distinct quotient values.
The quadratic scale of \(\sum\varphi(n)\) requires wide intermediates. Reduce modulo the problem modulus inside every operation if that is what the statement asks.


Derivation workflow

Name the wanted prefix \(F\).
Find \(g\) so \(h=f*g\) has an elementary prefix.
Sum \(h(n)\) for \(n≤N\), swap \(n=dk\), and isolate \(F(N)\).
Express coefficient sums on \([l,r]\) with prefix formulas.
Confirm every recursive argument is \(\lfloor N/l\rfloor\) and smaller than \(N\).

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
section: 3. Prime-sum sieve: the engine inside Min_25
text:
3. Prime-sum sieve: the engine inside Min_25
Min_25 first solves a narrower problem: quickly find sums over primes, such as \(\sum_{p\le w}p^k\), at every quotient state \(w=\lfloor N/l\rfloor\). Initialize
\[g_k(w)=\sum_{i=2}^{w}i^{k}.\]
At the start, \(g_k(w)\) is the sum over all integers \(2,\ldots,w\). Process primes \(p\) in increasing order. At the \(p\) stage, subtract the composites whose smallest prime factor is \(p\); for every state \(w\ge p^2\) this is
\[g_k(w)\mathrel{-}=p^{k}\left(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)-S_k(p-1)\right),\]
where \(S_k(p-1)=\sum_{q<p,q prime}q^{k}\). After processing all \(p≤\sqrt{N}\), \(g_k(w)=\sum_{q≤w,q prime}q^{k}\).
Why \(p^2\)? Any composite first removed at this stage has least prime factor \(p\), hence it is \(p\cdot x\) with \(x\ge p\). Just before the \(p\) stage, \(g_k(\lfloor w/p\rfloor)\) consists of two kinds of surviving entries: primes below \(p\), which are deliberately retained as final prime answers, and integers having no prime factor below \(p\). Only the second kind can be a valid cofactor \(x\), so \(S_k(p-1)\) removes the retained small primes. Updating states in descending order prevents the right side from using values already modified by the current prime. After all relevant stages, only prime contributions remain.
Worked sieve. For \(k=0,N=10\), initially \(g_0(10)=9\), counting \(2,\ldots,10\). The \(p=2\) update removes \(4,6,8,10\), leaving five entries. The \(p=3\) update removes \(9\), leaving the four primes \(2,3,5,7\). At \(w=5\), processing prime two before \(w=10\) would change the cofactor data used by larger states; descending order is what preserves the stage invariant.
For \(k=0\) this computes \(\pi(w)\), the number of primes at most \(w\). One array uses \(O(\sqrt N)\) space. An elementary upper bound on update count is \(O(N^{3/4})\): primes at most \(N^{1/4}\) have at most \(2\sqrt N\) states each, while larger primes can update only \(O(N/p^2)\) large states; \(N\sum_{j>N^{1/4}}j^{-2}=O(N^{3/4})\). Using prime-density estimates sharpens this to \(O(N^{3/4}/\log N)\) asymptotically for this prime-sum core, as discussed in the official ABC370 editorial. The simple bound already explains why the prime-sum stage is sublinear.

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
4. Full Min_25 sieve
Min_25 extends that prime-sum engine to a multiplicative function. Assume \(f\) is multiplicative, each \(f(p^{e})\) is computable in \(O(1)\), and the prime values, not necessarily all prime-power values, satisfy
\[f(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_kp^{k}\]
for small fixed \(K\). Run the prime-sum sieve for each required power \(k\); combine the arrays to obtain
\[G_f(x)=\sum_{p\le x}f(p).\]
The prime-sum sieve gives the contribution of prime numbers. To cover every composite exactly once, enumerate it by its least prime and the exact exponent of that prime. Index primes from \(p_0=2\) and set \(G_f(p_{-1})=0\). Define \(S(x,y)\) as the sum of \(f(n)\) for \(2\le n\le x\) whose least prime is at least \(p_y\). Calls maintain \(p_{y-1}\le x\) (with the \(y=0\) sentinel understood), so its prime-only base contribution is \(G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})\) and is zero when the interval contains no prime. For every possible least prime \(p_i\), enumerate an exponent \(e\ge1\). The term with \(S\) counts numbers \(p_i^e m\) where \(m>1\) has no prime factor at most \(p_i\); the separate term counts pure powers (the prime \(p_i\) itself is already in the base term):
\[
S(x,y)=G_f(x)-G_f(p_{y-1})+
\sum_{\substack{i\ge y\\p_i^2\le x}}
\sum_{\substack{e\ge1\\p_i^{e+1}\le x}}
\left(f(p_i^e)S(\lfloor x/p_i^e\rfloor,i+1)+f(p_i^{e+1})\right).
\]
Finally \(f(1)+S(N,0)=1+S(N,0)\) is the prefix, using the standard convention for a multiplicative function. The shift in the pure-power exponent is deliberate: as \(e=1,2,\ldots\), those terms list \(p_i^2,p_i^3,\ldots\) exactly once, while the cofactor term uses \(p_i^e\) as the exact valuation. The condition \(p_i^{e+1}\le x\) also safely ends the cofactor branch: any permitted nontrivial cofactor is at least \(p_{i+1}>p_i\). This decomposition is unique.
As a hand check, take \(f(n)=1\) and \(x=10\). The base term counts the four primes \(2,3,5,7\). The branch for least prime \(2\) contributes \(6,10\) from \(2\cdot\{3,5\}\) and the pure powers \(4,8\); the branch for least prime \(3\) contributes the pure power \(9\). Together with \(f(1)\) these are all ten integers, each assigned to exactly one least-prime branch.
Keep the enumeration cost separate from the prime-sum cost. Let \(E(N)\) be the number of \((i,e)\) branches actually visited by the displayed recursion from \((N,0)\). With \(O(1)\) local values and prime-prefix access, the cost is \(O((K+1)N^{3/4}+E(N))\) by the elementary prime-stage bound, with \(O((K+1)\sqrt N+\log N)\) storage for arrays and a depth-first stack. The logarithmic stack bound follows because each recursive step divides by at least two. A conservative \(E(N)=O(N)\) bound follows by assigning each call its product of selected prime powers: the strictly increasing prime indices give a unique factorization path for every product, and all products are at most \(N\). Practical enumeration is much smaller on common instances, but this is not a proof that every variant inherits the prime-sum bound. Count these branches when benchmarking the chosen library; optimized Min_25 variants require their own complexity analysis.
Applicability signals. \(N\) is around \(10^{9}–10^{12}\), the statement gives a multiplicative function through its prime powers, and its value at a prime is polynomial (examples: \(\varphi(p)=p-1\), \(\mu(p)=-1\), \(\sigma_k(p)=1+p^{k}\)).
Non-applicable cases. If \(f(p)\) depends on an arbitrary property of \(p\) for which no fast prime prefix exists, standard Min_25 has no base data. If only \(\mu/\varphi\) prefixes are needed, Du Jiao is simpler.

title: 14 — Advanced Summatory Sieves
text:
5. Powerful-number support
The third strategy attacks the problem from the opposite direction: instead of finding a convolution partner that simplifies the sum, find one that makes almost all of the terms vanish.
A positive integer is powerful if every prime dividing it has exponent at least two. For example, \(72=2^3\cdot3^2\) is powerful whereas \(12=2^2\cdot3\) is not. The count through \(N\) is \(O(\sqrt N)\) because every powerful integer has the unique representation
\[n=a^2b^3,\qquad b\text{ square-free}.\]
For each prime exponent \(e\ge2\), choose the unique \(e=2u+3v\) with \(v\in\{0,1\}\); the primes with \(v=1\) form \(b\). Consequently \(b\le N^{1/3}\) and \(a\le\sqrt{N/b^3}\). Summing over \(b\) gives \(\sqrt N\sum_b b^{-3/2}=O(\sqrt N)\) candidates. The requirement that \(b\) be square-free is what makes the representation unique.
This sparsity yields another generic strategy. Choose an easy multiplicative \(g\) agreeing with \(f\) on primes, and define
\[h=f*g^{-1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=h*g.\]
Because multiplicative functions have value \(1\) at \(1\), the prime-power convolution identity gives \(h(p)=f(p)-g(p)=0\). Multiplicativity then forces \(h(n)=0\) whenever any prime has exponent exactly one: its product over prime-power factors contains \(h(p)=0\). Thus \(h\) is supported on powerful numbers. Let \(G(x)=\sum_{n\le x}g(n)\). In the convolution \(f=h*g\), choosing a divisor \(d\) for the \(h\) factor leaves a \(g\) factor through \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\); summing those choices gives
\[F(N)=\sum_{d\le N\atop d\text{ powerful}}h(d)G(\lfloor N/d\rfloor).\]
Compute local prime-power coefficients from
\[f(p^{e})=\sum_{j=0}^{e}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}),\]
so \(h(1)=1\), \(h(p)=0\), and for \(e≥2\),
\[h(p^{e})=f(p^{e})-\sum_{j=0}^{e-1}h(p^{j})g(p^{e-j}).\]
Enumerate powerful numbers by DFS over increasing primes, choosing exponent zero or at least two; accumulate \(h(d)G(N/d)\). Prune when \(d·p²>N\). Alternatively enumerate the unique \(a²b³\) representation when the coefficient is easier to recover that way.
This method is attractive when \(G(x)\) is elementary or already available and \(h(p^{e})\) is cheap. Complexity is commonly around \(O(\sqrt{N} \operatorname{polylog} N)\) plus the cost of obtaining \(G\) and primes, but must be derived for the exact enumeration.

A common special case: perfect powers
To count integers \(n>1\) representable as \(a^{b}\) with \(a,b>1\), enumerate exponents but remove duplicate representations. If \(n=\prod_i p_i^{e_i}\), its maximal possible exponent is \(\gcd_i e_i\); thus \(n\) is a nontrivial perfect power exactly when this gcd exceeds one. Möbius inversion over exponents, or counting by the maximal exponent, avoids double counting. Integer kth roots must be corrected with exact 128-bit power comparisons—floating- point pow alone is unsafe near \(10^{18}\).


Worked powerful-support transformation
Let \(f(n)=\tau(n)\) and \(g(n)=2^{\omega(n)}\), where \(\omega(n)\) counts distinct prime factors. Both functions equal two at a prime. At \(p^e\), \(g(p^e)=2\) for \(e\ge1\). Local convolution gives \(h(p)=0\), \(h(p^2)=3-2=1\), and \(h(p^3)=4-(2+0+2)=0\). Continuing gives \(h(p^{2j})=1\) and \(h(p^{2j+1})=0\): the local generating-series quotient is
\[
\frac{\sum_{e\ge0}(e+1)t^e}{1+2t+2t^2+\cdots}
=\frac{1/(1-t)^2}{(1+t)/(1-t)}
=\frac1{1-t^2}.
\]
These are formal identities with constant-one denominators, valid over the integers without dividing coefficients. Thus \(h\) is the indicator of squares, and
\[\sum_{n\le N}\tau(n)=\sum_{a\le\sqrt N}G(\lfloor N/a^2\rfloor).\]
This is an identity, not automatically a fast algorithm: we still need cheap \(G\). Matching on primes makes support sparse but does not supply that prefix. For \(N=4\), \(G(4)=1+2+2+2=7\) and \(G(1)=1\), giving \(8\).
