title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
The vocabulary, in one page
Mathematical writing is terse mostly because the same handful of symbols appear everywhere. Here they are, with the reading you should hear in your head.
Sets. \(\mathbb Z\), \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathbb R\) are the integers, the rationals (fractions \(p/q\) of integers with \(q \ne 0\)), and the reals. \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) is the nonnegative integers. A set is an unordered collection with no repeats — think std::set, not std::vector; a sequence has order and may repeat. The empty set is \(\varnothing\), and \(|S|\) is the number of elements of a finite \(S\).
Index ranges. \([0,n)\) means the integers \(0, 1, \ldots, n-1\), the same half-open convention as a C++ loop. An indexed sum \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i\) has one term per index in that range.
Empty things. An empty sum is \(0\) and an empty product is \(1\). These are not arbitrary: they are the values that make recurrences correct at size zero, exactly as an accumulator is initialized to the identity of its operation. In the same spirit, there is exactly one empty sequence, so a formula counting sequences should return \(1\), not \(0\), at size zero. Off-by-one errors in combinatorics are almost always disagreements about this convention.
Functions. \(f : A \to B\) assigns one output in \(B\) to each input in \(A\). It is injective when different inputs give different outputs (no collisions), surjective when every element of \(B\) is hit, and bijective when both hold. A bijection between finite sets is a perfect matching between their elements, so it proves \(|A| = |B|\) — the single most useful proof technique in counting.
Indicators. \([P]\) is \(1\) when the proposition \(P\) is true and \(0\) otherwise. For instance \(\sum_{i=1}^{10} [\,2 \mid i\,] = 5\). Indicators let you move a condition out of the range of a sum and into the summand, which is often what unlocks an algebraic simplification.
Divisibility and floors. \(a \mid b\) (“\(a\) divides \(b\)”) means \(b = ak\) for some integer \(k\); its negation is \(a \nmid b\). The floor \(\lfloor x \rfloor\) is the greatest integer at most \(x\). Note \(\lfloor -3/2 \rfloor = -2\), while C++ integer division gives \(-1\): floor rounds down, the language truncates toward zero. Every chapter that uses floors means the mathematical one.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
section: Logic: what exactly must be proved?
text:
Logic: what exactly must be proved?
A surprising amount of contest debugging is really the discovery that you proved a different statement from the one you needed.
\(P \Rightarrow Q\) means: every instance satisfying \(P\) also satisfies \(Q\). Its converse \(Q \Rightarrow P\) is a genuinely different claim, and one of the two can hold while the other fails. \(P \Longleftrightarrow Q\) asserts both.
This matters constantly in reductions. When you say “the answer is yes exactly when the graph has a perfect matching”, you have made two claims: a yes-instance gives a matching, and a matching gives a yes-instance. Skipping the second is how you end up counting configurations that do not correspond to anything.






WarningWorked failure: a necessary condition is not a solution



If a positive integer is divisible by \(6\), then it is divisible by \(3\). The converse fails at \(n = 3\).
Practically: a necessary condition is a filter. It can prove an instance impossible, and that is valuable — checking parity or a gcd condition first can save an entire wrong approach. But passing the filter does not build a solution, and a solution written as “check the condition, then output yes” is correct only if you also proved sufficiency.


Quantifiers. \(\forall\) is “for every” and \(\exists\) is “there exists”. Their order is not decoration. “For every integer \(x\) there exists an integer \(y > x\)” is true. Swap the quantifiers — “there exists an integer \(y\) that is larger than every integer \(x\)” — and it is false. When reading a problem statement, note which quantity is allowed to depend on which; the dependency order is usually the whole difficulty of the problem.
To disprove a \(\forall\) statement, exhibit one counterexample. To negate “for every \(x\) there exists \(y\) with \(P(x,y)\)”, say “there exists an \(x\) such that every \(y\) fails \(P(x,y)\)” — negation flips each quantifier and negates the inside. Doing this mechanically is useful: the negation tells you exactly what a counterexample must look like, which is what your brute-force checker should search for.
Contrapositive and contradiction. The contrapositive of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\), and the two are equivalent — if \(P\) forced \(Q\), then failing \(Q\) rules out \(P\). Sometimes one direction is far easier to argue. To show that \(n^2\) even forces \(n\) even, assume instead that \(n\) is odd, write \(n = 2k+1\), and compute \(n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1\), which is odd. A proof by contradiction assumes the claim false and derives an impossibility; it is the right tool when the negation gives you something concrete to manipulate.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Induction: writing a correctness recurrence
Induction is the proof technique that most resembles code you already write. To prove a statement \(P(n)\) for every \(n \ge n_0\):

prove the base case \(P(n_0)\);
prove the step \(P(n) \Rightarrow P(n+1)\).

The base starts a chain, and the step propagates it to every index. In strong induction the step may assume \(P(k)\) for all valid \(k < n\), which is the exact analogue of a dynamic program reading every smaller state. In fact the correspondence is precise: a DP is correct when its transition is an induction step and its dependency graph reaches only already-computed states. Writing the induction is writing the correctness proof of your DP.
Worked example: a closed form. Let \(S_n = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n\), with \(S_0 = 0\). Claim: \(S_n = n(n+1)/2\). At \(n = 0\) both sides are \(0\). Assuming it at \(n\),
\[S_{n+1} = S_n + (n+1) = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + (n+1) = \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}.\]
Each equality is the definition, the induction hypothesis, or plain algebra — a good proof lets the reader label every step that way.
One warning that will recur for the rest of the book: this derivation lives in the integers and rationals, where dividing by \(2\) is harmless. If you evaluate \(n(n+1)/2\) modulo \(m\), divide the even factor by \(2\) before reducing, because \(2\) may have no inverse modulo \(m\) (it has none modulo \(4\), for instance). The identity is true; the naive modular translation of it is not.
Worked example: every integer factors into primes. A prime is an integer \(p \ge 2\) whose only positive divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Claim: every \(n \ge 2\) is a product of primes. Strong induction: if \(n\) is prime we are done; otherwise \(n = ab\) with \(2 \le a, b < n\), and the hypothesis factors both \(a\) and \(b\). Note carefully what this gives — existence of a factorization. That it is unique is a separate and harder fact, proved below from Bézout, and the gap between the two is not a technicality: uniqueness is what makes “compare prime signatures” a valid algorithm.






WarningFailed induction: all objects have the same color



Claim: in any set of objects, all objects have the same color. Base: a one-element set, trivially true. Step: given \(n+1\) objects, the first \(n\) share a color and the last \(n\) share a color, and the two groups overlap, so all \(n+1\) agree.
The conclusion is absurd, so the step must be broken — and it is, at exactly one place. Going from \(1\) to \(2\), the “first \(n\)” and “last \(n\)” groups are disjoint, so there is nothing to transfer the color through. An induction step must be valid at its first boundary, not merely for comfortable large \(n\). Whenever an induction feels too easy, test the step at the very smallest index.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Invariants, potentials, and extremal choices
Many contest problems ask whether a process can reach a target state. Searching the state space is hopeless when it is exponential; the mathematical move is to find a quantity that cannot change, and observe that the start and target disagree on it.
An invariant is a property preserved by every allowed transition. Proving one takes two steps: it holds initially, and if it holds before an arbitrary allowed move then it holds after.
A potential function assigns a number to a state and moves in a controlled direction. A nonnegative integer potential that strictly decreases proves termination, because a decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers is finite. A real-valued potential that merely decreases proves nothing: \(1, 1/2, 1/4,
\ldots\) decreases forever.






NoteWorked example: an obstruction and a matching construction



A board has a \(0\) or \(1\) in each cell. One move picks an allowed pair of cells and flips both.
Obstruction. The parity of the number of ones never changes: flipping two cells changes the count by \(-2\), \(0\), or \(+2\). So a board containing exactly one \(1\) can never become all zeros. This argument needed no search at all.
Is parity enough? Only once we say which pairs are allowed. Model cells as vertices and allowed pairs as edges. If that graph is connected, even parity is also sufficient: take a spanning tree, process vertices from the leaves upward, and flip a leaf together with its parent exactly when the leaf holds a \(1\). A cleared leaf is never touched again, so the invariant “all processed vertices are zero” is maintained. When only the root remains, it must be \(0\), because the total parity is even and everything else is zero. The construction costs \(O(V + E)\) with one traversal.
Notice the shape of the complete answer: an invariant proves that some instances are impossible, and a construction proves that all the others are possible. Either half alone leaves the problem unsolved.


An extremal argument picks a smallest, largest, or otherwise most extreme object and then exploits what that object is unable to do. It works because every finite nonempty set of integers has a minimum, and — more strongly — every nonempty set of nonnegative integers has one even if it is infinite.
Worked example: a finite tree has a leaf. Take a longest simple path in a tree with at least two vertices, and look at one endpoint \(u\). Could \(u\) have a neighbour besides the next vertex on the path? If that neighbour is off the path, the path was not longest. If it is elsewhere on the path, we have a cycle, and a tree has none. So \(u\) has degree one. This is the reason that “repeatedly strip leaves” is a legitimate induction on trees, used later in the matrix–tree theorem in Chapter 07.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
section: Euclid and Bézout: the first real tool
text:
Euclid and Bézout: the first real tool
Everything in Chapter 01 rests on one identity, so it is worth deriving rather than quoting.
For nonnegative integers \(a, b\) not both zero, \(g = \gcd(a,b)\) is the greatest positive integer dividing both. Division with remainder writes \(a = qb + r\) with \(0 \le r < b\) whenever \(b > 0\). The key observation is that an integer divides both \(a\) and \(b\) exactly when it divides both \(b\) and \(r = a - qb\): each of \(a\) and \(r\) is an integer combination of the other pair. The two pairs therefore have the same set of common divisors, hence the same greatest one:
\[\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, r).\]
The remainders strictly decrease and stay nonnegative, so the process stops — a potential-function argument — and the last nonzero remainder is \(g\). That is Euclid’s algorithm, and the proof above is the whole of its correctness.
Now track a little more information. Every remainder produced along the way is an integer combination \(au + bv\) of the original inputs: this is true of the starting values (\(a = a\cdot 1 + b \cdot 0\) and \(b = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 1\)), and subtracting \(q\) times one combination from another produces a combination again. Since \(g\) is one of the remainders, there exist integers \(u, v\) with
\[au + bv = g.\]
This is Bézout’s identity, and the running bookkeeping of \((u,v)\) is exactly what the extended Euclidean algorithm returns.
Small instance. For \(a = 30\), \(b = 18\): the remainders are \(12\), then \(6\), then \(0\), so \(g = 6\). Back-substituting, \(6 = 18 - 12 = 18 - (30 - 18) =
2 \cdot 18 - 30\). Hence \(30x + 18y = 6\) has the solution \((x,y) = (-1, 2)\).
When is \(ax + by = c\) solvable, and what are all the solutions? Solvable exactly when \(g \mid c\). Necessity is immediate: \(g\) divides every value the left-hand side can take. Sufficiency: multiply Bézout’s coefficients by \(c/g\). And when \(a, b > 0\), every solution is obtained from a single solution \((x_0, y_0)\) as
\[x = x_0 + \frac{b}{g}t, \qquad y = y_0 - \frac{a}{g}t, \qquad t \in \mathbb Z.\]
Why are there no others? Subtract two solutions to get \((a/g)\,\Delta x = -(b/g)\,\Delta y\). The integers \(a/g\) and \(b/g\) are coprime, so \(b/g\) divides \(\Delta x\) — this is Bézout again — which is precisely the parameterization above. Degenerate coefficients are handled directly; if both \(a\) and \(b\) are zero, the equation is solvable exactly when \(c = 0\).
This completeness statement is what contest problems actually need. They rarely ask for a solution; they ask for the smallest nonnegative one, or for the number of solutions in a window, and those questions are answered by the parameter \(t\), not by whatever pair extended Euclid happened to return.
Cost. Euclid performs \(O(\log \max(a,b))\) divisions on positive inputs, because the larger argument at least halves every two steps. That counts arithmetic operations; on big integers each division has its own bit cost.






NoteWhy prime factorization is unique



Suppose a prime \(p\) divides \(ab\) but not \(a\). Then \(\gcd(p,a) = 1\), so Bézout gives \(pu + av = 1\). Multiply by \(b\):
\[pub + abv = b.\]
Both terms on the left are divisible by \(p\) — the first visibly, the second because \(p \mid ab\) — so \(p \mid b\). Hence a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors.
Uniqueness follows: a prime appearing in one factorization of \(n\) must appear in any other, so cancel it from both and repeat. Two factorizations of the same integer therefore agree up to order.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Double counting and bijections
The last foundational habit is the one that makes combinatorics feel like programming rather than memorization: before rearranging a sum, name the objects its terms count. Then, if you can count the same collection a second way, the two answers must agree — and you have proved an identity without any algebra at all.
The handshake identity. In a finite undirected graph, count incidences: pairs \((v, e)\) where \(v\) is an endpoint of edge \(e\). Group by vertex and you get \(\sum_v \deg(v)\). Group by edge and you get \(2|E|\), since each edge has two endpoints. The two totals count one set, so they are equal. (With self-loops, define degree by counting endpoint occurrences, and the statement survives.)
Binomial coefficients from a bijection. Let \(\binom{n}{k}\) be the number of \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-element set; it is \(0\) when \(k < 0\) or \(k > n\). Count ordered lists of \(k\) distinct elements directly: \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\) choices. Now count them a second way: choose the underlying subset, then order it, which is \(\binom{n}{k} \cdot k!\) lists. Hence
\[\binom nk = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}, \qquad 0 \le k \le n,\]
where \(n!\) is the product of \(1\) through \(n\) and \(0! = 1\). The division is exact over the integers — the left side counts things. Over a modulus it needs its own justification, which is the subject of Chapter 04.
Splitting on whether one distinguished element is in the subset gives Pascal’s recurrence \(\binom nk = \binom{n-1}{k} + \binom{n-1}{k-1}\) for \(n \ge 1\): the subsets avoiding the element, plus the subsets using it.






NoteWorked example: a team and its captain



From \(n \ge 1\) people, choose a nonempty team and designate one member as captain. How many outcomes?
Count by team size. A team of size \(k\) can be chosen in \(\binom nk\) ways and has \(k\) captain choices, giving \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k \binom nk\).
Count by captain first. Pick the captain: \(n\) ways. Each of the remaining \(n-1\) people independently joins or does not: \(2^{n-1}\) ways.
Both describe the same outcomes, so
\[\sum_{k} k \binom nk = n\,2^{n-1}.\]
Check at \(n = 3\): the left side is \(1\cdot3 + 2\cdot3 + 3\cdot1 = 12\), and the right side is \(3 \cdot 4 = 12\). Note that the \(2^{n-1}\) counts subsets of the remaining people, not orderings of them — mixing up those two is the most common way a double count goes wrong.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Contest translation and checklist
Use a library routine only after your reduction has a written contract: what goes in, what comes out, and under what hypotheses. Keep four separate claims straight, because they fail in different ways:

the model faithfully describes the problem;
every valid solution is represented in the model (nothing is lost);
the algorithm returns the quantity actually asked for;
the resource bound fits the constraints.

A brute-force comparison on small inputs can refute any of the four, which makes it extremely worthwhile. It can never establish them for arbitrary inputs, which is why the derivation still has to exist.
Before coding, answer:

What is the domain, including the empty case, zero, and the boundary of every range?
Is my condition necessary, sufficient, or both — and which do I need?
Which concrete object does one summand, or one DP state, represent?
What is preserved by a transition, and what guarantees termination?
When I divide a count by a symmetry factor, are all the groups really the same size?
Does my complexity count arithmetic operations or actual machine work on numbers of this size?

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Exercises, hints, and solutions

1. Quantifiers and a counterexample — concept check
Negate the statement “every pair of nonzero residues modulo \(m\) has a nonzero product”. Then find the smallest \(m \ge 2\) for which the original statement is false.






TipHint and solution





Hint: the negation asserts the existence of a bad pair; look for a modulus that factors.
The negation is: “there exist two nonzero residues modulo \(m\) whose product is zero.” Modulo \(2\) and modulo \(3\), multiplying out all pairs shows no such pair exists. Modulo \(4\), \(2 \cdot 2 = 0\). The answer is \(m = 4\).
This is the first appearance of the theme that dominates Chapter 01: nonzero does not mean invertible. Modulo \(4\), the residue \(2\) is nonzero yet has no reciprocal, so any derivation that “divides by \(2\)” there is invalid.





2. Count the same marked subset twice — derivation
For \(n \ge 2\), derive \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} k(k-1)\binom nk = n(n-1)2^{\,n-2}\).






TipHint and solution





Hint: mimic the team-and-captain count, but mark an ordered pair.
Count pairs consisting of a subset together with an ordered pair of two distinct chosen members.
By subset size: a \(k\)-element subset admits \(k(k-1)\) ordered pairs, giving the left-hand side.
By marked pair first: choose the ordered pair in \(n(n-1)\) ways, then let each of the remaining \(n-2\) people independently join or not, giving \(2^{n-2}\).
Both count the same objects, so the identity holds. Check at \(n = 3\): the left side is \(2 \cdot 3 + 6 \cdot 1 = 12\) and the right side is \(3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 =
12\).





3. All bounded solutions — modelling
Find every pair of nonnegative integers with \(6x + 9y = 45\) and \(x \le 6\).






TipHint and solution





Hint: divide by the gcd first, then use the full parameterization rather than stopping at one solution.
Since \(\gcd(6,9) = 3\) divides \(45\), solutions exist; dividing through gives \(2x + 3y = 15\). One solution is \((0,5)\), and the general one is \(x = 3t\), \(y = 5 - 2t\).
Now impose the constraints: \(y \ge 0\) gives \(t \le 2\), and \(x \ge 0\) with \(x \le 6\) gives \(0 \le t \le 2\). The pairs are \((0,5)\), \((3,3)\), \((6,1)\).
Guessing a single solution would have reported one pair out of three. The parameterization is what makes the enumeration complete.





4. Flip graph on a disconnected board — synthesis
Extend the two-cell flip model to an allowed-pair graph that may be disconnected. State a necessary and sufficient condition for reaching the all-zero state, and give a construction.






TipHint and solution





Hint: a move never crosses between components, so each component carries its own invariant.
Every move flips two endpoints of one edge, so it stays inside a single connected component; the parity of ones is therefore invariant per component. Hence even parity in every component is necessary.
It is also sufficient: apply the spanning-tree leaf procedure independently in each component. An isolated vertex is its own component with no edges, so it must already hold \(0\) — its parity condition says exactly that.
Total cost is \(O(V+E)\), with at most \(V - 1\) flips across all components. The answer combines an obstruction with a matching construction, which is strictly stronger than either half.

title: 00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof
text:
Summary and reference sheet

An implication needs one direction; an equivalence needs two, and reductions almost always need two.
Negating a quantified claim tells you what a counterexample looks like — and therefore what your brute-force checker should hunt for.
Induction needs a valid base and a step that works at the first boundary. Strong induction is the proof form of a dynamic program.
An invariant proves impossibility; a construction proves possibility; a complete answer usually needs both.
A strictly decreasing nonnegative integer potential proves termination. A decreasing real quantity does not.
Euclid: \(\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)\). Bézout: \(au + bv = \gcd(a,b)\). Hence \(ax + by = c\) is solvable exactly when \(\gcd(a,b) \mid c\), and all solutions form the one-parameter family above.
A prime dividing a product divides a factor; this is why prime factorizations are unique.
A bijection or a double count proves an equality by describing one finite collection in two ways. Factorial division is exact over the integers and needs separate justification over a modulus.

Continue with modular algebra, where Bézout immediately becomes the theory of division modulo \(m\). Later, combinatorics, linear algebra, and probability build their own objects on the same foundations.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
You need unique factorization and double counting and modular fields and valuations.
By the end you should be able to reconstruct an arithmetic function from its values on prime powers, prove Möbius inversion instead of quoting it, turn a gcd restriction into a sum over multiples, and decide between sieving a bounded domain and factoring a handful of large values.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Definitions and notation
An arithmetic function assigns a coefficient to each positive integer — concretely, an array indexed from \(1\). Coefficients live in the integers or in a stated commutative ring, and no division is assumed unless a unit condition is stated.
The standard cast: \(\mathbf 1(n) = 1\) for all \(n\); \(\operatorname{id}(n) = n\); and \(\varepsilon(n)\), which is \(1\) at \(n=1\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Be careful to distinguish the pointwise product \(f(n)g(n)\) from Dirichlet convolution \(f*g\), introduced below; they are different operations and contest editorials rarely say which they mean.
A factorization \(n = \prod_p p^{e_p}\) has finitely many nonzero exponents, and \(1\) is the empty product. Zero is outside the domain of every divisor transform here.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
section: 1. Getting the prime factorization at all
text:
1. Getting the prime factorization at all
Everything below assumes you can see a number’s prime powers. For values up to \(10^7\) a sieve does it. For isolated 64-bit values it does not, and trial division by all primes up to \(2^{32}\) is far too slow. The standard pair of tools is Miller–Rabin to decide primality and Pollard–Rho to split composites.

Miller–Rabin: turning Fermat’s test into a real test
Fermat’s little theorem says a prime \(n\) satisfies \(a^{n-1} \equiv 1\). The converse is false, so a naive Fermat test has false positives. Miller–Rabin extracts more information from the same exponentiation by looking at the square roots encountered along the way.
Write \(n - 1 = d \cdot 2^s\) with \(d\) odd, and consider the chain
\[a^d, \; a^{2d}, \; a^{4d}, \; \ldots, \; a^{2^s d} = a^{n-1}.\]
If \(n\) is prime, the last value is \(1\), and in a field the only square roots of \(1\) are \(\pm 1\) (because \(x^2 - 1 = (x-1)(x+1)\) has at most two roots). So the chain must either start at \(1\) or hit \(-1\) before it first hits \(1\). A base \(a\) whose chain does neither is a witness: it proves \(n\) composite, with no probability attached.
A base that passes is only evidence, so several bases are tried. For unsigned 64-bit inputs the set
\[\{2,\ 325,\ 9375,\ 28178,\ 450775,\ 9780504,\ 1795265022\}\]
is known to be sufficient — it has been verified exhaustively over the whole range, so the test is deterministic there, not probabilistic. (The certificate is catalogued in the SPRP base database.) Handle \(n < 4\) and even \(n\) first, reduce every base modulo \(n\), and skip a base that reduces to zero rather than treating it as a witness. Cost: \(O(\log n)\) modular multiplications per base.






NoteBoth outcomes on small inputs



\(n = 21\): \(n - 1 = 5 \cdot 4\), so \(d = 5\), \(s = 2\). With base \(2\) the chain is \(2^5 = 11\), then \(11^2 = 121 \equiv 16\), then \(16^2 = 256 \equiv 4\). It never starts at \(1\) and never hits \(20 = -1\), so \(2\) witnesses that \(21\) is composite.
\(n = 2047 = 23 \cdot 89\) passes base \(2\) completely. One base is never enough; this is the smallest counterexample and the reason for the base list above.




Pollard–Rho: finding a factor you cannot see
Iterate \(f(x) = x^2 + c \bmod n\) from a random start. Modulo the unknown prime factor \(p\), this sequence must cycle after about \(\sqrt p\) steps by the birthday bound — but you cannot observe it modulo \(p\), only modulo \(n\).
The trick: if two iterates \(x, y\) collide modulo \(p\), then \(p \mid (x - y)\), so \(\gcd(|x-y|, n)\) is a nontrivial divisor of \(n\) — computed without ever knowing \(p\). Floyd or Brent cycle detection supplies the candidate pairs, and batching many differences into a single gcd makes it fast in practice. The expected time is heuristically \(O(\sqrt p)\) for the smallest factor \(p\), usually quoted as \(O(n^{1/4})\) for a balanced semiprime.
Pitfalls. Handle \(n < 2\) separately; use unsigned 128-bit multiplication; restart with a new \(c\) when the gcd comes back as \(n\) itself; remember the recursion receives prime powers as well as semiprimes, so re-test primality at each level; and accept that the runtime bound is heuristic, not worst-case.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
section: 2. Multiplicative functions: local data determines global
text:
2. Multiplicative functions: local data determines global
A function \(f\) is multiplicative when \(f(1) = 1\) and \(f(ab) = f(a)f(b)\) for coprime \(a, b\). Combined with unique factorization, this says something strong and very usable:
\[f(n) = \prod_p f(p^{e_p}).\]
A multiplicative function is completely specified by its values on prime powers. That is why sieves that build \(f\) one prime at a time are possible at all, and why “compute \(f\) for all \(n \le N\)” is an \(O(N)\) task rather than \(N\) independent factorizations.
The coprimality hypothesis is not decoration. \(f(ab) = f(a)f(b)\) can fail badly when \(a\) and \(b\) share a prime: \(\varphi(2)\varphi(2) = 1\) while \(\varphi(4) = 2\). Functions that do satisfy it unconditionally are called completely multiplicative; \(\operatorname{id}\) is, \(\varphi\) is not.








\(f(n)\)
value at \(p^e\)
what it counts




\(\varphi\)
\(p^e - p^{e-1}\)
units modulo \(n\)


\(\mu\)
\(-1\) if \(e = 1\), else \(0\)
the Dirichlet inverse of \(\mathbf 1\)


\(\tau\)
\(e + 1\)
divisors of \(n\)


\(\sigma_k\)
\(1 + p^k + \cdots + p^{ek}\)
\(k\)-th powers of the divisors, summed



Each entry is a small count, and each is worth deriving once.

Totient at \(p^e\): among the \(p^e\) residues, the non-units are exactly the \(p^{e-1}\) multiples of \(p\). Multiplicativity across different primes is CRT: a unit modulo \(ab\) is exactly an independent pair of units modulo \(a\) and modulo \(b\).
Divisor count and divisor sums: a divisor picks each exponent independently from \(0, \ldots, e_p\), which is a product over primes.
Möbius: define \(\mu(1) = 1\), \(\mu(n) = 0\) if any exponent exceeds one, and \(\mu(n) = (-1)^r\) for a product of \(r\) distinct primes. Multiplicative, again by independent choices per prime. Its meaning is inclusion–exclusion signs, made explicit in Section 3.


The linear sieve, and its one clever rule
Building all these up to \(N\) in \(O(N)\) rests on a single idea: visit each composite exactly once, through its least prime factor. Every composite \(x\) has a unique representation \(x = i \cdot p\) where \(p = \operatorname{lpf}(x)\) and \(i = x/p\), and this is the one the sieve emits.
Concretely, loop \(i = 2, \ldots, N\), and for each known prime \(p \le \operatorname{lpf}(i)\) with \(ip \le N\), emit \(ip\). The famous “break when \(p \mid i\)” rule is exactly the condition \(p \le \operatorname{lpf}(i)\); without it, composites are emitted several times and the running time degrades, but worse, the value updates become wrong.
The updates need to know whether \(p\) already divides \(i\), because that decides whether the exponent of \(p\) is fresh:

if \(p \nmid i\): \(\mu(ip) = -\mu(i)\) and \(\varphi(ip) = (p-1)\varphi(i)\);
if \(p \mid i\): \(\mu(ip) = 0\) and \(\varphi(ip) = p\,\varphi(i)\).

Both lines are just the prime-power table applied locally. For a general multiplicative \(f\) you additionally need to store, for each \(i\), the exponent of its least prime (or the value \(f\) takes on that prime power), since the local factor changes from \(f(p^e)\) to \(f(p^{e+1})\). Total cost: \(O(N)\) time and memory, producing primes, \(\mu\), \(\varphi\), and any similar function simultaneously.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
3. Dirichlet convolution and Möbius inversion
Convolution of arrays combines indices by addition. There is an analogous operation for arithmetic functions that combines indices by multiplication:
\[(f*g)(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)\,g(n/d),\]
the sum over all ordered factorizations \(n = d \cdot (n/d)\). For example \((\mathbf 1 * \mathbf 1)(6) = 4 = \tau(6)\), since each of the four divisors of \(6\) chooses one factorization.
Three structural facts, each with a one-line reason:

Associative: both \(((f*g)*h)(n)\) and \((f*(g*h))(n)\) expand to \(\sum_{abc = n} f(a)g(b)h(c)\) — the same ordered triples, grouped differently.
Commutative: swap the two factors of each factorization.
Multiplicativity is preserved: for coprime \(u, v\), every divisor of \(uv\) splits uniquely into a divisor of \(u\) times a divisor of \(v\), so the sum factors.

The identity element is \(\varepsilon\), since \((f * \varepsilon)(n) = f(n)\).

The key identity, and what it means
\[\mathbf 1 * \mu = \varepsilon .\]
Proof. For \(n\) with \(r \ge 1\) distinct prime factors, the divisors with \(\mu \ne 0\) are exactly the products of subsets of those primes, and \(\mu\) contributes \((-1)^{|S|}\):
\[\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d) = \sum_{S \subseteq [0,r)}(-1)^{|S|}
= \prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(1 - 1) = 0 .\]
For \(n = 1\) the empty product gives \(1\). So \(\mu\) is precisely the sequence of inclusion–exclusion signs, packaged so that “sum over divisors” can be undone.
Möbius inversion is now pure algebra. If \(F\) is the divisor-sum of \(f\), then \(F = f * \mathbf 1\); convolving both sides with \(\mu\) cancels \(\mathbf 1\) and returns \(f\):
\[F(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,F(n/d).\]
This is worth re-deriving rather than memorizing, because the same two lines handle every variant you meet (sums over multiples, sums over subsets, sums over a general poset).
Some identities that follow, and which you will use constantly:
\[\mathbf 1 * \varphi = \operatorname{id}, \qquad
\mu * \operatorname{id} = \varphi, \qquad
\mathbf 1 * \mathbf 1 = \tau.\]
Why \(\sum_{d \mid n}\varphi(d) = n\): classify each \(a \in \{1,\ldots,n\}\) by \(d = n/\gcd(a,n)\). Writing \(a = (n/d)b\), the valid \(b\) are exactly the \(\varphi(d)\) values in \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\) coprime to \(d\). Every \(a\) lands in exactly one class, so the classes partition \(n\) elements. The second identity is the first one inverted.


The gcd filter: the workhorse pattern
Here is the identity that solves the problem this chapter opened with:
\[[\gcd(x,y) = 1] = \sum_{d \mid x,\; d \mid y} \mu(d).\]
Why: the right side is \(\sum_{d \mid g}\mu(d)\) for \(g = \gcd(x,y)\), which is \(1\) when \(g = 1\) and \(0\) otherwise — exactly \(\varepsilon(g)\).
The payoff is that an exact, entangled condition on a pair becomes a weighted sum of independent conditions. Summing over all pairs,
\[\#\{(x,y) : \gcd(x,y) = 1\} = \sum_d \mu(d)\,A_d B_d,\]
where \(A_d\) and \(B_d\) count multiples of \(d\) in each coordinate — quantities that are usually trivial to compute. More generally, when the condition is “gcd equals \(g\)”, group the pairs by gcd, write down the resulting divisor relation, and invert it.






NoteWorked example: coprime pairs in a \(4 \times 4\) box



Count \((x,y)\) with \(1 \le x,y \le 4\) and \(\gcd(x,y) = 1\). For each \(d\) there are \(\lfloor 4/d\rfloor\) multiples in each coordinate, so
\[\sum_{d=1}^{4}\mu(d)\left\lfloor\frac4d\right\rfloor^2
= 16 - 4 - 1 + 0 = 11.\]
Verify by hand: the rows \(x = 1,2,3,4\) contribute \(4, 2, 3, 2\), total \(11\).
Now a warning about what the number means. For unordered pairs of distinct values, first remove the one coprime diagonal entry \((1,1)\) and then halve: \((11-1)/2 = 5\). Halving \(11\) directly would compound an ordered/unordered error with a diagonal error — and would not even be an integer.








NoteThe dynamic version



Maintain \(C_d\), the number of currently active values divisible by \(d\). Before inserting \(x\), the number of active values coprime to it is
\[\sum_{d \mid x}\mu(d)\,C_d,\]
and only square-free \(d\) contribute, so a value with \(r\) distinct primes costs \(2^r\) terms. Then increment \(C_d\) for those divisors. Deletion is the exact algebraic inverse: decrement first, then apply the same formula to the remaining set.
With active values \(\{2,3\}\), inserting \(6\) gives \(2 - 1 - 1 + 0 = 0\) new coprime pairs; inserting \(5\) gives \(2\). This is the whole reduction behind the first contest exercise below.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
section: 4. Divisor transforms: sieving a whole array at once
text:
4. Divisor transforms: sieving a whole array at once
When a problem is about all \(n \le N\) simultaneously, do not process values individually — transform the entire array.
The divisor zeta transform replaces each entry by the sum over its divisors, \(F[j] = \sum_{d \mid j} f[d]\). Looping over divisor–multiple pairs directly costs \(N(1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots) = O(N \log N)\), which is often fine. The faster route mirrors a multidimensional prefix sum, one prime at a time:

For each prime \(p\): for \(i\) increasing with \(ip \le N\), do f[i*p] += f[i].

Cost \(O(N \log\log N)\). The invariant that makes it correct: after processing a set of primes, \(f[x]\) holds the sum over exactly those divisors of \(x\) obtained by lowering the exponents of the processed primes, each counted once. Ascending \(i\) order is what lets a contribution travel up a whole prime-power chain (\(1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 8\)), and that is exactly why the inverse transform uses the same pairs in descending order with subtraction.
The multiple zeta transform reverses the divisibility direction: \(F[d] = \sum_{d \mid j} f[j]\), computed with f[i] += f[i*p] for \(i\) decreasing, and inverted by subtracting with \(i\) increasing.
Which one you need depends on the operation you are trying to diagonalize: divisor zeta linearizes LCM convolution, multiple zeta linearizes GCD convolution. The general poset statement appears in Chapter 08.
“Diagonalizes” means a double count. If \(h[x] = \sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = x} f[a]g[b]\), then
\[\sum_{d \mid x} h[d]
= \sum_{a \mid x}\sum_{b \mid x} f[a]g[b]
= F[x]\,G[x],\]
where the first equality holds because \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) \mid x\) is equivalent to (\(a \mid x\) and \(b \mid x\)). So: transform, multiply pointwise, transform back. Flip every divisibility sign and the same proof gives GCD convolution with the multiple transform.
Example. With \(f[1] = 2\), \(f[2] = 3\), \(f[3] = 5\), the transformed value at \(6\) is \(f[1] + f[2] + f[3] + f[6]\). This is the integer analogue of the subset zeta transform, with “submask” replaced by “divisor”.
Recognition. Reach for these when every operation replaces a value by all its divisors, when queries involve \(\gcd\) or \(\operatorname{lcm}\), or when values are bounded while the number of queries is large.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
section: 5. Quotient grouping: only \(O(\sqrt n)\) distinct floors
text:
5. Quotient grouping: only \(O(\sqrt n)\) distinct floors
Sums like \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lfloor n/i \rfloor\) look like \(n\) separate terms, but the quotient takes only about \(2\sqrt n\) distinct values — it changes rarely for large \(i\) and is large-but-few for small \(i\).
Precisely: \(\lfloor n/i \rfloor = q\) exactly when \(n/(q+1) < i \le n/q\), so once the quotient equals \(q\) at position \(l\), it stays constant up to
\[r = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{q} \right\rfloor,\qquad q = \left\lfloor\frac nl\right\rfloor.\]
Hence the loop for (l = 1; l <= n; l = r + 1) performs \(O(\sqrt n)\) iterations, each handling a whole block. Combine it with prefix sums of \(\mu\), \(\varphi\), powers, or whatever function the summand carries.
With two numerators in the same summand, compute the block end for each and take the minimum. Watch the degenerate case: once a quotient reaches zero it stays zero for the rest of the loop, and evaluating m/(m/l) with a zero quotient divides by zero.
A derivation worth internalizing, because it shows the two pictures are the same object:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lfloor\frac ni\right\rfloor
= \#\{(a,b) : ab \le n\}
= \sum_{k \le n}\tau(k).\]
The middle expression counts lattice points under a hyperbola; the left counts them column by column, the right by the product.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
section: 6. Dirichlet inverses and designing a prefix-sum recurrence
text:
6. Dirichlet inverses and designing a prefix-sum recurrence
If \(f(1)\) is invertible in the coefficient ring, \(f\) has a Dirichlet inverse \(g\) with \(f * g = \varepsilon\). It is computed greedily: the \(n=1\) equation determines \(g(1)\), and each larger equation contains exactly one new unknown, namely the \(d = 1\) term \(f(1)g(n)\). Solving for it,
\[g(1) = \frac{1}{f(1)}, \qquad
g(n) = -\frac{1}{f(1)}\sum_{\substack{d \mid n \\ d > 1}} f(d)\,g(n/d).\]
This is the mechanism behind a family of sublinear prefix-sum algorithms. Here is the design pattern. You want \(G(N) = \sum_{n \le N} g(n)\) for a hard \(g\). Find an easy convolution identity \(f * g = h\) with \(f\) and \(h\) both easy to sum. Then summing over \(n \le N\) and grouping by the \(f\)-factor,
\[\sum_{n \le N} h(n) = \sum_{d \le N} f(d)\, G\!\left(\left\lfloor \frac Nd \right\rfloor\right).\]
The \(d = 1\) term is \(f(1)G(N)\) — the unknown you want. Move it to the left, and evaluate the remaining sum by quotient grouping, which needs \(G\) only at the \(O(\sqrt N)\) distinct quotients. Memoize and recurse. That is the Du Jiao sieve, developed in Chapter 14.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
section: 7. Gaussian integers and sums of two squares
text:
7. Gaussian integers and sums of two squares
A different flavour of factorization, and a good illustration that “factorization” is a property of a ring rather than of numbers.
The Gaussian integers \(\mathbb Z[i]\) are the complex numbers \(a + bi\) with integer coordinates. Their norm \(N(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2\) is a nonnegative integer and is multiplicative: \(N(zw) = N(z)N(w)\), because \(N(z) = z\bar z\) and conjugation respects products. Multiplicativity of the norm is precisely what makes “is \(n\) a sum of two squares?” a question about factorization.
\(\mathbb Z[i]\) also supports Euclidean division: to divide \(\alpha\) by nonzero \(\beta\), round each coordinate of the complex quotient \(\alpha/\beta\) to a nearest integer. Each coordinate is off by at most \(1/2\), so the remainder has norm at most \(N(\beta)/2 < N(\beta)\). With division-with-remainder come Euclid, Bézout, and — as in Chapter 00 — unique factorization into irreducibles. The units are the four elements of norm one, \(\pm 1, \pm i\). In code, test the few rounding candidates with exact integer arithmetic; floating point picks the wrong quotient for large coordinates.
Fermat’s two-square theorem. A positive integer \(n\) is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\) occurs in \(n\) with an even exponent.






NoteWhy the criterion is true





Necessity. Suppose \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\) divides \(a^2 + b^2\) with \(p \nmid b\). Then \((a/b)^2 = -1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), so \(-1\) is a quadratic residue — but Euler’s criterion from Chapter 01 gives \((-1)^{(p-1)/2} = -1\) for \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\). Contradiction, so \(p \mid b\) and then \(p \mid a\). Remove \(p^2\) and repeat: the exponent of \(p\) must be even.
Sufficiency. For \(p \equiv 1 \pmod 4\), cyclicity of \(\mathbb F_p^\times\) supplies \(t\) with \(t^2 \equiv -1\). Put \(\delta = \gcd(p, t+i)\) in \(\mathbb Z[i]\). It is not a unit: otherwise Bézout multiplied by \(t - i\) would force \(p \mid t - i\), impossible since the imaginary coordinate is \(-1\). It is not an associate of \(p\) either, since \(p \nmid t+i\). As \(\delta \mid p\), its norm divides \(p^2\), and we just excluded norms \(1\) and \(p^2\); hence \(N(\delta) = p\), i.e. \(p\) is a sum of two squares. Together with \(2 = N(1+i)\), even powers of \(3 \bmod 4\) primes, and multiplicativity of the norm, every allowed \(n\) is representable.



Constructing a representation. For \(p \equiv 1 \pmod 4\), find a square root of \(-1\) modulo \(p\) (Tonelli–Shanks) and run Cornacchia’s Euclidean descent to obtain \(p = x^2 + y^2\). For \(p^e\), raise the Gaussian integer: \((x + yi)^e\), not the coordinates separately. The remaining local cases are explicit: \(2^e = N((1+i)^e)\), and a \(3 \bmod 4\) prime with exponent \(2e\) contributes \(p^{2e} = (p^e)^2 + 0^2\). Combine local pieces with the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity, which is nothing but \(N(zw) = N(z)N(w)\) written out:
\[(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2) = (ac - bd)^2 + (ad + bc)^2 .\]
Normalize signs and ordering only at the very end.
Worked example. \(65 = 5 \cdot 13\) with \(5 = N(2+i)\) and \(13 = N(3+2i)\). Multiply in \(\mathbb Z[i]\): \((2+i)(3+2i) = 4 + 7i\), giving \(65 = 4^2 + 7^2\). Multiplying coordinates separately would give \(6^2 + 2^2 = 40\), which is not even the right number — norms multiply, coordinates do not.
This construction produces a representation. Counting all representations is a separate task requiring you to track the choice of conjugate at each prime and quotient by the unit symmetries.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Contest checklist

Multiplicative is not completely multiplicative: \(\varphi(p^2) \ne
\varphi(p)^2\).
Decide whether your divisor formula uses \(f(d)\) or \(f(n/d)\) before you code it; the two differ whenever \(f\) is not symmetric in that swap.
\(\mu(n) = 0\) as soon as a prime square divides \(n\); only square-free divisors ever contribute.
Frequency transforms need a bounded value domain. For a few large values, factor them and do inclusion–exclusion over their prime subsets instead.
Quotient blocks must use 64-bit division, and with several floors the block end is the minimum over all of them.
Pollard–Rho returns a multiset of factors with repetitions; compress it before enumerating divisors or subsets.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Ordered practice

1. Mike and Foam — Codeforces 547C

Level: Advanced · Language: English/Russian
Trains: dynamic coprime-pair counting via square-free divisor inclusion–exclusion.
Editorial: official Round 305 tutorial



Hint 1

On insertion, count active values sharing no prime factor with the new value.



Hint 2

Enumerate subsets of its distinct prime factors and maintain counts divisible by each product.



Hint 3

The signs are exactly the Möbius values of square-free divisors; make deletion the algebraic inverse of insertion.



2. Steps to One — Codeforces 1139D

Level: Advanced · Language: English/Russian
Trains: expectation grouped by gcd, divisor transforms/Möbius.
Editorial: official Round 548 tutorial



Hint 1

The current gcd is a sufficient Markov state and can only move to a divisor.



Hint 2

Count numbers whose gcd with a state is exactly each divisor using inversion.



Hint 3

Move the self-loop probability to the left side of the expectation equation.



3. Cubic? — AtCoder ABC238 G

Level: Advanced · Language: English/Japanese
Trains: prime-exponent vectors modulo three; offline range-query invariants.
Editorial: official contest editorial



Hint 1

A product is a cube iff every prime valuation is \(0 \bmod 3\).



Hint 2

Represent the changing exponent vector by a collision-resistant fingerprint or maintain it with Mo’s algorithm.



Hint 3

Prefix states are equal exactly when the intervening range has zero exponent vector; account carefully for randomized-hash risk.



4. Alex and a TV Show — Codeforces 1097F

Level: Mastery · Language: English/Russian
Trains: divisor-closure sets, Möbius inversion modulo two, bitset acceleration.
Editorial: official Hello 2019 editorial



Hint 1

Store each set through parity of how many elements are multiples of every possible divisor.



Hint 2

Union-like operations become XOR/AND on bitsets in the transformed domain.



Hint 3

Recover membership of \(v\) by Möbius inversion; modulo two, only square-free multiples matter.



5. Coprime Arrays — Codeforces 915G

Level: Mastery · Language: English/Russian
Trains: counting by gcd, divisor zeta transform, inversion.
Editorial: official Educational Round 36 tutorial



Hint 1

First count arrays whose every element is divisible by \(d\).



Hint 2

This counts gcds that are multiples of \(d\); invert over the divisibility poset.



Hint 3

The task needs every upper bound, so take differences of the Möbius formula and accumulate contributions over divisor–multiple pairs.







TipEditorial guidance: all upper bounds





Let \(B(i)=\sum_{d\le i}\mu(d)\lfloor i/d\rfloor^n\) and \(B(0)=0\), for the positive array length \(n\). The floor changes from \(i-1\) to \(i\) only when \(d\mid i\), so \(B(i)-B(i-1)=\sum_{d\mid i}\mu(d)((i/d)^n-(i/d-1)^n)\). Precompute powers, add these differences over all \(i=dt\le k\), then prefix sum. Cost is \(O(k\log n+k\log k)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(k)\) memory. For \(n=3,k=4\), the counts are \(1,7,25,55\). Apply the statement’s final XOR/output aggregation only after reducing each count as specified. Recomputing a full inversion for every upper bound would be too slow.





6. Number Challenge — Codeforces 235E

Level: Capstone · Language: English/Russian
Trains: prime-power decomposition, multiplicative local contributions, memoized state DP.
Editorial: official Round 146 tutorial



Hint 1

Process primes one at a time and fix their exponents in each of the three chosen integers.



Hint 2

If the exponents are \(x,y,z\), this prime contributes the factor \(x+y+z+1\) to the divisor count.



Hint 3

Memoize a state consisting of the three remaining upper bounds and the next allowed prime; divide each bound by successive prime powers.

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Exercises with solutions

1. A multiplicativity trap — concept check
Compute \(\tau(12)\), \((\mu * \mathbf 1)(12)\), and \(\varphi(12)\) from prime powers. Then explain why \(\tau(12) \ne \tau(6)\tau(2)\).






TipHint and solution





Hint: check the coprimality hypothesis before using multiplicativity.
From \(12 = 2^2 \cdot 3\): \(\tau(12) = 3 \cdot 2 = 6\) and \(\varphi(12) = (4-2)(3-1) = 4\). The square-free divisors of \(12\) are \(1, 2, 3, 6\) with signs \(1, -1, -1, +1\), so \((\mu * \mathbf 1)(12) = 0\), as \(\mathbf 1 * \mu = \varepsilon\) predicts.
But \(\tau(6)\tau(2) = 4 \cdot 2 = 8 \ne 6\). Multiplicativity applies only to coprime arguments, and \(6\) and \(2\) share the prime \(2\). Splitting at a shared prime double-counts that prime’s exponent choices.





2. Recover an arithmetic function — derivation
Suppose \(\sum_{d \mid n} f(d) = n^2\) for every positive \(n\). Find \(f(p^e)\) and \(f(12)\).






TipHint and solution





Hint: at a prime power, subtract consecutive equations.
At \(p^e\) the divisors are \(1, p, \ldots, p^e\), so subtracting the equation at \(p^{e-1}\) from the one at \(p^e\) leaves \(f(p^e) = p^{2e} - p^{2e-2}\) for \(e \ge 1\), with \(f(1) = 1\).
Möbius inversion says \(f = \mu * \operatorname{id}^2\), a convolution of two multiplicative functions, hence multiplicative. Therefore \(f(12) = f(4)f(3) = (16-4)(9-1) = 96\).
Interpretation: \(f(n)\) counts ordered pairs of residues modulo \(n\) such that the pair and \(n\) have joint gcd one — the prime-by-prime exclusion of pairs both divisible by \(p\) is exactly the factor \(p^{2e} - p^{2e-2}\).





3. Equal gcd with a fixed value — modelling
For positive integers \(m, k\), count the \(1 \le x \le m\) with \(\gcd(x,k) = d\), using only square-free divisors.






TipHint and solution





Hint: substitute \(x = dy\) to turn “gcd equals \(d\)” into “gcd equals \(1\)”.
If \(d \nmid k\) the answer is \(0\). Otherwise \(x = dy\) with \(y \le \lfloor m/d \rfloor\) and \(\gcd(y, k/d) = 1\). Applying the gcd filter,
\[\sum_{e \mid k/d}\mu(e)\left\lfloor \frac{m}{de} \right\rfloor .\]
For \(m = 10\), \(k = 12\), \(d = 2\): \(5 - 2 - 1 + 0 = 2\), realized by \(x = 2\) and \(x = 10\).
Only square-free \(e\) contribute, so after factoring \(k/d\) this is \(O(2^{\omega(k/d)})\) terms, where \(\omega\) counts distinct primes.





4. Regroup a floor sum — synthesis
Derive \(\sum_{i=1}^{N} i\lfloor N/i \rfloor = \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sigma_1(n)\), then give an algorithm using \(O(\sqrt N)\) arithmetic operations.






TipHint and solution





Hint: both sides count weighted lattice points under a hyperbola.
The left side gives weight \(i\) to each pair \((i,j)\) with \(ij \le N\). Group those pairs by the product \(n = ij\): the weights are the divisors \(i\) of \(n\), summing to \(\sigma_1(n)\). Hence the two sides agree.
For the algorithm, use quotient grouping: on a block \([l,r]\) where the quotient is the constant \(q\), the contribution is \(q \cdot (l+r)(r-l+1)/2\). That division by \(2\) is exact over the integers — divide the even factor before reducing modulo anything, since \(2\) need not be a unit.
Check at \(N = 5\): \(5 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 21\), and \(\sigma_1(1..5) = 1+3+4+7+6 = 21\).

title: 02 — Multiplicative Number Theory
text:
Summary and reference sheet

A multiplicative function is determined by its prime-power values; that is what makes \(O(N)\) sieves and prime-by-prime derivations possible. Shared primes break naive splitting.
Dirichlet convolution sums over factorizations \(n = ab\). It is associative, commutative, has identity \(\varepsilon\), and preserves multiplicativity.
\(\mathbf 1 * \mu = \varepsilon\) is inclusion–exclusion over prime subsets; Möbius inversion is that identity plus associativity, not a separate fact.
The gcd filter \([\gcd = 1] = \sum_{d \mid \gcd}\mu(d)\) converts an exact entangled condition into independent counts of multiples.
Divisor zeta ascends prime-power chains, multiple zeta descends; each inverse reverses the direction and subtracts. They diagonalize LCM and GCD convolution respectively.
Costs: linear sieve \(O(N)\); direct divisor sums \(O(N\log N)\); prime-wise transforms \(O(N \log\log N)\); quotient grouping \(O(\sqrt N)\) blocks.
64-bit factorization has a deterministic primality contract (Miller–Rabin with the fixed base set) and a heuristic splitting runtime (Pollard–Rho).
\(n\) is a sum of two squares exactly when every prime \(\equiv 3 \pmod 4\) has even exponent; build representations by multiplying Gaussian integers, never coordinates.

title: 03 · Practice — Advanced Combinatorics
text: Work these in order. The concept checks below are small enough to verify by hand, which is exactly what makes them useful: they catch a wrong model before it costs you a submission. Foundation entries isolate one tool; later entries deliberately mix modelling with algebra. Hints stop before implementation details, so you keep the interesting part.

title: 03 · Practice — Advanced Combinatorics
text:
Concept checks with solutions

A. Named rooms and unnamed teams
Split four labelled people into two nonempty teams. How many answers are there if the teams are unnamed? What changes if the teams are named red and blue? This is the \(k!\) trap from the chapter opening, at its smallest.






TipHint





Count assignments to named teams, then examine the number of names for each unlabelled partition.









NoteSolution





There are \(2^4-2=14\) assignments using both names. Each unlabelled partition has exactly two namings, so the answers are \(7\) and \(14\). Empty teams would break this simple correspondence if the requested number of nonempty blocks were not fixed. This is \(S(4,2)=2S(3,2)+S(3,1)=7\).





B. Forbidden diagonal
Derive the number of permutations of four labels with no fixed point.






TipHint





Any selection of diagonal cells is a nonattacking rook placement.









NoteSolution





Here \(r_k=\binom4k\). Thus the answer is \(24-4\cdot6+6\cdot2-4\cdot1+1=9\). For general \(n\), the same reasoning gives \(\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk(n-k)!\). The cancellation proof of IE justifies every sign; no modular division is needed.





C. Exactly one shared value
Let \(f,g:[2]\to[3]\) each be injective. Count ordered pairs for which exactly one aligned position has \(f(i)=g(i)\).






TipHint





Use marked counts \(b_1,b_2\), or first fix \(f\) and the shared position.









NoteSolution





There are six choices for \(f\). For either chosen shared position, the other value of \(g\) must avoid both the shared value and the other value of \(f\); exactly one of the three target names remains. Hence the answer is \(6\cdot2=12\). Alternatively \(b_1=6\cdot2\cdot2=24\), \(b_2=6\), and \(a_1=b_1-2b_2=12\).

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
Count the ways to color three beads of a circular necklace black or white, where rotating the necklace does not create a new necklace.
There are \(2^3 = 8\) colored strings and \(3\) rotations, so the answer is \(8/3\). Which is not an integer, so something is wrong.
The mistake is assuming every necklace is counted the same number of times. BBB looks identical under all three rotations — it is counted once. BBW gives three distinct strings — it is counted three times. Dividing by \(3\) treats these the same, and it does not work.
The fix is a beautiful one: instead of averaging over objects, average over moves. For each rotation, count how many colorings it leaves unchanged, and take the mean. Here: the identity fixes all \(8\), and each of the two genuine rotations fixes only the \(2\) constant colorings, so
\[\frac{8 + 2 + 2}{3} = 4.\]
And indeed there are four: all-black, all-white, one black, one white. This chapter explains why that trick is not a coincidence, and how to use it when the objects being colored carry constraints of their own.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Use bijections and double counting, inclusion–exclusion, and modular units. Weighted inventories use coefficient extraction, introduced locally below.
You should finish able to write down the exact symmetry group for a problem, prove the averaging rule instead of trusting it, derive the cycles of a move on positions, count constrained fixed objects, and say precisely when dividing by \(|G|\) is legal in a modular ring.
All sets and groups here are finite. The notation \(X/G\) means the set of orbits, not division. A permutation is a bijection of positions; its cycles are the loops you traverse by applying it repeatedly, and distinct cycles share no position.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 1. From “the same up to a move” to a group action
text:
1. From “the same up to a move” to a group action
A finite group \(G\) is a set of allowed moves with an associative composition, an identity move, and an inverse for each move. It acts on a set \(X\) of objects when each \(g \in G\) gives a map \(x \mapsto g \cdot x\), the identity fixes everything, and \(g\cdot(h\cdot x) = (gh)\cdot x\) — that last law just says composing moves and multiplying in the group agree.
Two objects are “the same” when a move carries one to the other. The equivalence class is the orbit \(Gx\): every version of \(x\) reachable by allowed moves. One orbit = one object up to symmetry, so the quantity a problem asks for is \(|X/G|\).
The stabilizer \(G_x\) is the set of moves that leave \(x\) unchanged. The first theorem ties the two together:
\[|Gx|\cdot|G_x| = |G|. \tag{1}\]
Proof. Send each move \(g\) to the object \(g \cdot x\); the image is exactly the orbit. If \(h \cdot x = y\), then the moves landing on \(y\) are precisely the products \(hs\) with \(s \in G_x\) — every such product works, and conversely \(g\cdot x = h \cdot x\) forces \(h^{-1}g \in G_x\). So every orbit element has exactly \(|G_x|\) preimages, and the \(|G|\) moves split into \(|Gx|\) equal groups. (Those groups are called cosets of the stabilizer.) \(\square\)
Equation (1) is exactly the reason naive division fails. For the three-bead necklace, BBB has \(|G_x| = 3\) and orbit size \(1\), while BBW has \(|G_x| = 1\) and orbit size \(3\). Orbits have different sizes, so no single divisor can fix the count.
Recognition — write the move set first. Everything downstream depends on getting this right:

necklaces: rotations, the cyclic group \(C_n\), size \(n\);
bracelets (you may flip them over): rotations and reflections, the dihedral group \(D_n\), size \(2n\);
a square grid under quarter turns: a small geometric permutation group;
interchangeable colors: a second action, usually handled by cycle types or by another layer of Burnside.

And check one thing: the moves must preserve validity. If a move can turn a valid object into an invalid one, its orbits are not the equivalence classes the problem is asking about.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
2. Burnside’s lemma
Let \(\operatorname{Fix}(g) = \{x : g\cdot x = x\}\). Burnside’s lemma (also Cauchy–Frobenius) states
\[|X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\left|\operatorname{Fix}(g)\right|. \tag{2}\]
It is startling at first because the summand is a different count for every move, and nothing in it obviously refers to orbits.
Proof by double counting. Count the pairs \((g,x)\) with \(g \cdot x = x\). Grouping by \(g\) gives the right-hand numerator. Grouping by orbit instead: in an orbit \(O\), equation (1) says each object has \(|G|/|O|\) fixing moves, so the orbit contributes
\[|O| \cdot \frac{|G|}{|O|} = |G|\]
pairs — the same total for every orbit, large or small. So the numerator is \(|G|\) times the number of orbits. \(\square\)
That is the real content: the averaging exactly compensates for uneven orbit sizes, because a small orbit is made of objects with correspondingly large stabilizers.
The coloring special case. If \(X\) is all colorings of \(v\) positions with \(c\) named colors, a move \(g\) permutes the positions into cycles. A coloring fixed by \(g\) must be constant along each cycle, and each cycle chooses its color independently, so
\[|\operatorname{Fix}(g)| = c^{z(g)}, \quad z(g) = \#\text{cycles of } g.\]
Almost every Burnside computation reduces to counting cycles.

Necklaces, worked out
Rotation by \(r\) on \(n\) positions jumps by \(r\) each step and first returns after \(n/\gcd(n,r)\) steps, so it has \(\gcd(n,r)\) cycles. Then (2) gives
\[
N(n,c) = \frac1n\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}c^{\gcd(n,r)}
= \frac1n\sum_{d \mid n}\varphi(n/d)\,c^{d}. \tag{3}
\]
The second form groups rotations by their cycle count, which is what you actually want after factoring \(n\): writing \(r = du\) and \(n = dv\) for the rotations with \(\gcd(n,r) = d\) gives \(0 \le u < v\) with \(\gcd(u,v) = 1\), i.e. exactly \(\varphi(v) = \varphi(n/d)\) of them. (The identity is \(d = n\) with \(\varphi(1) = 1\).)
At \(n = 3\), \(c = 2\) this reproduces the opening computation: \((8+2+2)/3 = 4\).
Bracelets need their own cycle analysis. Reflections must be examined by parity of \(n\), which is why a memorized necklace formula cannot answer a bracelet question:

\(n\) odd: every reflection axis passes through one position and pairs up the rest — \(1 + (n-1)/2\) cycles.
\(n\) even: half the axes pass through two positions (\(2 + (n-2)/2\) cycles) and half pass between positions (\(n/2\) cycles).

At \(n = 4\), \(c = 2\): rotations give \(16 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 24\), the two vertex-axis reflections give \(2^3\) each and the two edge-axis reflections \(2^2\) each, another \(24\). So bracelets \(= 48/8 = 6\) and necklaces \(= 24/4 = 6\) — equal here, by coincidence. At \(n = 6\), \(c = 2\): rotations sum to \(84\) (\(14\) necklaces), reflections add \(3\cdot 16 + 3 \cdot 8 = 72\), giving \(156/12 = 13\) bracelets. The two counts differ as soon as some necklace is not its own mirror image.






NoteNon-faithful actions are fine



For \(n = 1, 2\) several formal dihedral moves induce the same permutation of positions. We still sum over all \(2n\) formal group elements. Burnside holds regardless: each distinct induced permutation simply appears the same number of times, top and bottom.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 3. Pólya: keeping track of how many of each color
text:
3. Pólya: keeping track of how many of each color
Burnside with \(c^{z(g)}\) answers “how many necklaces”, but not “how many necklaces with exactly three red and two blue beads”. To keep the inventory, attach a marker variable \(y_i\) to color \(i\), and let a cycle of length \(j\) painted color \(i\) contribute \(y_i^{\,j}\) — because that single choice uses color \(i\) exactly \(j\) times.
Record the cycle structure of the whole group in the cycle index
\[Z_G(s_1, s_2, \ldots) = \frac1{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\prod_{j \ge 1}s_j^{\,c_j(g)}, \tag{4}\]
where \(c_j(g)\) is the number of length-\(j\) cycles of \(g\). Substituting
\[s_j \leftarrow y_1^{\,j} + \cdots + y_c^{\,j}\]
makes the coefficient of \(y_1^{a_1}\cdots y_c^{a_c}\) equal to the number of symmetry classes using exactly \(a_i\) positions of color \(i\). Setting every \(y_i = 1\) recovers plain Burnside, since each \(s_j\) becomes \(c\).
Smallest possible example. Two positions, group = {identity, swap}. The identity has two \(1\)-cycles and the swap has one \(2\)-cycle, so \(Z = \tfrac12(s_1^2 + s_2)\), which substitutes to
\[\tfrac12\left((y_1+y_2)^2 + y_1^2 + y_2^2\right).\]
The coefficient of \(y_1y_2\) is \(\tfrac12(2 + 0) = 1\): the two mixed colorings form a single class. Note why the swap contributed nothing there — it fixes no mixed coloring, which is precisely why its term is \(y_1^2 + y_2^2\) and not \((y_1+y_2)^2\).
Weighted states. If each position may hold a state of some nonnegative integer weight, with inventory \(A(x) = \sum_w a_w x^w\) (\(a_w\) finite, counting available states of weight \(w\)), substitute \(s_j \leftarrow A(x^j)\): a cycle of length \(j\) repeats its chosen state \(j\) times, multiplying the weight by \(j\). Then \([x^s]\) selects total weight \(s\). For instance a swapped pair of positions holding positive integers has inventory \(x^2 + x^4 + \cdots = x^2/(1-x^2)\), since both positions must hold the same value. Truncate everything at the requested total weight.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 4. Constraints go inside the fixed-point count
text:
4. Constraints go inside the fixed-point count
This is where most Burnside solutions go wrong. Burnside is only the outer average; the inner count must already respect the problem’s constraints. The procedure per group element is:

find its cycles on the atomic positions;
contract each cycle to a single node — a fixed object is constant on it;
count the valid assignments to the contracted structure;
add that to the numerator.

Contraction can change the structure in ways that matter. If an edge’s two endpoints collapse into one node, that self-loop makes a proper coloring impossible — the fixed count is zero. Contraction may also create parallel edges, usually harmless for proper colorings but relevant for weights.

Worked example: proper colorings of a triangle
Count proper \(3\)-colorings of a triangle up to rotation.
The identity fixes \(3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6\). Each nonidentity rotation contracts all three vertices into one node, turning every edge into a self-loop, so it fixes \(0\) proper colorings. Burnside gives
\[\frac{6 + 0 + 0}{3} = 2,\]
the two cyclic orders of the three colors.
Using the unrestricted formula \(c^{z(g)}\) instead would give \((27 + 3 + 3)/3 = 11\) — a count of all colorings up to rotation, proper or not. The constraint must live inside each term, never be applied after averaging.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 5. Symmetric groups: sum over cycle types, not permutations
text:
5. Symmetric groups: sum over cycle types, not permutations
When the group is \(S_n\) (say, all relabellings of \(n\) vertices), summing over \(n!\) elements is hopeless. But if the fixed count depends only on the cycle lengths — which it does whenever the action is built from positions — then all permutations of the same cycle type contribute equally, and you can sum over the integer partitions of \(n\) instead.
A type \(1^{m_1}2^{m_2}\cdots\) with \(\sum_i i\,m_i = n\) contains
\[\frac{n!}{\prod_i i^{m_i}m_i!} \tag{5}\]
permutations. The denominator has a concrete meaning: start from all \(n!\) linear orderings cut into cycles of the prescribed lengths, then quotient by rotating each cycle of length \(i\) (\(i^{m_i}\)) and by reordering the \(m_i\) cycles of equal length (\(m_i!\)). Relatedly, two permutations are conjugate (\(g \mapsto hgh^{-1}\)) exactly when they share a cycle type, since conjugation only renames entries.
If the objects carry both vertex colors and edges, there are two induced actions to handle: a fixed coloring is constant on each vertex cycle, while a fixed edge set is constant on each unordered-pair cycle. Requirements like “every color is used” go inside that fixed count, typically by inclusion–exclusion over the missing colors.

Induced cycles on pairs, derived
A vertex permutation with cycles of lengths \(a_1, \ldots, a_r\) acts on unordered vertex pairs. Two cases:

Pairs across two cycles of lengths \(a, b\): a pair returns to itself after \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\) steps, and there are \(ab\) such pairs, giving \(ab/\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = \gcd(a,b)\) pair cycles.
Pairs inside one cycle of length \(a\): classify by circular distance \(1, \ldots, \lfloor a/2\rfloor\); each distance forms one orbit (the opposite-pair class, when \(a\) is even, has size \(a/2\) rather than \(a\)).

So the number of induced pair cycles is
\[e = \sum_{i=1}^{r}\left\lfloor \frac{a_i}{2}\right\rfloor
+ \sum_{1 \le i < j \le r}\gcd(a_i, a_j),\]
and a fixed simple graph independently includes or excludes each whole pair cycle: \(2^e\) of them.
Check on three vertices. Type \((2,1)\) gives \(e = 1 + 1 = 2\): the edge inside the swapped pair is a cycle by itself, and the two edges to the fixed vertex form one orbit — \(4\) invariant graphs. Over all of \(S_3\) the three types contribute \(1\cdot 8 + 3 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 2 = 24\), so there are \(24/6 = 4\) unlabelled simple graphs on three vertices: with zero, one, two, or three edges. Correct.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
text:
6. Arithmetic and modelling checks

Dividing by \(|G|\) modulo a prime \(p\) requires \(p \nmid |G|\). Otherwise divide exactly over the integers first, or rearrange (see Section 7).
A reflection and a rotation of the same order need not have the same cycle structure — derive cycles, do not guess them.
If the colors are also interchangeable, position-Burnside alone still treats color names as distinct; you need to model the color symmetry too.
Exact multiplicities need coefficient extraction from (4), not \(c^{\,\text{cycles}}\).
Before coding: take a \(2\)- or \(3\)-position toy case, enumerate raw objects, group the orbits by hand, and compare against your Burnside numerator.

title: 05 — Group Actions, Burnside, and Pólya
section: 7. Costs, the division trick, and a reference table
text:
7. Costs, the division trick, and a reference table
For an explicitly listed group acting on \(v\) positions, cycle decomposition costs \(O(v)\) per element, so \(O(|G|v)\) plus the fixed-object counting. Necklace divisor grouping costs one modular exponentiation per divisor after factoring \(n\). Summing over the cycle types of \(S_n\) visits the integer partitions of \(n\), with the edge-cycle formula costing \(O(n^2)\) gcds per type — useful in practice, but partition enumeration is itself the limiting factor, not a polynomial-time algorithm.






TipDividing by \(|G|\) when it is not a unit



The Burnside numerator \(A\) is always divisible by \(g = |G|\) as an integer, even when \(g\) is \(0\) modulo the requested modulus \(m\). Compute \(A \bmod gm\) instead: writing \(A = qgm + r\) with \(0 \le r < gm\), divisibility gives \(g \mid r\) and
\[\frac Ag \equiv \frac rg \pmod m .\]
This needs your fixed-count algorithm to run modulo \(gm\) and that modulus to fit your arithmetic model, but it avoids an inverse that does not exist.


Before implementing, name five things: the positions, the moves, what makes an object valid, what a cycle constraint forces, and the ring in which the final division happens. Then test a case with a nontrivial stabilizer.

title: 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms
text:
Here is a familiar situation. You have a DP array f[k] = number of ways to reach total size \(k\) using the first group of items, and g[k] for the second group. Combining the groups means
\[h[k] = \sum_{i+j=k} f[i]\,g[j],\]
which is \(\Theta(n^2)\) if you write the double loop — and is exactly polynomial multiplication if you call f and g polynomials. Doing it in \(O(n\log n)\) instead is often the entire difficulty of a problem.
That is the point of view of this chapter: a polynomial is a compact description of size-indexed choices, \([x^k]A(x)\) is the answer at total size \(k\), and multiplication is “split a total between two independent parts”. Once you see convolution in a merge, a dozen fast operations become available — evaluation at many points, division, shifting the variable, multiplying thousands of small factors — and each one has an algebraic precondition that quietly decides whether your submission is correct.
We assume your library already contains a tested convolution routine. What this chapter supplies is why the operations work and when they are legal.
