title: 11 — Set Power Series
section: Definitions: a polynomial whose labels cannot repeat
text:
Definitions: a polynomial whose labels cannot repeat
Let \(U=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and let \(R\) be a commutative ring with identity. A set series is a table \(f[S]\in R\) for every \(S\subseteq U\). For \(S\subseteq U\), write \(x^S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\); this is a monomial, not an ordinary integer power. We impose \(x_i^2=0\) for each label. The resulting algebra is
\[R[x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}]/(x_0^2,\ldots,x_{n-1}^2).\]
Multiplying \(x^Ax^B\) returns \(x^{A\cup B}\) if \(A,B\) are disjoint, and zero otherwise. For example, \(x^{\{0,1\}}x^{\{1,2\}}=0\), but \(x^{\{0\}}x^{\{1,2\}}=x^{\{0,1,2\}}\). The empty-set coefficient is the constant term. The multiplicative identity has coefficient one at the empty set and zero elsewhere.
Suppose \(f[T]\) counts a first structure on labels \(T\), and \(g[S\setminus T]\) counts a second structure on the remaining labels. Summing over the choice of the first label set gives subset convolution:
\[ (f*g)[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]g[S\setminus T]. \]
Every label is assigned to exactly one of the two structures. Over all masks, the naive cost is \(\sum_S2^{|S|}=3^n\): each label is outside \(S\), in the first part, or in the second part.
Example. On \(\{0,1\}\), suppose \(f[\{0\}]=2\), \(f[\{1\}]=3\), \(g[\{0\}]=5\), \(g[\{1\}]=7\), with all other coefficients zero. Then \((f*g)[\{0,1\}]=2\cdot7+3\cdot5=29\). An ordinary size polynomial would also combine two structures using the same label, which is forbidden here.

title: 11 — Set Power Series
section: Ranked convolution and the overlap invariant
text:
Ranked convolution and the overlap invariant
The naive \(3^n\) is already better than brute force, but the transforms of Chapter 08 handle union convolution in \(O(n2^n)\) — they just do not enforce disjointness. The trick is to track cardinality alongside the union, and let arithmetic detect overlaps: if \(A \cup B = S\) and \(|A| + |B| = |S|\), then \(A\) and \(B\) must be disjoint.
Separate a series by cardinality before applying the subset zeta transform:
\[\widehat f_k[S]=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq S\\|A|=k}}f[A],
\qquad 0\le k\le n.\]
For each \(S\), multiply the rank polynomials and retain ranks \(0\) through \(n\):
\[H_k[S]=\sum_{i=0}^k\widehat f_i[S]\widehat g_{k-i}[S]
=\sum_{\substack{A,B\subseteq S\\|A|+|B|=k}}f[A]g[B].\]
These pairs may overlap. Now Möbius-invert each rank layer. For a fixed pair \((A,B)\), its contribution to inverted entry \(S\) is multiplied by
\[\sum_{A\cup B\subseteq T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}
=\begin{cases}1,&A\cup B=S,\\0,&A\cup B\ne S.\end{cases}\]
Indeed, every element of \(S\setminus(A\cup B)\) can be included or excluded, producing \((1-1)^{|S\setminus(A\cup B)|}\). Thus the inverted layer is
\[h_k[S]=\sum_{\substack{A\cup B=S\\|A|+|B|=k}}f[A]g[B].\]
Finally take \(k=|S|\). Since \(|A|+|B|=|A\cup B|+|A\cap B|\), this equality forces \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). Therefore \(h_{|S|}[S]=(f*g)[S]\).






WarningDo not clear intermediate overlap layers



Input layers above \(|S|\) are zero. Product layers above \(|S|\) can be necessary: Möbius inversion needs them to cancel overlaps. On \(U=\{0,1\}\), let \(f[\{0\}]=g[\{0\}]=1\). Then \(H_2[\{0\}]=H_2[U]=1\). Inversion subtracts the first from the second and correctly returns zero. Clearing \(H_2[\{0\}]\) prematurely creates a false disjoint pair on \(U\).


There are \(n+1\) zeta/inverse transforms, each costing \(O(n2^n)\) additions/subtractions, and \(O(n^2)\) rank products for each mask. The total is \(O(n^22^n)\) ring operations and \(O(n2^n)\) coefficient storage. A ring with subtraction suffices; factorials and field division play no role in this multiplication algorithm. OR convolution differs: it keeps overlap and does not enforce \(|A|+|B|=|S|\).

title: 11 — Set Power Series
text:
Functions of a set series
With a fast product in hand, we can run the whole exp/log story from Chapter 09 here — and this is where connected-component counting actually happens.
Let \(g[\varnothing]=0\). Any product of more than \(n\) copies of \(g\) must repeat a label, so \(g^{n+1}=0\). This property is nilpotence. It makes substitution into an infinite formal series finite.
When \(1,2,\ldots,n\) are units in \(R\), define
\[\exp(g)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{g^k}{k!},\qquad
\log(1+g)=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{k-1}\frac{g^k}{k}.\]
Over \(\mathbb F_p\), the sufficient local condition is \(p>n\). The usual finite formal identities show these operations are inverse. We will also derive partition recurrences that work without dividing by these integers.
What does \(g^k/k!\) count? A term of \(g^k[S]\) chooses an ordered list of \(k\) disjoint nonempty blocks covering \(S\), with weight equal to the product of their \(g\)-values. Each unordered partition has exactly \(k!\) orders, because its nonempty blocks have distinct label sets. Hence
\[[x^S]\exp(g)=\sum_{\pi\text{ a partition of }S}\prod_{B\in\pi}g[B].\]
The empty set has one partition with no blocks; its product is one. This finite partition sum makes sense over any commutative ring even when the displayed factorial quotients do not.
Three-label example. If \(g[B]=1\) for every nonempty \(B\), the contributions on three labels are one one-block partition, three two-block partitions, and one three-block partition. The answer is five. If singleton blocks have weight \(a\) and larger blocks have weight zero, the answer on any \(S\) is \(a^{|S|}\): only the singleton partition survives.

Connected objects and a division-free recurrence
Let \(A[S]\) count all objects on \(S\) and \(C[S]\) count connected ones. Assume every object has a unique partition into nonempty connected components, and the allowed choices and weights factor across that partition. Then \(A=\exp(C)\), so \(C=\log(A)\) where the quotient formulas are legal.
For a formula valid over any coefficient ring, choose the least label \(v\in S\). Its component has one uniquely determined label set \(T\) containing \(v\). Therefore
\[A[S]=\sum_{\substack{T\subseteq S\\v\in T}}C[T]A[S\setminus T],
\qquad
C[S]=A[S]-\sum_{\substack{T\subsetneq S\\v\in T}}C[T]A[S\setminus T].\]
Use \(A[\varnothing]=1\) and process nonempty masks by increasing size. The second formula isolates the term \(T=S\). Each object appears once because its component containing \(v\) is unique. Enumerating these transitions costs \(O(3^n)\) operations and \(O(2^n)\) storage.
Graph example. For all simple graphs on a fixed vertex subset, \(A[S]=2^{\binom{|S|}{2}}\). Two vertices have \(A=2\), so \(C=2-1=1\). Three vertices have \(A=8\): subtract the all-singleton graph and three graphs with a connected pair plus an isolated vertex, leaving \(C=8-1-3=4\). They are the three paths and the triangle.

title: 11 — Set Power Series
section: Fast exp, inverse, and log without factorial division
text:
Fast exp, inverse, and log without factorial division
The special relation \(x_i^2=0\) supplies a short recurrence. Split off one label, writing a series as \(f=f_0+x_{n-1}f_1\), where both parts use only the other \(n-1\) labels. The coefficient \(f_1[S]\) equals the old coefficient at \(S\cup\{n-1\}\).
For \(g[\varnothing]=0\), let \(E_0\) be its partition exponential on the smaller universe. The distinguished label belongs to exactly one component; choosing its other labels gives
\[E(g_0+x_{n-1}g_1)=E(g_0)+x_{n-1}\bigl(E(g_0)*g_1\bigr).\]
Compute \(E(g_0)\) recursively and perform one subset convolution. With the ranked multiplier the recurrence is \(T(n)=T(n-1)+O(n^22^n)\), giving \(T(n)=O(n^22^n)\). This operation equals the factorial exponential wherever that formula exists and supplies its combinatorial extension otherwise.
An ordinary multiplicative inverse requires only that \(f[\varnothing]\) be a unit. If \(u=f_0^{-1}\), direct multiplication and \(x_{n-1}^2=0\) give
\[f^{-1}=u-x_{n-1}(u*u*f_1).\]
This is another \(O(n^22^n)\) recursion. Finally, for \(A[\varnothing]=1\), connected extraction obeys
\[L(A_0+x_{n-1}A_1)=L(A_0)+x_{n-1}(A_0^{-1}*A_1).\]
This follows by inverting the exponential split: \(A_1=A_0*C_1\). Recompute smaller inverses if desired; the geometric sum of their \(O(k^22^k)\) costs is still \(O(n^22^n)\). The resulting \(L\) is the inverse of the partition exponential over any ring, and agrees with the displayed formal logarithm when its denominators are units. It is not permission to evaluate \(1/k\) in small characteristic.

title: 11 — Set Power Series
text:
Composition and power projection
For an ordinary polynomial \(F(z)=\sum_{k=0}^m a_kz^k\), substitution \(F(g)=\sum_{k=0}^{\min(m,n)}a_kg^k\) is defined whenever \(g[\varnothing]=0\). Successive subset multiplications give the explicit bound \(O(n^32^n)\) when \(m\le n\). More specialized composition algorithms improve this; do not infer their cost from a single convolution. For an EGF \(\sum F_kz^k/k!\), use unit factorials or interpret coefficients by the corresponding weighted partition sums.
Power projection reverses the question. Given weights \(w[S]\), compute
\[b_k=\sum_{S\subseteq U}w[S]\,[x^S]g^k\qquad(0\le k\le n).\]
For fixed \(g\), composition is a linear map from \((a_k)\) to the subset table. Its transpose maps \(w\) to \((b_k)\), because
\[\sum_S w[S]\,[x^S]F(g)=\sum_k a_kb_k.\]
This equality explains the word “transpose” without an extra combinatorial assumption. Computing successive powers gives the same \(O(n^32^n)\) baseline. A transposed implementation of a faster linear composition circuit can share its asymptotic operation count; that is an additional library contract, not an unexplained property of the basic multiplier.

title: 11 — Set Power Series
text:
Contest translation: coloured bipartite graphs
For Lights Out on Connected Graph, ARC105 F, assign a bit \(s_v\) to whether vertex \(v\) is flipped an odd number of times. An edge \(uv\) becomes blue exactly when \(s_u+s_v=1\) in \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus the retained graph must be bipartite, and the problem asks for connected bipartite spanning subgraphs.
The count easier to obtain is coloured bipartite subgraphs. For every vertex set \(S\) and every colour class \(T\subseteq S\), choose any subset of original edges crossing \(T,S\setminus T\). If \(e(T,S\setminus T)\) is their number, set
\[A[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}2^{e(T,S\setminus T)}.\]
Each summand counts graphs with that particular two-colouring. A bipartite graph with \(k\) components has \(2^k\) colourings, including a factor two for an isolated vertex. Therefore \(C=L(A)\) counts connected graphs with a colouring, and the answer for nonempty \(U\) is \(C[U]/2\). The modulus \(998244353\) makes two a unit. Summing first and dividing all \(A[S]\) by two would be wrong for disconnected graphs.
For the official limit \(n\le17\), a practical baseline uses \(O(3^n)\) cut terms and the distinguished-component recurrence; ranked multiplication can accelerate the latter. Precompute induced-edge counts \(e(S)\) so crossing counts are \(e(S)-e(T)-e(S\setminus T)\). The partition coefficient is maintained exactly throughout, rather than deduplicating colourings afterward.

title: 11 — Set Power Series
text:
Problem-solving checklist

Must the two objects use disjoint labels, or is overlap allowed?
What does the empty-set coefficient mean?
Are components uniquely determined and weights multiplicative?
Are you counting uncoloured objects, coloured objects, or objects with an extra mark?
Are divisions legal, or should you use the distinguished-component recurrence?
Have intermediate product ranks survived until Möbius inversion?

title: 11 — Set Power Series
text:
Exercises with hints and solutions

Partition check. Give weight two to a singleton and weight three to a pair. What is the partition exponential on two labels?
Hint: list partitions. Solution: the singleton partition contributes \(2\cdot2=4\) and the one-block partition contributes 3, so the answer is 7.
Characteristic trap. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), let \(g=x_0+x_1\). Why is “compute \(g^2/2\)” invalid, and what is the partition exponential’s two-label coefficient?
Hint: ordered and unordered partitions are different computations. Solution: \(g^2=2x_0x_1=0\), and two has no inverse. The unique partition into two singleton blocks still has weight one, so the division-free answer is one.
Connected extraction. How many connected simple graphs exist on three labelled vertices?
Hint: subtract component partitions from eight. Solution: one empty graph and three single-edge graphs are disconnected, giving four. This also checks the earlier recurrence.
Coloured failure. For a two-vertex graph with one possible edge, compute \(A\) and \(C\) for the coloured bipartite model.
Hint: the empty graph has four colourings. Solution: \(A[U]=4+2=6\), each singleton has \(A=2\), and \(C[U]=6-2\cdot2=2\). Dividing \(C[U]\) by two yields the unique connected graph. Dividing \(A[U]\) by two instead yields three, not the two uncoloured graphs.
Projection model. If \(g\) has coefficient one on singletons and zero elsewhere, and \(w\) selects the full universe, determine every \(b_k\).
Hint: count ordered singleton blocks. Solution: only \(k=n\) can cover \(U\); its coefficient is \(n!\). Hence \(b_n=n!\) and the other \(b_k\) vanish, with the arithmetic interpreted in the coefficient ring.

For a sustained modelling exercise, attempt ARC105 F before reading the reduction above. Chapter 20 supplies a synthesis check on the complete four-vertex graph.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Read Bézout and units and polynomials. Bernoulli preprocessing also uses formal power series; interpolation does not.
You should finish able to prove degree bounds, evaluate huge polynomial sums, count lattice points without enumeration, and convert rational and quadratic constraints into integer recurrences. Symbols \(n, d\) are nonnegative integers unless stated otherwise, and inequalities concern ordered integers, never residues.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
1. Polynomial interpolation
Over a field \(K\), a polynomial of degree at most \(d\) is determined by its values at \(d+1\) distinct points: if two such polynomials agreed there, their difference would have more roots than its degree, so it is zero. That is the entire reason huge-index polynomial sums are cheap — the infinite function is really \(d+1\) numbers.
Lagrange interpolation writes the polynomial down:
\[P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{d} y_i\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-x_j}{x_i-x_j}.\]
The factor for index \(i\) is \(1\) at \(x_i\) and \(0\) at all other samples, so the sum assigns the requested value at each point. At arbitrary points this costs \(O(d^2)\) for one query. When \(x_i=i\), prefix/suffix products and factorials reduce one query to \(O(d)\) after \(O(d)\) preprocessing:
\[\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{x-j}{i-j}
=\frac{\prod_{j<i}(x-j)\prod_{j>i}(x-j)}{i!(-1)^{d-i}(d-i)!}.\]
Preconditions are not cosmetic: sample points must be distinct and their differences invertible. In \(\mathbb F_p\), the points \(0,\ldots,d\) therefore require \(d<p\). For many arbitrary queries use a product tree and multipoint evaluation.
The unit-difference condition also licenses interpolation over a commutative ring, but the field root-bound proof does not: \(x^2-1\) has four roots \(1,3,5,7\) modulo 8. Over a field, the root bound follows by dividing out one factor \((x-a)\) for each distinct root.






NoteExample: reconstructing a quadratic



Suppose \(P(0)=1,P(1)=2,P(2)=5\) and \(\deg P\le2\) over \(\mathbb Q\). At \(x=4\), the Lagrange basis values are \(3,-8,6\), so \(P(4)=3-16+30=17\). The polynomial is \(x^2+1\). Without the degree bound, adding \(x(x-1)(x-2)\) preserves all three samples but changes the answer.


For consecutive evaluation, prefix product \(L_i=\prod_{0\le j<i}(x-j)\) and suffix product \(R_i=\prod_{i<j\le d}(x-j)\) omit exactly the forbidden factor. Multiply \(y_iL_iR_i\) by inverse factorials and \((-1)^{d-i}\). If \(x\) equals a sample point, return that sample directly. For \(d<p\), reduce a huge integer query modulo \(p\) only after proving the desired function is represented by this polynomial.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
2. Finite differences and polynomial sums
Define \(\Delta P(x)=P(x+1)-P(x)\) over any coefficient ring. It is the discrete analogue of a derivative: the leading \(x^d\) terms cancel, so the degree drops by at least one. It drops by exactly one when the leading coefficient times \(d\) is nonzero; this can fail in small characteristic, as \(\Delta(x^p)=1\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). When \(1,\ldots,d\) are units, repeated differences give the Newton expansion
\[P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d} \Delta^k P(0){x\choose k}.\]
For example, \(\Delta(x^2)=2x+1\) and \(\Delta^2(x^2)=2\). This Newton basis is ideal when values are consecutive or arguments shift repeatedly. Over a characteristic-zero field (more generally a \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra), or when \(1,\ldots,d+1\) are units in the coefficient ring, it also proves that if \(P\) has degree \(d\), then
\[S(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}P(i)\]
has degree \(d+1\), because \(\Delta S=P\) and its leading coefficient is the leading coefficient of \(P\) divided by \(d+1\). Therefore evaluate \(S(0),\ldots,S(d+1)\) directly and interpolate at huge \(n\). More generally, the needed condition is that all denominators in this Newton/interpolation basis are units. In small characteristic, \(S\) may not be representable by a polynomial of the expected degree, so the ordinary consecutive-point method is not licensed.
Here is the basis derivation. When \(1,\ldots,d\) are units, define \(\binom{x}{k}=x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)/k!\). Pascal’s identity gives \(\Delta\binom{x}{k}=\binom{x}{k-1}\) for \(k\ge1\). These polynomials have distinct degrees and unit leading coefficients and therefore form a basis through degree \(d\). In \(P=\sum_k a_k\binom{x}{k}\), apply \(\Delta^j\) and set \(x=0\): only \(a_j\) survives. Thus \(a_j=\Delta^jP(0)\). Summation is then telescoping:
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\binom{i}{k}
=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left(\binom{i+1}{k+1}-\binom{i}{k+1}\right)
=\binom{n}{k+1}.\]
For \(P(x)=x^2\), the difference coefficients are \(0,1,2\); hence \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^2=\binom n2+2\binom n3=n(n-1)(2n-1)/6\). At \(n=4\), this is \(1+4+9=14\). The identity is exact over integers, but evaluating it modulo 2 or 3 needs integer cancellation, not division by 6.
Recognition signal: a fixed exponent or degree, an enormous upper bound, and a modular answer. Do not interpolate when the degree depends on \(n\), or when the sample denominators vanish modulo the chosen prime.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
3. Floor sum via Euclidean descent
Define
\[F(n,m,a,b)=\sum_{0\le i<n}\left\lfloor\frac{ai+b}{m}\right\rfloor,\]
with nonnegative inputs and \(m>0\). Geometrically this counts the lattice points under a line of rational slope, and the whole algorithm is one idea: strip the part of the line you can sum in closed form, then swap the axes. Swapping turns the slope into its reciprocal, which is exactly the step of the Euclidean algorithm — hence \(O(\log m)\) iterations.
First strip quotient parts. Writing \(a=q_am+a'\) and \(b=q_bm+b'\) separates full multiples of \(m\), whose floors are ordinary arithmetic progressions:
\[a=q_am+a',\quad b=q_bm+b'.\]
Exactly,
\[
F(n,m,a,b)=q_a\frac{n(n-1)}2+q_bn+F(n,m,a',b').
\]
Now consider the normalized remainder with \(0\le a,b<m\). The sum counts lattice points \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i<n\) and \(1\le j\le(ai+b)/m\). Let \(y=an+b\), the numerator one step beyond the final \(i\); this is the boundary used by the half-open rectangle. If \(y<m\), no point reaches the first horizontal level and the remainder is zero. Otherwise \(a>0\); put \(q=\lfloor y/m\rfloor\) and \(r=y\bmod m\). On horizontal row \(1\le j\le q\), substitute \(t=n-i\) in \(jm\le ai+b=y-at\); the number of points on that row is \(\lfloor((q-j)m+r)/a\rfloor\). Summing and reindexing \(q-j=0,\ldots,q-1\) swaps the axes and yields
\[F(n,m,a,b)=F(\lfloor y/m\rfloor,a,m,y\bmod m)\]
after the parameter update \((n,m,a,b)\leftarrow(\lfloor y/m\rfloor,a,m,y\bmod m)\). Normalize again at the start of the next iteration: the new numerator coefficient is the old modulus and may be at least the new denominator. For example, \(F(4,7,3,2)=0+0+1+1=2\), and the update gives \(F(2,3,7,0)\); stripping \(7=2\cdot3+1\) gives \(2+F(2,3,1,0)=2\). This is the Euclidean algorithm geometrically, so there are \(O(\log m)\) iterations.
The horizontal count is between zero and \(n\): for \(j\ge1\), \(y-jm<an\) because \(b<m\). A top row may be empty; for \(F(1,2,1,1)\), \(y=2\) but the only actual floor is zero. The empty row makes the half-open update uniform. Maintain original answer = accumulated stripped terms + current F. Both normalization and axis swap preserve this invariant. Stop on \(n=0\), or after normalization when \(an+b<m\); if \(a=0\), the latter holds automatically. The logarithmic bound counts arithmetic operations.
Use __int128 when its range covers the proven product bounds. For negative \(a\) or \(b\), use mathematical floor division to normalize them; C++ truncation is not floor division. A library routine can have overflow semantics different from exact mathematics; the AtCoder contract returns modulo \(2^{64}\) on overflow.
Applications include counting lattice points, sums of residues, Beatty sequences, and recursively counting points constrained by rational lines.
The residue sum follows from \(u=m\lfloor u/m\rfloor+(u\bmod m)\):
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(ai+b)\bmod m
=a\frac{n(n-1)}2+bn-mF(n,m,a,b).\]
For \((4,7,3,2)\) the residues \(2,5,1,4\) sum to \(12=18+8-14\). For \((n,m,a,b)=(3,5,-1,0)\) the floors are \(0,-1,-1\) and residues \(0,4,3\). Truncating division toward zero breaks this normalization.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
4. Continued fractions
The same Euclidean descent, read as approximation rather than as counting: each quotient tells you how far you can go along one direction before the best rational approximation of a real number changes.
Euclid’s quotients form the finite simple continued fraction of a positive rational number, and the same process gives an infinite expansion for an irrational number \(\alpha\):
\[\alpha=[a_0;a_1,\ldots].\]
This means \(a_0+1/(a_1+1/(a_2+\cdots))\), with \(a_0=\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\) and subsequent \(a_i\) positive integers. Invert the fractional part repeatedly to find the quotients. For rationals, stop at an integer; choose the final coefficient greater than one unless there is only one coefficient. A finite truncation is a convergent. For example, \(13/5=[2;1,1,2]\).
Convergents satisfy
\[P_i=a_iP_{i-1}+P_{i-2},\qquad Q_i=a_iQ_{i-1}+Q_{i-2},\]
starting with \((P[-2],P[-1])=(0,1)\) and \((Q[-2],Q[-1])=(1,0)\). Substitution in the nested fractions proves these recurrences. They give \(2/1,3/1,5/2,13/5\) for the example. The determinant \(D_i=P_iQ_{i-1}-P_{i-1}Q_i\) obeys \(D_i=-D_{i-1}\), so \(D_i=\pm1\); in particular every convergent is reduced. For the tail \(t=[a_{i+1};a_{i+2},\ldots]>1\),
\[\alpha=\frac{tP_i+P_{i-1}}{tQ_i+Q_{i-1}},\qquad
\left|\alpha-\frac{P_i}{Q_i}\right|
=\frac1{Q_i(tQ_i+Q_{i-1})}.\]
This explains alternating sides and rapidly decreasing errors. The adjacent determinant also makes these integer vectors a basis of \(\mathbb Z^2\); expressing a competing \((p,q)\) in this basis is the mechanism behind the best-approximation theorem below. Its specified error measure is essential. For an irrational \(\alpha\), its convergents are best approximations of the second kind: no fraction \(p/q\) with \(0<q<Q_i\) has a smaller value of \(|q\alpha-p|\) than \(|Q_i\alpha-P_i|\). (For a rational input, the final convergent is the number itself.) The recurrence is just the record of successive Euclidean quotients, so it also supplies the Bezout-like identity below. For other bounded-denominator objectives, the optimum may be a convergent or an intermediate (semiconvergent), so derive the relevant comparison rather than citing “best approximation” without a definition. Adjacent convergents obey \(P_iQ_{i-1}-P_{i-1}Q_i=\pm1\), a built-in error check.
Use continued fractions for rational approximation, modular inequalities, and Pell equations. Intermediate fractions replace the next quotient by \(1\le t\le a_i\): \((tP_{i-1}+P_{i-2})/(tQ_{i-1}+Q_{i-2})\). For approximating \(13/5\) with denominator at most 3 in absolute error, \(8/3\) beats the convergent \(5/2\), since \(1/15<1/10\). An optimum need not be a convergent. Rational Euclid takes logarithmically many arithmetic steps. Compare by exact cross products with a proved width bound or big integers; 128 bits do not cover arbitrary input lengths.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
5. Pell equations
Pell equations are how contests hide exponentially growing answers behind tiny input. Solutions are not found by search; they are generated, by repeatedly multiplying one fundamental solution.
For nonsquare \(D>0\), Pell’s equation is
\[x^{2}-Dy^{2}=1.\]
The continued fraction of \(\sqrt D\) is periodic. The first convergent satisfying the equation gives the fundamental solution \((x_1,y_1)\) with \(x_1,y_1>0\). Multiplication of numbers \(x+y\sqrt D\) preserves \(x^2-Dy^2\), proving powers remain solutions. The stronger theorem is that every solution with \(x>0,y>0\) follows from
\[(x_k+y_k\sqrt D)=(x_1+y_1\sqrt D)^{k},\]
or the recurrence
\[x'=x_1x+Dy_1y,\qquad y'=x_1y+y_1x.\]
The converse needs descent. Write \(\varepsilon=x_1+y_1\sqrt D>1\) for the least positive norm-one unit. Given another \(u=x+y\sqrt D>1\), choose \(k\) with \(1\le v=u\varepsilon^{-k}<\varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon^{-1}=x_1-y_1\sqrt D\), \(v\) still has integer coefficients and norm one. They are \((v+v^{-1})/2>0\) and \((v-v^{-1})/(2\sqrt D)\ge0\). Unless \(v=1\), this contradicts minimality of \(\varepsilon\). Thus \(u=\varepsilon^k\); norm preservation alone would not establish completeness.
For \(D=2\), \([1;2,2,\ldots]\) gives fundamental pair \((3,2)\), then \((17,12)\) and \((99,70)\). Searching convergents suffices because a Pell solution satisfies \(|x/y-\sqrt D|=1/(y^2(x/y+\sqrt D))<1/(2y^2)\), and the continued-fraction approximation criterion says a reduced fraction this close must be a convergent. Periodicity and existence of a solution are classical quadratic-surd theorems, separate from the power-generation argument. The integer expansion maintains \((\sqrt D+m)/d\) with \(d\mid D-m^2\):
\[m'=da-m,\quad d'=(D-m'^2)/d,\quad
a'=\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor\sqrt D\rfloor+m'}{d'}\right\rfloor.\]
Start with \(m=0,d=1,a=\lfloor\sqrt D\rfloor\). Bounded reduced surd states yield periodicity. This avoids cumulative floating-point error; the number of convergents is not uniformly \(O(\log D)\), and the fundamental solution may have many more bits than \(D\).
For \(x^{2}-Dy^{2}=N\), existence and seed generation are subtler; do not assume the \(N=1\) theorem transfers unchanged. Contest tasks often bound the search enough to find seeds and then advance each orbit by the fundamental unit.
Values grow exponentially. Use big integers or stop with division-based overflow checks before multiplication.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
section: 6. Linear Diophantine equations and CRT viewpoint
text:
6. Linear Diophantine equations and CRT viewpoint
For \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), the equation \(ax+by=c\) has an integer solution iff \(g=\gcd(a,b)\) divides \(c\): the left side is always a multiple of \(g\), and Bézout constructs one whenever that necessary condition holds. Extended Euclid finds \(u,v\) with \(au+bv=g\); scale by \(c/g\). All solutions are
\[x=x_0+k\frac bg,\qquad y=y_0-k\frac ag.\]
To prove completeness, subtract solutions: \(a\Delta x=-b\Delta y\). For nonzero coefficients, coprimality of \(a/g,b/g\) implies \(b/g\) divides \(\Delta x\), and substitution determines \(\Delta y\). If one coefficient is zero, its nonzero partner fixes one variable and the other is free, consistently with the formula. Here \(g>0\) and \(k\) ranges over all integers.
If \(a=b=0\), all integer pairs solve the equation when \(c=0\), and none solve when \(c\ne0\); keep that degenerate case outside an extended-gcd routine.
Intersect this parameterization with sign or interval constraints using correct floor/ceiling division. A congruence \(ax\equiv c\pmod m\) is the same equation \(ax+my=c\); after dividing by \(\gcd(a,m)\), invert in the reduced modulus.
For \(6x+9y=30\), take \((x_0,y_0)=(2,2)\) to obtain \(x=2+3k,y=2-2k\). Nonnegativity requires \(\lceil-2/3\rceil\le k\le1\), yielding \((2,2),(5,0)\). A linear objective becomes linear in \(k\), so its minimum on a bounded feasible interval is at an endpoint; zero slope makes all points tie. Check separately whether the feasible interval is empty or unbounded.
For nonlinear-looking determinant constraints such as \(ad-bc=k\), fixing two variables often reduces the rest to Bézout. For quadratic forms, factorization, modular obstructions, descent, or Pell reduction may apply.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
7. Stern–Brocot and modular extrema
Start with boundaries \(a/b=0/1\) and \(c/d=1/0\), the latter denoting infinity. Their mediant is \((a+c)/(b+d)\). Boundaries maintain \(bc-ad=1\), so the mediant is reduced and lies strictly between them. For a target in this interval, replace the lower or upper boundary by the mediant according to its side. The determinant invariant is preserved. To see that every positive reduced \(p/q\) is reached, write it uniquely as \((ua+vc)/(ub+vd)\) with positive integers \(u,v\) while it is strictly between the boundaries. Comparing with the mediant subtracts the smaller of \(u,v\) from the larger. Euclid eventually gives \(u=v=1\). The strict interval choices also prove uniqueness: this is the Stern–Brocot tree.
Repeated same-side updates can be batched: replacing the lower bound \(t\) times gives \((a+tc)/(b+td)\). Solve the exact denominator and target inequalities for the largest legal integer \(t\), observing whether the target bound is strict. The run lengths relate to continued-fraction quotients, with initial/final adjustments depending on the sentinel and endpoint conventions. Use the inequalities as the contract, not a memorized unqualified run sequence.
Functions such as \(\min_{0\le i<n} (ai+b) \bmod m\) use the same Euclidean geometry as floor_sum: quotient away full multiples, then swap axes after the first wrap. Keep half-open interval conventions consistent.
An alternative derived contract avoids a new recursive template. For a proposed threshold \(0\le t<m\), write \(ai+b=qm+r\) with \(0\le r<m\). Then
\[[r<t]=1+\left\lfloor\frac{ai+b}{m}\right\rfloor
-\left\lfloor\frac{ai+b+m-t}{m}\right\rfloor.\]
Thus the count below \(t\) is \(n+F(n,m,a,b)-F(n,m,a,b+m-t)\). For \(n>0\), binary-search the first \(t\in[1,m]\) whose count is positive and return \(t-1\). This costs \(O(\log^2m)\) arithmetic operations. Direct Euclidean minimum algorithms can remove a logarithm, but need their own interval invariant. For \(n=0\) there is no minimum.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
8. Bernoulli numbers and Faulhaber sums
Section 2 computed one power sum at one degree. If a problem needs the closed form for many degrees, there is a single generating function that produces them all at once.
Bernoulli numbers are defined by
\[\frac{x}{e^{x}-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}B_k\frac{x^{k}}{k!}.\]
With the convention \(i^0=1\) even at \(i=0\), they give for \(d\ge0\)
\[\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^{d}=\frac1{d+1}\sum_{j=0}^{d}{d+1\choose j}B_j n^{d+1-j}.\]
To derive the formula, count the exponential weight of each summand:
\[\sum_{d\ge0}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i^d\right)\frac{x^d}{d!}
=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}e^{ix}
=\frac{e^{nx}-1}{e^x-1}
=\frac{e^{nx}-1}{x}\frac{x}{e^x-1}.\]
The coefficient of \(x^d\), multiplied by \(d!\), chooses degree \(j\) from the Bernoulli factor and degree \(d-j\) from the other factor; this yields the displayed binomial coefficient. The proof is over \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\), or truncated over a ring where the denominators through \(d+1\) are units. The first terms are \(B_0=1,B_1=-1/2,B_2=1/6\), giving sums \(n\), \(n(n-1)/2\), and \(n(n-1)(2n-1)/6\). The formal quotient \(x/(e^x-1)\) means the inverse of \((e^x-1)/x\), whose constant term is 1; it is not inversion of a zero-constant series. To obtain degree \(d\), form the exponential through degree \(d+1\).
This computes all power-sum formulas through one FPS inversion and factorial scaling. Check the \(B_1\) sign convention and require all denominators through \(d+1\) to be invertible. For one degree and one query, consecutive-point interpolation is often simpler; Bernoulli preprocessing wins for many degrees.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
9. Pitfalls

C++ % and / on negatives do not implement Euclidean remainder/floor division.
Lagrange denominators vanish if the interpolation degree reaches the modulus.
Inferring “it is polynomial” from samples is not a proof; establish a degree bound.
\(a*n+b\) can overflow before the floor sum shrinks it.
Pell recurrences need all seed orbits for generalized equations.
Extended-GCD coefficients may overflow even if the final normalized answer fits.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
10. Practice, in order

Advanced — The Sum of the k-th Powers, CF 622F. Consecutive-point interpolation.


Hints


The prefix sum is a polynomial in \(n\) of degree \(k+1\).
Evaluate it at \(0,\ldots,k+1\) directly.
Use prefix/suffix Lagrange products for one huge query.


Advanced — S = 1, AtCoder ABC340 F. Bézout and determinant construction.


Hints


Rewrite the required area as an equation of the form \(Xb-Ya=±2\).
Check the gcd divisibility condition.
Scale extended-Euclid coefficients and map signs carefully.


Mastery — Cowmpany Cowmpensation, CF 995F. Tree DP whose answer is polynomial.


Hints


First solve for small color bounds with a tree DP.
Prove each subtree’s count is a polynomial and bound its degree by subtree size.
Evaluate enough consecutive points, then interpolate at \(D\).


Mastery — Sum of Min of Mod of Linear, AtCoder ARC182 E. Floor sums inside a modular-minimum decomposition. Official English editorial.


Hints


Sort and deduplicate the offsets; compare every candidate with the smallest offset.
The active minimum changes exactly when \((Ck+A_i) \bmod M\) wraps.
Counts of wraps and sums of one linear residue sequence are differences of floor_sum calls.

title: 13 — Discrete Sums and Diophantine Tools
text:
Exercises with solutions

1. Concept check: polynomiality before interpolation
Compute \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(i^2+1)\) as a polynomial and evaluate at \(n=4\). Why do four sampled values suffice? Hint: summation raises the degree by one over \(\mathbb Q\).






NoteSolution





The answer is \(n+n(n-1)(2n-1)/6\), degree three, and its value at 4 is 18. The degree proof licenses four samples; four samples alone do not prove the function is cubic. Modulo a prime \(p>3\), these rational coefficients and the four consecutive sample differences are valid units. For smaller moduli, evaluate the integer formula by exact cancellation or use a different basis.





2. Application: a residue threshold
Among \(i=0,1,2,3\), how many residues \((3i+2)\bmod7\) are below 3? Derive the general threshold count rather than enumerate a large \(n\). Hint: compare floors before and after adding \(m-t\).






NoteSolution





The residues \(2,5,1,4\) give two. The general formula is \(n+F(n,m,a,b)-F(n,m,a,b+m-t)\); here it is \(4+2-4=2\). For \(t=0\) it gives zero, and for \(t=m\) it gives \(n\), checking both boundaries. Two floor sums cost \(O(\log m)\) arithmetic operations, even for negative \(a,b\) after mathematical floor normalization.





3. Advanced: an interval Diophantine optimum
Find nonnegative integers satisfying \(6x+9y=30\) that minimize \(2x+5y\). Hint: optimize the single integer parameter, not both original variables.






NoteSolution





\(x=2+3k,y=2-2k\), with \(k=0,1\). The objective is \(14-4k\), so choose \(k=1\) and obtain \((5,0)\) with cost 10. Extended Euclid and interval intersection cost \(O(\log\max(|a|,|b|))\) arithmetic steps in the general case. Verify the original equation and bounds after mapping coordinates.





4. Synthesis: square triangular numbers
Find the first three positive integers that are both a square and a triangular number, where the \(n\)th triangular number is \(n(n+1)/2\). Hint: complete the square in \(n(n+1)=2m^2\).






NoteSolution





Multiply by 4 and add 1: \((2n+1)^2-8m^2=1\). The fundamental solution for \(D=8\) is \((x,m)=(3,1)\), and multiplying by \(3+\sqrt8\) produces \((17,6),(99,35)\). Thus \(n=(x-1)/2\) is \(1,8,49\), and the numbers are \(1,36,1225\). All generated \(x\) stay odd. Conversely every positive solution of the original problem gives a positive Pell solution, so the fundamental-unit descent proves completeness. Enumerating \(n\) up to the largest answer ignores the exponentially spaced structure; generate units with big integers instead.

title: 15 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
Every chapter so far handed you the topic in its title. That is the one luxury a real contest never gives. A World Finals statement is about tiles, tokens, or roads; it never says “use a formal logarithm here” or “invert this over the divisor poset”. By the time you recognize the technique, the hard part is already done.
So this chapter contains no new mathematics. It trains the missing step: turning a story into a precise mathematical object, and continuing to sharpen that object until one of the earlier chapters becomes unavoidable. “Sum a function over all pairs” becomes a written sum over \((i,j)\) — and only then does grouping by \(\gcd(i,j)\) suggest Möbius inversion. “Count drawings up to relabelling” becomes a named group acting on a named set — and only then does Burnside apply. That intermediate model is the thing worth practising.
A capstone attempt should therefore begin without opening the topic tags in this repository, and the model should be written down and argued over as a team before anyone starts coding.

title: 15 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
Prerequisites and learning objectives
Complete the relevant branches of the learning path: modular algebra, divisor identities, symmetry, polynomials, FPS, transforms, and discrete sums. This is a synthesis workshop, so its structure is a sequence of attempts and editorial arguments. The objective is to produce a model, a complete reduction, a complexity bound, and an independent small oracle without being told the technique first. Existing chapter problems are intentionally revisited.
For an untagged attempt, use only this statement list and stop reading the chapter until your scheduled hint time: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The circuit below is instructor guidance and deliberately exposes prerequisites.

title: 15 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
Recognition protocol
Before coding, write answers to these questions. A good answer is a sentence or equation which could be checked on a three-element example, not a technique name such as “probably NTT.”

What is the mathematical object: residue class, multiplicative function, polynomial/FPS, labelled class, group action, linear operator, random variable, or lattice sum?
Which operation is expensive: pairwise product, convolution, coefficient extraction, repeated transition, divisor sum, or enumeration of symmetric copies?
Which change of basis makes that operation pointwise or triangular?
What is the coefficient ring, and which divisions/roots actually exist?
What brute-force oracle can test the first 20–100 cases?

The ordered set below revisits a few chapter problems in a deliberately tag-free setting and adds one synthesis problem. Treat each as a 3–5 hour team session, not a normal single-person rating drill. Before reading a hint, insist on a proposed invariant: “this table stores …,” “this coefficient counts …,” or “these two configurations are equivalent because ….”

title: 15 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
Timed-attempt rules

Do not inspect tags, hints, or editorials for the first 90 minutes.
At 90 minutes, compare the three best models you considered. For each, say exactly which object it counts and why it is insufficient or promising. Open only Hint 1 if none gives the target complexity.
At 150 minutes, open Hint 2 and require a written derivation before coding.
At 210 minutes, open Hint 3. Stop after five hours and study the official analysis; continuing an unproductive implementation is not endurance training.
Re-solve from a blank file six weeks later. A remembered code template does not count unless you can re-derive its contract.

title: 15 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
Worked miniature: models before machinery
Count triples of nonnegative integers \((x,y,z)\) with \(x+y+z=N\) and \(x\) even. For \(N=3\), the possible \(x\) values 0 and 2 contribute 4 and 2 pairs, giving 6. A direct model is \(\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}(N-2j+1)\). Writing \(h=\lfloor N/2\rfloor\), this equals \((h+1)(N+1-h)\) in \(O(1)\) integer arithmetic. A second model assigns weights \(t^{2j}\) to \(x\) and \(t^y,t^z\) to the others, obtaining \([t^N](1-t^2)^{-1}(1-t)^{-2}\). Both count the same objects, but the closed sum is cheaper for one query. Dividing the unrestricted count \(\binom{N+2}{2}\) by two fails at \(N=3\): it gives 5 instead of 6 because even and odd values of \(x\) do not have equal numbers of completions. Technique recognition includes deciding when an advanced tool is unnecessary.

title: 15 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
Capstone circuit

1. AtCoder AGC 047 C — Product Modulo (Mastery)

Statement · official editorial · English/Japanese
Prerequisites: cyclic multiplicative groups, primitive roots, convolution.
Why here: the hard step is recognizing that a group isomorphism turns a distribution of products into additive convolution.



Hint 1 — recognition

Pairs involving zero contribute zero; after separating them, nonzero residues modulo the fixed prime form a cyclic group.



Hint 2 — reduction

Map each nonzero value to its discrete-log index under a primitive root; multiplication becomes cyclic addition of indices.



Hint 3 — algorithm

Convolve the frequency array and fold indices modulo \(p-1\). Convert each exponent back to its residue, then correct ordered-pair and diagonal contributions to obtain the required unordered-pair sum.







NoteEditorial guidance: exact convolution and pair correction





Let \(g\) generate the nonzero residues modulo the statement’s prime \(p\). Build \(f_e=\#\{i:A_i=g^e\bmod p\}\) for \(0\le e<p-1\), excluding zeros. The ordinary integer convolution \(h=f*f\) counts ordered index pairs by exponent sum. Therefore the answer is
\[\frac12\left(\sum_{j=0}^{2p-4}h_j(g^{j\bmod(p-1)}\bmod p)
-\sum_i(A_i^2\bmod p)\right).\]
Every diagonal occurs once in the first sum; every pair of different indices occurs twice. Division by 2 is exact integer division: the final sum is not modulo \(p\). Coefficients can be as large as \(n^2\), so one convolution modulus need not recover them. Use an exact integer-convolution contract or sufficient CRT range and width for the final weighted sum. Time is \(O(p\log p+n)\) with a bounded number of transform primes, space \(O(p+n)\) or \(O(p)\) while streaming the diagonal sum. For the toy prime 7 and values \(2,3,0\), the only nonzero unordered product is 6. Reducing the final sum modulo the input prime or forgetting diagonal subtraction solves a different problem.





2. Codeforces 338D — GCD Table (Capstone)

Statement · official analysis · English/Russian
Prerequisites: LCM bounds, linear congruences, generalized CRT.
Why here: a local gcd pattern must first be converted into compatible global row/column congruences, then checked against construction bounds.



Hint 1

Choose a row divisible by every requested entry.



Hint 2

Each desired gcd imposes a congruence on the starting column modulo that entry.



Hint 3

Merge non-coprime congruences, then verify every gcd explicitly; CRT consistency alone is not the full proof.







NoteEditorial guidance: why the smallest row suffices





Index the desired entries by \(0\le t<k\) and set \(L=\operatorname{lcm}_t a_t\). Any feasible row \(r\) is divisible by \(L\), so reject when \(L>n\), stopping LCM multiplication before overflow. If \(r,j\) works, then \(a_t\mid L\) and \(L\mid r\) imply \(a_t\mid\gcd(L,j+t)\mid\gcd(r,j+t)=a_t\). Thus row \(L\) works at the same column.
The necessary congruences are \(j\equiv-t\pmod{a_t}\). Merge them by generalized CRT. The merged modulus is \(L\); choose its least positive representative \(j\) (residue zero means \(j=L\)). All larger representatives have the same gcds with \(L\) and worse width bounds. Check \(j+k-1\le m\) and every exact gcd; these checks are sufficient by construction. Compatible congruences alone can fail: desired entries \((2,1,3)\) yield \(L=6,j=4\), but the third gcd is \(\gcd(6,6)=6\), not 3. This also explains why choosing a larger multiple of \(L\) cannot repair it. Cost is \(O(k\log L)\) arithmetic steps with bounded intermediate integers, excluding bit-complexity factors.





3. Codeforces 1097F — Alex and a TV Show (Mastery)

Statement · official Hello 2019 editorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: divisor zeta/Möbius transforms and arithmetic over \(\mathbb F_2\).
Why here: it combines a non-obvious coordinate system with a representation chosen specifically for a million online operations.



Hint 1

Query parity suggests storing every multiset in a vector space over \(\mathbb F_2\).



Hint 2

Find a transform in which multiset union is addition and the pairwise-GCD product is pointwise multiplication.



Hint 3

Use divisor-incidence vectors packed into bitsets; derive the inverse coefficient needed to recover one exact value.







NoteEditorial guidance: transformed online multisets





Let \(M\) bound all values and \(c(v)\) be multiplicity parity. Store \(z(d)=\sum_{d\mid v}c(v)\) in \(\mathbb F_2\), the parity of divisible entries. Union becomes coordinatewise addition, hence bitwise XOR. For a pairwise-gcd product, \(d\mid\gcd(a,b)\) precisely when \(d\) divides both arguments, so its \(z(d)\) is the product of the two \(z(d)\) values, hence bitwise AND. A singleton \(v\) initializes bits at the divisors of \(v\).
Möbius inversion recovers one value: \(c(v)=\sum_{k\le M/v}\mu(k)z(kv)\) modulo 2. Thus precompute a bit mask containing \(kv\) for squarefree \(k\); query the parity of the popcount after AND with that mask. Each operation costs \(O(M/w)\) machine words in a dense bitset implementation, with \(O((n+M)M/w)\) words for mutable states and precomputed masks; \(w\) is the word width. All destination assignments must read the old source states, including aliasing inputs. For \(\{2,3\}\), divisible parities at 1,2,3 are \(0,1,1\); inversion gives \(c(1)=0+1+1=0\), illustrating why the first transformed bit is total parity, not multiplicity of 1.





4. Codeforces 438E — The Child and Binary Tree (Capstone)

Statement · GF/FPS derivation · English
Prerequisites: combinatorial decomposition, NTT, FPS inverse and square root.
Why here: the combinatorial equation is short; recognizing and safely computing its algebraic solution is the real test.



Hint 1

Write a generating function for the allowed root weights and decompose a tree at its root.



Hint 2

The two ordered child slots produce a quadratic functional equation.



Hint 3

Select the formal root with the correct constant term and evaluate it using FPS square root and inverse, truncated after every operation.







NoteEditorial guidance: the correct formal root





Let \(C(x)=\sum_{c\text{ allowed}}x^c\) and let \(T(x)\) count nonempty trees. Positive vertex weights give \(C(0)=T(0)=0\). Each root selects its weight and two ordered, possibly empty, child slots, giving \(T=C(1+T)^2\). Set \(F=1+T\). Then \(F=1+CF^2\) and rationalizing its quadratic solution gives
\[F=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1-4C}},\qquad \sqrt{1-4C}(0)=1.\]
The other square-root branch has the wrong constant term. This form avoids dividing by \(C\), a series with zero constant term. Over the problem’s field, 2 is invertible and the square root with constant 1 is uniquely liftable; the denominator has constant 2. Truncate modulo \(x^{m+1}\), then output positive coefficients of \(F\). With quasi-linear polynomial multiplication, Newton square root and inverse take \(O(\mathcal M(m))\) under the usual regularity assumption, or the safe \(O(\mathcal M(m)\log m)\) generic bound. For allowed weights 1 and 2, expanding the combinatorial equation gives \(T=x+3x^2+9x^3+\cdots\), an independent check before invoking FPS machinery.





5. Codeforces 995F — Cowmpany Cowmpensation (Capstone)

Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: tree counting, polynomial-valued DP, finite differences or interpolation.
Why here: it requires proving that a huge-domain answer is a low-degree polynomial before any fast evaluation is possible.



Hint 1

Parameterize a subtree by the largest label it may use.



Hint 2

Children multiply; adding the parent takes a prefix sum, so track how the polynomial degree changes.



Hint 3

Compute enough consecutive values and evaluate the resulting bounded-degree polynomial at the large argument.







NoteEditorial guidance: subtree degree is the resource





Let \(F_v(d)\) count legal salaries in \(v\)’s subtree, all at most \(d\). If \(v\) has salary \(t\), every child subtree has the bound \(t\). Therefore
\[F_v(d)=\sum_{t=1}^d\prod_{u\text{ child of }v}F_u(t),\quad F_v(0)=0.\]
A leaf has \(F_v(d)=d\). Inductively, the product degree is at most the sum of child subtree sizes, and finite summation raises it by one; hence degree at most \(|\text{subtree}(v)|\). Compute values for all \(d=0,\ldots,n\) in a postorder traversal, using pointwise products then prefix sums. This costs \(O(n^2)\) field operations and \(O(n^2)\) straightforward storage. Interpolate the root at \(D\) in \(O(n)\) with consecutive samples. The problem’s prime is greater than \(n\), so the factorial denominators are units. A root with two leaf children has \(F(d)=\sum_{t=1}^d t^2\), giving 5 at \(d=2\). The huge salary bound is a polynomial argument, not a DP dimension.





6. AtCoder ABC 284 Ex — Count Unlabeled Graphs (Capstone)

Statement · official editorial, JA
Prerequisites: Burnside, conjugacy classes of \(S_n\), integer partitions, induced permutation actions, surjective colorings.
Why here: applying Burnside is easy; compressing \(n!\) group elements and counting both vertex-color and edge orbits is the mastery step.



Hint 1

Model an object as a surjective \(K\)-coloring of labelled vertices together with an edge subset, acted on by relabeling vertices.



Hint 2

Group vertex permutations by cycle type rather than enumerating them.



Hint 3

For each vertex cycle type, fixed colorings are constant on vertex cycles and invariant edge sets are constant on pair cycles. Enforce that every color appears before averaging.







NoteEditorial guidance: two induced orbit counts





For a permutation with cycle lengths \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_c\), a fixed coloring assigns one of the \(K\) distinguished colors to each cycle and uses all colors. Its count is \(U(c,K)=\sum_{j=0}^K(-1)^j\binom Kj(K-j)^c\): each summand excludes a chosen set of missing colors, and a coloring missing \(r>0\) colors has total weight \((1-1)^r=0\). The convention \(0^0=1\) handles empty index sets.
For edges between two vertex cycles of lengths \(a,b\), a pair returns after \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\) steps, giving \(ab/\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=\gcd(a,b)\) orbits. Within a length-\(a\) cycle, circular distances \(1,\ldots,\lfloor a/2\rfloor\) give that many orbits. Thus
\[e(\lambda)=\sum_i\lfloor\lambda_i/2\rfloor
+\sum_{i<j}\gcd(\lambda_i,\lambda_j).\]
Each edge orbit is either wholly absent or present, giving \(2^{e(\lambda)}\). If \(m_j\) cycles have length \(j\), define \(z_\lambda=\prod_j j^{m_j}m_j!\). Burnside grouped by cycle type yields \(\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}U(c,K)2^{e(\lambda)}/z_\lambda\). The answer prime exceeds \(n\), licensing all denominators. Enumerating partitions and evaluating pair gcds costs \(O(p(n)n^2+nK)\) with surjection counts precomputed by their Stirling recurrence; \(p(n)\) is the partition count. For \(n=3,K=1\), types \(1+1+1,2+1,3\) contribute \(8/6,4/2,2/3\), totaling 4. For \(K=2\) the same sum is 12. Dividing labelled graphs by \(n!\) directly would ignore nontrivial stabilizers.





7. Codeforces 914G — Sum the Fibonacci (Capstone)

Statement · official tutorial · English/Russian
Prerequisites: ranked subset convolution and AND/OR/XOR transforms.
Why here: the expression must be separated into several distributions, each diagonalized by a different transform, then recombined without losing ordered multiplicities.



Hint 1

Replace indices by a frequency distribution over their bitmask values.



Hint 2

Construct the OR-with-disjointness, singleton, and XOR distributions separately.



Hint 3

Apply the appropriate transform to each stage, include the Fibonacci weights at the right time, and audit whether tuples are ordered.







NoteEditorial guidance: three weighted distributions





Let \(f[s]\) count input occurrences on \(B\) bits. Build \(A[u]=\sum_{x\mathbin{\vert}y=u,\ x\mathbin{\&}y=0}f[x]f[y]\) by ranked subset convolution, \(C[v]=f[v]\), and \(D[w]=\sum_{x\mathbin{\oplus}y=w}f[x]f[y]\) by XOR convolution. These describe the first pair, middle index, and final pair of the five-tuple. Indices may coincide: the statement imposes no distinctness correction.
Multiply each distribution at mask \(s\) by the ordinary Fibonacci number \(F_s\) modulo the answer prime. Now combine the three arrays by AND convolution, using superset zeta transforms, pointwise triple multiplication, and inverse superset transform. If the result is \(H\), answer \(\sum_{i=0}^{B-1}H[2^i]\): these and only these masks have one set bit. Fibonacci weights belong before the AND convolution because they depend on three separate masks, not only their final intersection. Complexity is \(O(B^2 2^B+n)\) time and \(O(B2^B)\) memory; the answer modulus is odd, so the XOR transform length \(2^B\) is a unit. For inputs 1 and 2, there are two disjoint ordered first pairs (OR 3), two unequal final pairs (XOR 3), and two middle choices, each contributing \(F_3^2F_1=4\) or \(F_3^2F_2=4\): total 32. Filtering repeated indices would erase valid terms.





8. Luogu P3768 — A Simple Math Problem (Capstone)

Statement, ZH · solution index, ZH, login required
Prerequisites: gcd extraction, totient identities, weighted summatory functions, Du Jiao recursion, quotient blocks.
Why here: several familiar identities must be composed before the desired summatory function even becomes visible.



Hint 1

Extract the gcd in the double sum and rewrite the coprime part with a totient identity.



Hint 2

Identify the weighted totient prefix that the quotient blocks require.



Hint 3

Derive a convolution recurrence for that prefix and evaluate polynomial block sums with explicitly licensed denominators.







NoteEditorial guidance: weighted totient summation





Use \(g=\sum_{d\mid g}\varphi(d)\) inside the desired double sum. Interchange finite sums and write multiples as \(i=da,j=db\):
\[\sum_{i,j\le n}ij\gcd(i,j)
=\sum_{d\le n}d^2\varphi(d)
\left(\sum_{a\le\lfloor n/d\rfloor}a\right)^2.\]
Thus quotient blocks need \(S(x)=\sum_{d\le x}d^2\varphi(d)\). Let \(f(d)=d^2\varphi(d)\) and \(g(d)=d^2\). Their Dirichlet convolution is \((f*g)(m)=m^2\sum_{d\mid m}\varphi(d)=m^3\). Summing through \(x\) gives
\[S(x)=\left(\frac{x(x+1)}2\right)^2
-\sum_{l=2}^x l^2 S(\lfloor x/l\rfloor).\]
Group equal quotients and use exact square-sum differences for each block’s coefficient. Precompute \(S\) through a cutoff \(T\), memoize larger quotient arguments, and use the summatory-sieve chapter’s bound \(O(T+n/\sqrt T)\) arithmetic operations for \(T\ge\sqrt n\), giving \(O(n^{2/3})\) at \(T\asymp n^{2/3}\); memory includes \(O(T)\) prefix storage. The outer quotient sum costs \(O(\sqrt n)\) lookups after recursion. Here the official statement specifies a prime greater than \(5\cdot10^8\), so 2 and 6 are units; in a generalized composite-modulus version, cancel integer factors before reduction. At \(n=2\), direct terms are \(1,2,2,8\), totaling 13; the transformed terms are \(1\cdot3^2+4\cdot1^2=13\).

title: 15 — Mixed Mathematics Capstones
text:
Original synthesis exercises

A. Reuse the model, change the observable
In Problem 1’s setting, find the number of unordered index pairs whose product residue belongs to a given set \(R\), rather than their sum of residues. Hint: change the final weight, not the convolution.






NoteSolution





Use the same exponent-pair distribution, weight exponent \(j\) by \([g^{j\bmod(p-1)}\in R]\), subtract diagonal indicators, and divide by two. If \(0\in R\), add pairs with at least one zero: for \(z\) zero inputs this is \(z(n-z)+\binom z2\). Separating zero was valid for a residue sum because its weight was zero; it is not automatically valid for a new observable.





B. A weighted root breaks the guessed degree
Change the salary count so that each assignment is weighted by the product of all salaries. What degree bound replaces subtree size? Hint: conditioning on the root salary contributes an additional factor of \(t\).






NoteSolution





The recurrence becomes \(G_v(d)=\sum_{t=1}^d t\prod_uG_u(t)\). A leaf has degree 2; inductively, multiplication, the root factor, and summation give degree at most \(2|\text{subtree}(v)|\). Use \(2n+1\) samples and require the corresponding factorial denominators to be units. Reusing the unweighted \(n+1\) samples would silently interpolate the wrong polynomial.

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
A contest problem: you may repeatedly XOR a binary string with a shifted copy of itself, and you want the smallest number of steps to reach a target. Try to attack that as a string problem and you drown in cases.
Read the string as a polynomial over \(\mathbb F_2\) — bit \(i\) is the coefficient of \(x^i\) — and the shift-XOR is multiplication by \(1 + x^{\text{shift}}\). The question becomes: what is the smallest \(L\) with \(g \mid 1 + x^L\)? And that is answered by the factor structure of \(g\): the multiplicative order of \(x\) in each irreducible factor, combined across factors. (This is exactly problem 5 below.)
That is the shift this chapter asks you to make. So far polynomials have been coefficient arrays you convolve fast. Here the useful representation is the factorization, because it turns questions about repetition, periodicity, and roots into questions about irreducible factors and their multiplicities. Three recurring signals:

repeating a linear process becomes taking powers in a polynomial quotient;
finding all roots becomes extracting linear factors;
a period or order question becomes the order of \(x\) modulo each irreducible.

Prerequisites: fields and units, polynomial arithmetic, and linear maps for Berlekamp’s method. Recall that in a field every nonzero element can be divided by — the property the whole chapter leans on.
After this chapter you should be able to explain how irreducibles create extension fields, separate multiplicity from degree, derive the Frobenius factor-degree tests, and tell certification apart from mere reconstruction.
The plan is a pipeline, and it is worth keeping the shape in mind: strip repeated factors, then group the remaining factors by degree, then split equal-degree groups, then certify. Each stage exists because the next one assumes something the previous stage guarantees.

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Euclidean algebra and quotient fields
Everything below is built from one fact: polynomials over a field support long division with remainder, so they behave like integers — gcds, Bézout, and modular arithmetic all carry over.
Fix a prime \(p\). The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues modulo \(p\). A polynomial is monic when its leading coefficient is one. A positive-degree polynomial is irreducible if it has no factorization into two positive-degree polynomials over the coefficient field. Constants are units, not irreducible factors.
For nonzero \(B\), long division gives unique \(Q,R\) with
\[A=BQ+R,\qquad R=0\text{ or }\deg R<\deg B.\]
The leading term can be cancelled because the leading coefficient of \(B\) is invertible. Repeated division produces a monic gcd and a Bezout identity \(UA+VB=\gcd(A,B)\), just as for integers.
For a monic modulus \(M\) of degree \(d\ge1\), the quotient \(\mathbb F_p[x]/(M)\) identifies polynomials whose difference is divisible by \(M\). Every residue has one representative of degree below \(d\). There are \(p^d\) representatives: each of its \(d\) coefficients has \(p\) choices.






NoteWhen is the quotient a field?



The residue of \(A\) is invertible exactly when \(\gcd(A,M)=1\). Bezout supplies an inverse; conversely, an inverse supplies a Bezout identity modulo \(M\). The quotient is therefore a field exactly when \(M\) is irreducible. If \(M=BC\) with both degrees positive, the nonzero residues \(B,C\) multiply to zero, which is impossible in a field.


Example: four elements from a quadratic. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), \(M=x^2+x+1\) has neither 0 nor 1 as a root. A reducible quadratic has a linear factor, so \(M\) is irreducible. Set \(\alpha=x\bmod M\). Then \(\alpha^2=\alpha+1\) and
\[\alpha(\alpha+1)=\alpha^2+\alpha=1.\]
The field consists of \(0,1,\alpha,\alpha+1\), and \(\alpha\) has multiplicative order three.
Failed shortcuts. Having no field roots certifies irreducibility only in degrees two and three: \((x^2+x+1)^2\) is a reducible quartic without an \(\mathbb F_2\) root. Composite coefficient moduli introduce another failure: modulo 4, the leading coefficient 2 cannot be inverted, since \(2\cdot2=0\).

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Stage 1: remove multiplicities
Why first? Because the next stage represents the quotient ring as a product of fields, and a repeated factor makes that false. Squeeze out repetition before anything else.
Write a monic input as \(f=\prod_i h_i^{e_i}\) with distinct monic irreducibles \(h_i\). It is square-free when every multiplicity \(e_i\) is one. Repeated factors prevent its quotient from being a product of fields.
The formal derivative is defined algebraically by \((x^k)'=kx^{k-1}\). For \(f=h^eu\) with \(h\nmid u\),
\[f'=e h^{e-1}h'u+h^eu'.\]
An irreducible over \(\mathbb F_p\) has nonzero derivative: otherwise it would be a \(p\)th power. If \(p\nmid e\), the exponent of \(h\) in \(\gcd(f,f')\) is exactly \(e-1\); if \(p\mid e\), that exponent is \(e\). Thus the gcd detects repetition but does not always lower each multiplicity by one.
A square-free decomposition can use the following invariant-driven procedure:

Set \(c=\gcd(f,f')\), \(w=f/c\), and \(i=1\).
While \(w\ne1\), set \(y=\gcd(w,c)\) and \(z=w/y\). Emit nonconstant \(z\) with multiplicity \(i\). Replace \(w\) by \(y\), replace \(c\) by \(c/y\), and increase \(i\).
Any remaining \(c\ne1\) is a \(p\)th power. Take its formal \(p\)th root, recurse, and multiply the returned multiplicities by \(p\).

For a factor with \(p\nmid e\), \(w\) initially contains one copy; successive iterations remove copies from \(c\) until the factor is emitted at \(i=e\). Factors whose multiplicities are divisible by \(p\) remain entirely in \(c\). This explains both the loop and the residual recursion.
Taking a \(p\)th root over \(\mathbb F_p\) divides exponents by \(p\) and leaves coefficients unchanged, since
\[\left(\sum_j a_jx^j\right)^p=\sum_j a_j^px^{jp}=\sum_j a_jx^{jp}.\]
The intermediate binomial coefficients vanish modulo \(p\). Over an extension field the coefficients also require inverse Frobenius; the stated procedure uses the prime field.
Mixed example. In \(\mathbb F_2[x]\), take \(f=x^2(x+1)^3\). Then \(f'=x^2(x+1)^2\), so initially \(c=x^2(x+1)^2\) and \(w=x+1\). The loop emits \(x+1\) at multiplicity three and leaves \(c=x^2\). Its square root returns \(x\) at multiplicity two. Handling only the top-level case \(f'=0\) would miss this residual square.

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Stage 2: Frobenius and degree decomposition
The key identity of this stage separates factors by degree using nothing but modular exponentiation and gcd — no candidate irreducibles are ever enumerated.
In characteristic \(p\), the map \(a\mapsto a^p\) preserves sums and products. It is called Frobenius. In a field of \(p^e\) elements every nonzero element satisfies \(a^{p^e-1}=1\), by the finite-group order theorem. Including zero gives \(a^{p^e}=a\).
Let \(h\) be irreducible of degree \(e\) and \(\alpha=x\bmod h\). Its Frobenius orbit has length exactly \(e\). To prove this, let the orbit length be \(t\). The polynomial
\[\prod_{j=0}^{t-1}(X-\alpha^{p^j})\]
has coefficients fixed by Frobenius. Those fixed elements are exactly \(\mathbb F_p\), since \(X^p-X\) has at most \(p\) roots and already has all \(p\) base-field elements as roots. Thus the orbit polynomial belongs to \(\mathbb F_p[X]\) and is divisible by the minimal polynomial \(h\), giving \(e\le t\). Meanwhile \(\alpha^{p^e}=\alpha\) gives \(t\le e\). Consequently \(t=e\).
Therefore \(h\) divides \(x^{p^d}-x\) exactly when \(e\mid d\). The derivative of \(x^{p^d}-x\) is \(-1\), so its factors do not repeat. We have proved
\[x^{p^d}-x=\prod_{\substack{h\text{ monic irreducible}\\\deg h\mid d}}h.\]
This turns factor degrees into gcd queries without enumerating candidate irreducibles. For square-free \(f\), maintain \(r=f\), \(H=x\bmod r\), and \(d=1\). While \(r\ne1\) and \(2d\le\deg r\):

Replace \(H\) by \(H^p\bmod r\), giving \(H\equiv x^{p^d}\pmod r\).
Compute \(b=\gcd(r,H-x)\). Emit nonconstant \(b\) as the product of degree-\(d\) factors.
Divide \(r\) by \(b\), reduce \(H\) modulo the new \(r\) if necessary, and increase \(d\).

Before iteration \(d\), all factors of \(r\) have degree at least \(d\). The gcd therefore selects degree exactly \(d\): smaller divisor degrees have already been removed. At termination any nonconstant residual is irreducible, because two remaining factors would require total degree at least \(2d\). Emit it with its own degree.
Example. For
\[f=(x+1)(x^2+x+1)(x^3+x+1)\quad\text{over }\mathbb F_2,\]
the degree-one gcd returns \(x+1\). The degree-two gcd on the residual returns \(x^2+x+1\). The remaining cubic is irreducible; checking 0 and 1 also verifies this independently.

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Stage 3: equal-degree splitting and Berlekamp
After stage 2 you hold blocks whose factors all share one degree, so no deterministic degree test can separate them further. The standard escape is randomness: pick a random element and let a gcd read off which hidden factors it “labels” the same way.
Suppose the square-free block \(b=h_1\cdots h_k\) has \(k\ge2\) factors of degree \(d\). Polynomial CRT gives
\[\mathbb F_p[x]/(b)\cong\prod_{j=1}^k\mathbb F_{p^d}.\]
A uniformly random polynomial \(a\) of degree below \(\deg b\) gives independent uniform field coordinates. First compute \(\gcd(a,b)\): a proper nontrivial gcd already splits the block. Retry if \(a=0\bmod b\). When the gcd is one, every coordinate is nonzero.
For odd \(p\), put \(q=p^d\). In a field with \(q\) elements, exactly half of the nonzero elements are squares, and \(a_j^{(q-1)/2}\) is respectively \(+1\) or \(-1\). Thus
\[g=\gcd\bigl(b,a^{(q-1)/2}-1\bigr)\]
collects factors receiving sign \(+1\). Conditional on nonzero coordinates, a useful split has probability \(1-2^{1-k}\ge1/2\). Retry when \(g=1\) or \(g=b\), otherwise recurse on the proper factors. This is Cantor–Zassenhaus: randomness labels hidden factors and gcd extracts a label class. The answer is exact; randomness affects running time.
For \(p=2\), use a fresh uniformly random residue \(a\) without conditioning it to be a unit, and use the trace
\[T(a)=a+a^2+a^{2^2}+\cdots+a^{2^{d-1}}\pmod b.\]
In each field coordinate, \(T(a)^2=T(a)\), so the result is a bit. The trace is a nonzero linear map: its defining polynomial has degree \(2^{d-1}<2^d\) and cannot vanish on the whole field. Its two values are therefore equally frequent. The gcd \(\gcd(b,T(a))\) selects trace-zero factors with the same split probability. Evaluate by repeated squaring and addition.
Berlekamp’s alternative. On representatives of degree below \(n=\deg b\), Frobenius is an \(\mathbb F_p\)-linear map \(Q\). In the CRT coordinates, the kernel of \(Q-I\) consists of arbitrary base-field constants on each factor. Its dimension is the number of factors. Find a kernel basis with your linear-algebra library. For basis vectors \(v\) and \(c\in\mathbb F_p\), gcds with \(v-c\) separate the factors: if two coordinates agreed on every basis vector they would agree on the whole kernel, contrary to the availability of independent coordinate labels. Enumerating \(p\) constants is useful for small fields; it is not independent of \(p\).

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Stage 4: roots and certification
The distinct linear factors of nonzero \(f\) form \(\gcd(f,x^p-x)\). Split this square-free product and read roots from \(x-a\). Recover their multiplicities from the earlier decomposition.
Reconstruction alone does not certify a complete factorization: returning the input itself passes that check. Also certify that every returned factor is irreducible. A monic degree-\(d\) polynomial \(h\) is irreducible exactly when
\[x^{p^d}\equiv x\pmod h,\qquad
\gcd\bigl(h,x^{p^{d/\ell}}-x\bigr)=1
\quad\text{for every prime }\ell\mid d.\]
The first condition makes \(h\) square-free with factor degrees dividing \(d\). Any proper divisor degree \(e\) divides \(d/\ell\) for some prime \(\ell\mid d/e\), contradicting a gcd condition. For degree one the gcd list is empty. Check these tests, multiply the factors with multiplicities, and restore the input’s leading scalar.

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Contest contract and complexity
The input is a nonzero polynomial over a specified prime field. Normalize its leading coefficient. Nonzero constants have an empty factor list; zero has no finite factorization of this form.
Let \(M(n)\) bound multiplication and reduction modulo a degree-\(n\) polynomial, and \(G(n)\) bound gcd. Binary modular exponentiation to exponent \(E\) costs \(O(M(n)\log E)\). The distinct-degree procedure uses at most \(n\) Frobenius steps and gcds, hence costs
\[O\bigl(n(M(n)\log p+G(n))\bigr).\]
With quadratic multiplication and Euclid this is \(O(n^3\log p)\) field operations. This is a conservative baseline, not the fastest known factorization bound. At block degree \(m\), an odd-field splitting trial costs \(O(M(m)d\log p+G(m))\); a binary trace costs \(O(dM(m)+G(m))\). Proper splits terminate the recursion. Including zero-coordinate splitting, each trial has a constant success probability, so the expected retries are bounded. Berlekamp additionally requires a dense kernel computation, cubic in block degree, and the subsequent splitting gcds.
Keep polynomials trimmed and gcds monic. Compare small-degree results with trial division by every monic candidate of degree at most half the input degree. Distinguish a splitter retry from an input that violates the field contract.

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Problem-solving checklist

Is the coefficient domain a field? Is the input zero or constant?
Do you need roots, factor degrees, irreducibles, or multiplicities?
Have you separated repetition before using polynomial CRT?
Does the Frobenius residue use the current modulus?
Does verification check irreducibility as well as reconstruction?

title: 17 — Finite-Field Polynomial Algebra
text:
Exercises with hints and solutions

Inverse. Invert \(x+1\) modulo \(x^2+x+1\) over \(\mathbb F_2\).
Hint: multiply by \(x\). Solution: \((x+1)x=x^2+x\equiv1\), so the inverse is \(x\).
Multiplicity. Recover the factor multiplicity in \((x+1)^6\) over \(\mathbb F_3\).
Hint: its derivative is zero. Solution: take the formal cube root \((x+1)^2\). Its square-free decomposition returns multiplicity two; scaling by three recovers six.
Certificate. Which Frobenius gcd tests suffice for a degree-six candidate?
Hint: list proper divisors of six. Solution: after the \(p^6\) identity, possible factor degrees are \(1,2,3,6\). Gcd tests at \(p^3\) and \(p^2\) exclude 1,2,3. Only degree six remains.
Order with repetition. Find the least positive \(L\) such that \((x+1)^3\mid x^L+1\) over \(\mathbb F_2\).
Hint: write \(L=2^tu\), \(u\) odd. Solution: \(x^L+1=(x^u+1)^{2^t}\). The derivative of \(x^u+1\) is nonzero at 1, so its root there is simple. The multiplicity is exactly \(2^t\), giving least \(L=4\). Ignoring repetition incorrectly gives one.
Contest application — Long Binary String, CF1698G. The official input length is at most 35; no enlarged constraint is assumed.
Editorial guidance: remove the initial power of \(x\) from the input polynomial to obtain \(g\) with constant term one. A two-bit target requires \(g\mid1+x^L\). For each distinct irreducible \(h\), find the order of \(x\) modulo \(h\), which divides \(2^{\deg h}-1\). Take the lcm of these odd orders, then multiply by the smallest power of two at least the largest factor multiplicity. The initial zero prefix fixes the earliest possible first bit; the minimum gap maximizes the string lexicographically. Treat the zero input separately and prove that the multiplier fits the finite allowed string. Chapter 20 develops a small complete instance.

title: 19 — Holonomic Methods: D-Finite Series and P-Recursive Sequences
text:
“Compute the \(10^{12}\)-th term” normally means: find a linear recurrence with constant coefficients and exponentiate its matrix. Now try it for the number of involutions on \(n\) labels (permutations that are their own inverse). The recurrence is a two-liner — the last label is fixed, or paired with one of the other \(n-1\) labels:
\[I_n = I_{n-1} + (n-1)I_{n-2}.\]
The transition matrix is no longer constant; it depends on \(n\). Matrix powering is simply the wrong tool, and pretending otherwise gives a confidently wrong answer.
Sequences like this — factorials, central binomials, involutions, almost every labelled-structure count — satisfy recurrences whose coefficients are polynomials in the index. They are called P-recursive, their generating functions satisfy linear differential equations, and they come with their own toolkit:

the recurrence and the differential equation are two views of the same object, and each is easy to get from the other;
the class is closed under sums, products, and many substitutions, so you can build complicated sequences from simple ones and still have a recurrence;
a distant term costs \(\widetilde O(\sqrt N)\) rather than \(O(N)\), by grouping consecutive index-dependent transitions into one polynomial matrix.

One hazard runs through all of it. A polynomial leading coefficient can vanish, either at a genuine index or only after reducing modulo a prime, and at that index the recurrence determines nothing. Watching denominators is not pedantry here; it is the main way these methods break.
Prerequisites: polynomials, formal differentiation, generating functions, and linear recurrences and systems. Work over a characteristic-zero field such as \(\mathbb Q\) when deriving the theory. Reduction modulo a prime comes after checking every denominator.
The objectives are to translate a differential equation into a recurrence with correct boundaries, prove a guessed recurrence, use closure properties with their hypotheses, and evaluate a distant term without pretending an index-dependent matrix is constant.
